findings.title: Disabling the listener removes protection for an existing TLS key
findings.detail: The request says the TLS key is read-denied in every agent sandbox. When the listener is disabled, startup returns before registering the previously generated key with the process-local deny registry. The key remains on disk, and editor sandboxes do not otherwise deny the worker TLS directory.
findings.suggestion: Register the existing key path for the daemon lifetime independently of whether the listener is enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables workers after having enabled them, then starts a run. An editor agent can read the retained coordinator TLS private key.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:30 calls `startWorkerListener(..., factory.cfg.workers.listen)` before integrations start. No persistent registry survives restart: src/util/private-reads.ts:4 uses `new Map<string, number>()`.
verification.trigger: Disable workers after creating their TLS material, restart, then start an editor agent. Where generic sandbox restrictions permit reading the data directory, the editor can read the retained private key. Duplicate of C6.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
findings.detail: The key file is created before openssl runs, but a failed or interrupted generation leaves it behind. The next start sees incomplete TLS material and throws instead of generating a certificate, so a transient failure prevents the daemon from starting whenever the worker listener is configured.
findings.suggestion: Generate the certificate and key in temporary files and publish them together, cleaning up incomplete generation safely.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped or openssl fails after the empty key file is created but before the certificate is written; every subsequent daemon start fails with "Incomplete worker TLS material".

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:17 rejects partial material with `throw new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material")`; line 18 creates key.pem before OpenSSL runs at lines 19–39. Its catch only performs `release(); throw error;` at lines 46–47. src/cli/daemon.ts:30 awaits the listener, and lines 44–46 propagate startup errors.

findings.title: A changed pinned certificate is retried indefinitely without an explanation
findings.detail: The request requires the coordinator fingerprint to be pinned. Although the transport detects a mismatch, the heartbeat loop catches that error along with transient connection failures and retries forever. The operator receives no indication that the certificate changed and that intervention is required.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the initial TLS connection
candidates.detail: The initial connection accepts any certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that connection. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request to the real coordinator, return its code and secret to the worker, and present its own certificate. The owner sees the same code on both sides and approves it; the attacker then observes the claim and issued token. Pinning the attacker's certificate on subsequent requests does not prevent this. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is never authenticated or used to bind the exchange.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to both endpoints' certificate fingerprints and the pairing exchange, so relaying through a different TLS certificate changes the code or causes verification to fail.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies the real coordinator's pairing response, and forwards the approved claim while terminating both TLS connections.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
candidates.detail: Private read protection is an in-memory registry. Pairing releases the token and fingerprint registrations on return, and `runWorker` registers them only in the worker CLI process. A daemon running gates or agents in a separate process therefore does not include those files in its sandbox deny paths. The coordinator TLS key has the same lifetime problem when its listener is disabled after the key has been created. Mode 0600 does not protect files from another process running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the configured worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that constructs agent or gate sandboxes, independent of whether a worker or listener is currently running.
candidates.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, then run a factory daemon and a gate on the same machine; the daemon's sandbox is built without the worker token path registered, allowing a gate with access to that path to read the token.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate creation permanently blocks restart
candidates.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before invoking OpenSSL. If generation fails, times out, or the process stops before both files are complete, the next start either rejects the incomplete pair or tries to parse invalid material. No cleanup or recovery occurs, so the worker listener or pairing command continues to fail on every subsequent start.
candidates.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names, validate them, and publish them only after successful generation; clean up incomplete temporary material on failure.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped after creating the empty key file but before OpenSSL creates the certificate; every later listener start throws `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
candidates.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. The displayed code comes from the coordinator but is not bound to that certificate or to an authenticated exchange. An intermediary can relay the pairing request and code unchanged, obtain the pairing secret and issued token, and leave the worker pinned to the intermediary's certificate even though the owner compared matching codes.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange so a relaying intermediary cannot obtain a usable token or substitute its certificate.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, forwards the request to the real coordinator, and relays its code. The owner approves the matching code; the attacker claims the token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

candidates.title: Permanent TLS and configuration errors are retried silently forever
candidates.detail: The heartbeat loop catches every request exception and retries without a deadline or diagnostic. This includes a changed coordinator fingerprint and malformed coordinator URL, neither of which can be repaired by retrying. The worker remains running but never sends another heartbeat, and the owner receives no explanation.
candidates.suggestion: Retry only transient transport failures with a bounded policy; propagate permanent validation and certificate-pin failures with their original reason.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing. Every heartbeat fails fingerprint validation, but the worker silently retries indefinitely instead of reporting that it must be paired again.

candidates.title: Existing TLS key loses sandbox protection when the listener is disabled
candidates.detail: The TLS key is registered with the sandbox deny list only when the listener starts. After a listener has created the key, restarting the daemon with workers.listen unset skips registration even though the key remains on disk. Agent sandboxes that can read that data directory can then read the coordinator's private key, contrary to the requirement that it be denied in every agent sandbox.
candidates.suggestion: Register protection for existing worker TLS material independently of whether the listener is enabled, and retain it for the daemon lifetime.
candidates.failure_scenario: Enable the listener once, then disable it and restart the daemon with the data directory outside the default home deny paths. A subsequent agent can read worker-tls/key.pem.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
candidates.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before running openssl, but its error path leaves partial files behind. A timeout, failed openssl invocation, or interruption can therefore leave only the empty key or other incomplete material. Every later start rejects the incomplete material, requiring manual cleanup.
candidates.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths and publish them only after successful generation, cleaning up partial temporary files on failure.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before openssl writes cert.pem. Subsequent starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Credential read protection ends with the pairing process
candidates.detail: The worker token and coordinator fingerprint are registered in an in-memory deny list only while `pairWorker` or `runWorker` holds them. Pairing releases both registrations before exiting, and a separately running daemon has its own deny list. Likewise, an existing coordinator TLS key is not registered when the listener is disabled. An agent sandbox created by that daemon therefore does not receive these paths as private-file denies.
candidates.suggestion: Register persisted worker credential and TLS-key paths in every process that constructs agent sandbox policies, independently of whether pairing, the worker loop or the listener is currently running.
candidates.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, exit the pairing command, and run an agent through a separate daemon using the same data directory: that daemon's private-file deny list does not contain the stored worker token or coordinator fingerprint.

candidates.title: Privacy probe masks the cross-process credential protection gap
candidates.detail: The real-Seatbelt test creates the TLS material and registers both worker files in the same process that starts the gate, retaining all registrations throughout the probe. It consequently passes even if a daemon started separately after pairing has no credential paths in its in-memory deny list.
candidates.suggestion: Add a real-Seatbelt probe that persists credentials, releases the pairing registrations, and launches the gate from an independently initialized daemon or process; cover an existing TLS key with the listener disabled as well.
candidates.failure_scenario: The current implementation releases the registrations after pairing, yet this test retains them and reports all three files denied.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
candidates.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that untrusted connection. An active intermediary can forward the request to the real coordinator, relay its code to the worker, and retain the returned pairing secret. The owner and worker see matching codes, but the intermediary can claim the approved token and the worker pins the intermediary's certificate.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the human-compared code to both the coordinator certificate fingerprint and the pairing exchange, so relaying a coordinator response through a different TLS certificate changes the code.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies `/worker/pair` to the coordinator, and relays the real code. After the owner approves it, the attacker claims the worker token.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
candidates.detail: `protectPrivateFile` maintains an in-memory registry. Pairing releases its registrations before exiting, and `runWorker` registers the files only in the worker process. A separately running daemon on the same machine does not receive those registrations when it constructs Claude or Codex sandbox policies, so its agents can read the persistent worker token and coordinator fingerprint. Mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that launches agents, including when the worker is stopped, and cover separate-process sandbox behavior.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a worker and a factory daemon under the same user. An agent launched by the daemon reads `<data>/worker/token` and impersonates that worker.

candidates.title: Disabling the listener leaves its existing TLS key unprotected from agents
candidates.detail: The TLS key is added to the process-local private-read registry only when the listener is enabled. After an owner removes `workers.listen` and restarts the daemon, the existing key remains on disk but is no longer included in agent sandbox deny paths. An agent running as the same user can read it, compromising the certificate trusted by already paired workers if the listener is later re-enabled.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent TLS key path independently of whether the listener is currently enabled, or securely remove and rotate the material when disabling it.
candidates.failure_scenario: A coordinator previously enabled workers, then starts with the listener disabled. A tool-enabled agent reads `<data>/worker-tls/key.pem` before the listener is enabled again.

candidates.title: Store untrusted heartbeat fields only after redaction
candidates.detail: Heartbeat capabilities are serialized directly into SQLite. Several worker-controlled strings can contain coordinator credentials or private strings, but sanitization occurs only when listing workers. This leaves the unredacted values in persistent storage even though the trust-boundary rules require redaction before storage.
candidates.suggestion: Redact and apply private-string policy to worker-supplied capability fields before persisting them, while preserving the fields needed for version matching.
candidates.failure_scenario: A paired worker sends a coordinator credential or private string in `osVersion`; the value is written verbatim to the workers table.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied in the daemon's agent sandboxes
candidates.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. The deny registry is process-local, but pairing and the worker loop run as separate CLI processes from the daemon. Their registrations are also released when those commands exit. A daemon on the same machine therefore does not add these files to its agent sandbox deny lists; mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that can launch agents and gates, including when the worker command is not running.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator. An agent launched by its daemon reads the token under the worker data directory and uses it to impersonate the worker.

candidates.title: Disabling the listener removes protection for an existing TLS key
candidates.detail: The request says the TLS key is read-denied in every agent sandbox. When the listener is disabled, startup returns before registering the previously generated key with the process-local deny registry. The key remains on disk, and editor sandboxes do not otherwise deny the worker TLS directory.
candidates.suggestion: Register the existing key path for the daemon lifetime independently of whether the listener is enabled.
candidates.failure_scenario: An owner disables workers after having enabled them, then starts a run. An editor agent can read the retained coordinator TLS private key.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
candidates.detail: The key file is created before openssl runs, but a failed or interrupted generation leaves it behind. The next start sees incomplete TLS material and throws instead of generating a certificate, so a transient failure prevents the daemon from starting whenever the worker listener is configured.
candidates.suggestion: Generate the certificate and key in temporary files and publish them together, cleaning up incomplete generation safely.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped or openssl fails after the empty key file is created but before the certificate is written; every subsequent daemon start fails with "Incomplete worker TLS material".

candidates.title: A changed pinned certificate is retried indefinitely without an explanation
candidates.detail: The request requires the coordinator fingerprint to be pinned. The operator receives no indication that the certificate changed and that intervention is required.

findings.title: Credential read protection ends when pairing exits
findings.detail: The private-file deny registry is process-local, and pairing releases both credential paths before exiting. A separate daemon on the worker machine therefore does not register those files in its agent sandbox deny rules; running the worker in another process does not share its registrations either. The same lifecycle problem affects an existing coordinator TLS key when its listener is disabled.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of whether the worker listener or client is running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is paired, the pairing command exits, and an agent launched by a separate local daemon reads the worker token from the data directory.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47–48 saves the fingerprint and token through `privateFile`, then :55–57 executes `cert.release()` and `for (const release of held) release()`. src/util/private-reads.ts:21 removes released paths with `privatePaths.delete(p)`; :4 makes the registry process-local.
verification.trigger: Pairing completes and exits, leaving credential files on disk without persistent sandbox registration. A separate daemon's editor can read the token because its deny policy does not include that path.

findings.title: Permanent TLS and configuration failures retry forever
findings.detail: The catch treats every request error as transient and retries indefinitely without logging the original error. A changed certificate fingerprint, malformed coordinator URL, or invalid stored pin therefore leaves the worker silently looping instead of reporting the failure and requiring corrective action.
findings.suggestion: Retry only transient transport errors with an appropriate bound, and propagate certificate, pin and configuration errors with their original cause.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing; every heartbeat fails fingerprint verification, but the worker remains running indefinitely with no diagnostic.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:114–115 rejects a changed pin with `new Error("Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed")`. src/workers/client.ts:99–102 catches every request exception and returns `undefined`; :93 loops `for (;;)`, and :106–107 sleeps and caps only the delay at 10 seconds.
verification.trigger: The coordinator certificate changes, or the coordinator URL is permanently invalid. Every heartbeat exception is silently discarded and retried indefinitely, leaving the worker running without heartbeats or an actionable error.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the key path before invoking OpenSSL, but failures leave generated or partial files in place. The next start either rejects the incomplete pair or reads invalid material, so a transient interruption permanently blocks the worker listener until the files are manually removed.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths, clean them up on failure, and publish the completed pair only after validation.
findings.failure_scenario: OpenSSL times out or the process stops after creating key.pem but before writing cert.pem; subsequent daemon starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18–19 writes key.pem before `await sh(...)`, whose timeout is 30 seconds (:38). The catch (:45–47) performs no file cleanup. The next invocation reaches :17: `if (existsSync(keyPath) || existsSync(certPath)) throw new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material");`. src/cli/daemon.ts:30 awaits listener startup and :44–46 propagates its failure.
verification.trigger: OpenSSL fails, times out, or is interrupted before creating cert.pem, leaving key.pem behind. With the listener configured, subsequent daemon starts repeatedly fail. This is the same defect as C3.

findings.title: Worker credentials lose sandbox protection when pairing exits
findings.detail: Protection is held in a process-local registry and released when pairing finishes. A separate daemon or agent process does not inherit that registration, even though the token and coordinator fingerprint remain on disk. The real-Seatbelt test explicitly registers synthetic files in the same process that launches the gates, so it does not exercise this lifecycle or cross-process case.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that constructs an agent sandbox, and test access from a separately started process after pairing has finished.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine pairs a worker, the pairing command exits, and a separate local factory process launches an agent sandbox that can otherwise reach the worker data directory; the persisted token and fingerprint are absent from that process's private-read registry.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47-48 persists credentials using `privateFile(...)`; lines 55-57 then execute `for (const release of held) release()`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 defines the process-local `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()`, and line 21 removes released entries with `privatePaths.delete(p)`.
verification.trigger: Pairing completes and exits. A separate factory process receives no deny registrations for the persisted worker credentials; an agent whose readable paths include that directory can read the token despite its 0600 mode, since it runs as the same user.

findings.title: No test covers claiming an approved pairing after coordinator restart
findings.detail: The implementation reconstructs an issued token from the persistent TLS key so that a worker can claim it after a restart, but the pairing tests approve and claim within one listener lifetime. A regression in key reuse or token reconstruction would leave an approved worker unable to pair without being caught.
findings.suggestion: Approve a pending request, restart the listener and store, then claim with the original secret and verify that the returned token authenticates a heartbeat.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator restarts after the owner approves a pending request but before the worker claims its token.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:67–68 immediately calls `workers.approve(pending.code)` followed by `call("/worker/pair/claim", { secret: pending.secret })`; the approval test repeats this at lines 84–85. The listener restart test at test/workers.test.ts:123–126 only checks `expect((await listen()).tls.fingerprint).toBe(fingerprint)`, without an approved pairing or token claim.
verification.trigger: Coordinator restarts after approval but before token claim: no test exercises token reconstruction and authentication across that restart. This confirms a coverage gap, not a demonstrated runtime failure.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator certificate
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the coordinator generates a random code that is unrelated to either endpoint's certificate. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request and response unchanged, present its own certificate to the worker, and relay the subsequent claim. The owner and worker see the same code, but the worker pins the attacker's certificate and sends it the issued token.
findings.suggestion: Bind the displayed pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange, and verify that binding on both sides before issuing or accepting credentials.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies requests to the real coordinator, and forwards the unchanged pairing code. After approval, the attacker receives the worker token while the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-28 makes the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; lines 33 and 39 print the returned code and pin `first.fingerprint`. src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`, and lines 114-115 check the certificate only when `options.pin !== undefined`. src/db/workers.ts:89 returns `{ token: this.issued(w) }` to whoever holds the approved pairing secret.
verification.trigger: An active interceptor terminates the initial TLS connection and relays pairing and claim requests to the real coordinator. The unchanged code passes owner comparison, while the interceptor obtains the token and the worker pins the interceptor's certificate.

findings.title: Worker credential deny registrations do not protect other processes
findings.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory, process-local deny list, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A separately running daemon or agent process therefore never registers the worker credential paths. Its agent sandbox can consequently lack the explicit denies required for these files, even while the worker is running in another process.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of the worker process and pairing command.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator with a tool-enabled agent. The worker runs as a separate process, so the coordinator's agent sandbox does not receive the worker token and fingerprint deny entries.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:87-88 registers the token and fingerprint through `privateFile(...)` only inside `runWorker`. src/workers/tls.ts:52 implements this using `protectPrivateFile(path)`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4,30 stores and exposes registrations through the module-local `privatePaths` map. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 builds sandbox denials from `...privateReadPaths()`.
verification.trigger: Worker and coordinator run in separate processes on the same machine. The coordinator's registry lacks the worker credential paths, allowing its tool-enabled agent to read them whenever the directory is otherwise accessible.

findings.title: Pairing can be relayed through an attacker-controlled coordinator
findings.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins that certificate after receiving the pairing response. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the pair request and the unchanged code to the real coordinator, then relay the claim request after owner approval. The codes match, but the attacker obtains the issued token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is stored but is never authenticated or used to bind the claim.
findings.suggestion: Bind approval and token delivery to authenticated coordinator and worker identities so that relaying a matching code cannot disclose the worker token or substitute the pinned coordinator.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pairs over a network controlled by an attacker who proxies both pairing endpoints to the real coordinator; the owner sees the same code and approves, after which the proxy receives the worker token.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:103 accepts the initial certificate with `rejectUnauthorized: false`; lines 114-115 enforce only an already supplied pin. src/workers/client.ts:27 supplies no initial pin and line 39 trusts `first.fingerprint`. src/db/workers.ts:61 returns `{ code, secret, expiresAt: ... }`, and lines 83-89 issue the approved token based solely on that secret.
verification.trigger: An attacker-controlled TLS proxy forwards both pairing endpoints and preserves the displayed code. Owner approval authorizes the real pending request, but the proxy knows its secret and receives the issued worker token.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not registered for denial in the daemon's sandboxes
findings.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. Their protection is held only in the pairing or worker CLI process's in-memory private-path registry and is released when that process exits. A separate daemon on the same machine does not register these paths when it starts, so its sandbox policy can permit access to them. The real-Seatbelt test creates and protects all files in the same process as the gate, so it does not cover this deployment.
findings.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that launches agent or gate sandboxes, independently of whether the worker CLI is running, and test across the actual process boundary.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a worker and a coordinator, with its data directory in a location readable by an agent sandbox; after pairing, a gate launched by the separate daemon reads the worker token and fingerprint.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47-48 registers the persisted credential paths, then lines 55-57 release those registrations. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 keeps registrations in a process-local map. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 derives deny paths from that process's `privateReadPaths()`; src/server/workers.ts:16 initializes only the coordinator's `worker-tls` certificate.
verification.trigger: After pairing, a separate daemon launches a gate whose allowed read paths include the worker data directory. The daemon never registered the worker token or fingerprint, so the gate can read those same-user files.

findings.title: The coordinator TLS key is unprotected when the listener is disabled
findings.detail: The request says the TLS key must be read-denied in every agent sandbox. The key path is registered only when the worker listener starts. After a listener has generated the key, disabling `[workers] listen` and restarting leaves the private key on disk without registering it in the daemon's sandbox deny policy. Re-enabling the listener later reuses that key.
findings.suggestion: Register the existing coordinator key path for sandbox denial independently of whether the listener is enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables the listener after pairing workers, then runs an agent with read access to the data directory; the agent reads the persisted key and can impersonate the coordinator when the listener is re-enabled.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15–16 returns before registering protection when disabled: `if (!listen) return undefined; const tls = await certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"));`. Protection is registered only inside `certificate`: src/workers/tls.ts:12–14, `const keyPath = join(home, "key.pem") ... const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. Existing keys persist and are reused (src/workers/tls.ts:16,41–43). Agent deny paths incorporate registered files: src/harness/read-policy.ts:190, `const denyRead = policySpellings([...credentials, ...privateReadPaths()], true, fs);`.
verification.trigger: After generating TLS material, disable workers.listen and restart the daemon. The persisted key receives no private-file deny registration. An agent with read access to that data directory can read the same-user 0600 key, compromising the coordinator identity trusted by paired workers.

findings.title: An approved pairing that fails before token storage cannot be retried
findings.detail: An approved name is always rejected by `pair`, even if the worker never received or saved its token. A transient failure after approval therefore leaves the worker unable to pair again until the owner explicitly revokes it.
findings.suggestion: Provide a safe recovery path for an approved but unclaimed pairing, or report the required revoke-and-repair action clearly.
findings.failure_scenario: The owner approves a request, but the worker process exits before its next claim; restarting `limitless worker pair` with the same name receives a refusal.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:78-80 persists `state='approved'` during approval. src/workers/client.ts:30-38 holds the pairing secret only in the local `pending` variable; credentials are written only after a successful claim at lines 45-48. A restarted invocation calls `/worker/pair` again (lines 23-29), but src/db/workers.ts:43-46 rejects all existing approved names, regardless of expiry.
verification.trigger: After owner approval, the worker exits before claiming or storing its token. Restarting pairing with the same name is refused, and the lost in-memory secret prevents resuming the claim. Owner revocation is required before pairing again.

verdicts.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates key.pem before awaiting OpenSSL: `writeFileSync(keyPath, "", { flag: "wx", mode: 0o600 });`. verdicts.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18–19 writes key.pem before `await sh(...)`, whose timeout is 30 seconds (:38). The catch (:45–47) performs no file cleanup. verdicts.evidence: docs/GUIDE.md:236 says, "Changing the coordinator's certificate requires pairing again." findings.title: Treat a worker confinement failure as a terminal failure
findings.detail: A check reporting a confinement failure is rejected as an invalid result, which calls workers.fail. After the retry is exhausted, the LAN executor runs the gates locally and can return a pass. This converts a failed security check into a successful gate result.
findings.suggestion: Preserve confinement failures as a distinct terminal failure and propagate them through the gate result without retrying them into a pass.
findings.failure_scenario: Both worker attempts report a Seatbelt launch failure, but the local fallback executes successfully; the overall gate is reported as passing.

verification.evidence: src/workers/protocol.ts:65 rejects confinement failures: `.refine((r) => !r.confinementError && !launchFailure(r.output), "Worker confinement failed")`. src/server/workers.ts:131-133 handles that rejection with `workers.fail(id, ...)`. src/db/workers.ts:260 transitions using `j.attempt < 2 ? "queued" : "failed"`. src/gates/lan.ts:73-89 then runs the local executor and returns its result: `workers.complete(handle.id, run, true); return workers.sanitize(run);`.
verification.trigger: Both worker attempts report confinement failures. They become infrastructure failures, and a successful local fallback replaces them with a passing GateRun instead of preserving a terminal confinement failure.

findings.title: Do not discard failed checks received before an infrastructure failure
findings.detail: Check events from a worker are persisted and forwarded, but the final result is replaced by the next attempt or local fallback if that worker disconnects before posting its GateRun. A later pass therefore erases an already observed failing check, contrary to the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve and account for validated failing check results across attempts when producing the final gate outcome.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a failing test check and loses its connection before posting the final result; the retry or local fallback passes, so the run receives a passing GateRun.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:68–72 collects stored events separately, then returns only the final result: `events.push(...stored.slice(index))` and `if (job.state === "done" && job.result) return JSON.parse(job.result) as GateRun`. The local fallback likewise returns its own run at src/gates/lan.ts:86–89: `workers.complete(handle.id, run, true); return workers.sanitize(run);`. src/gates/executor.ts:211–215 sends check events to hooks but returns `execution.result` without reconciling prior failures.
verification.trigger: A worker posts a failing check, then disconnects before submitting its GateRun. Infrastructure recovery retries elsewhere or locally; if that execution passes, the returned GateRun passes without retaining the earlier failure.

findings.title: Do not retry certificate pin failures indefinitely
findings.detail: The catch treats every workerRequest exception as a transient connection error. That includes an invalid coordinator URL or a changed pinned TLS fingerprint, so the worker silently retries forever instead of surfacing the security or configuration failure. The retry has no deadline.
findings.suggestion: Classify request errors and propagate certificate validation and configuration failures; bound retries for transient transport errors.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator presents a certificate whose fingerprint differs from the stored pin. The worker stays running and retries indefinitely without reporting the fingerprint mismatch.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:114-115 rejects a mismatched pin with `new Error("Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed")`. src/workers/client.ts:146-148 catches every request rejection and returns `undefined`; :139 loops `for (;;)`, while :157-158 sleeps and caps the retry delay at 10 seconds.
verification.trigger: A coordinator presents a certificate differing from the stored pin. The worker silently retries until externally aborted, discarding the fingerprint mismatch error.

findings.title: The credential test does not establish worker-side redaction
findings.detail: The worker and coordinator run in the same process and share the credential registry. The test registers the secret globally and checks only the stored coordinator result and events, so coordinator-side sanitization can make it pass even if the worker sends the credential in plaintext.
findings.suggestion: Inspect the outgoing worker event and result bodies before coordinator processing, or run the worker in a separate process with a credential unknown to the coordinator.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker-side redaction is removed and a gate prints a worker-only credential; the shared coordinator registry still redacts the stored output, so this test passes while the credential crosses the connection.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:659 registers `registerCredential("WORKER_OUTPUT_TEST", secret)`. The helper calls `runWorker(...)` in the same process (test/workers.test.ts:459), sharing the module-level `credentialValues` registry (src/util/proc.ts:667). Assertions inspect only stored data: `expect(jobs[0]?.result).not.toContain(secret)` and the equivalent events assertion (test/workers.test.ts:681-682). Coordinator storage independently sanitizes both: `events.push(this.sanitize(event))` (src/db/workers.ts:238) and `JSON.stringify(this.sanitize(run))` (src/db/workers.ts:291).
verification.trigger: Worker-side redaction regresses and raw credential output crosses the connection; the shared coordinator registry sanitizes it before storage, so the test's assertions still pass. This establishes a test gap, not a current credential leak.

findings.title: The bundle test never exercises distinct head and base commits
findings.detail: The shared request fixture assigns the same commit to headSha and baseSha. Consequently, the end-to-end bundle test cannot detect an implementation that bundles only the head, even though the request requires both commits to be available on the worker.
findings.suggestion: Create distinct base and head commits and have a worker gate verify that both requested commits are present.
findings.failure_scenario: Bundle creation omits baseSha when it differs from headSha; the existing end-to-end test still passes because its two SHAs are identical.

verification.evidence: The bundle fixture assigns `baseSha: sha` and `headSha: sha` (test/workers.test.ts:123-124), and the end-to-end test uses `const req = await request(true)` (test/workers.test.ts:657). Production currently includes both via `const refs = [...new Set([request.headSha, request.baseSha].filter(Boolean))]` (src/server/workers.ts:88), but identical fixture SHAs exercise only one ref.
verification.trigger: Bundle creation regresses to including only headSha; the existing end-to-end test still passes because baseSha equals headSha, leaving distinct-base bundle coverage missing.

findings.title: Reconcile streamed check failures with the final result
findings.detail: The coordinator validates each check event and the final GateRun independently. It accepts a passing final result even if the same lease previously reported that check as failed. The failed event is stored, but it does not influence the returned GateRun, so an inconsistent worker response can turn an observed failure into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Validate the final run against the check events recorded for the current lease and treat inconsistent results as an infrastructure failure.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a valid failed event for a requested check, then posts a valid GateRun reporting that same check as passed; the coordinator completes the job with the passing result.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:135-136 stores events independently from completion: `if (action === "events" && event.success) workers.event(id, event.data); else if (result.success) workers.complete(id, result.data.run);`. src/workers/validation.ts:25-48 validates the final run against requested checks without consulting stored events. src/db/workers.ts:290-291 writes that final run directly with `UPDATE gate_jobs SET state='done',result=?...`.
verification.trigger: A leased worker submits a schema-valid failed check event, then a schema-valid passing final result for the same requested check and SHA. The coordinator accepts the contradictory passing result and completes the job.

findings.title: Coordinator-only credentials can be truncated before redaction
findings.detail: runLocalGates truncates output on the worker after redacting only credentials registered on that worker. The coordinator subsequently redacts the already-truncated value using its own credentials. If the tail boundary cuts through a coordinator credential that the worker does not know, the coordinator sees only a fragment and literal credential redaction cannot remove it before the event or result is stored.
findings.suggestion: Ensure coordinator-only credentials cannot be cut before coordinator-side redaction, such as by sending bounded raw output with enough overlap for coordinator redaction before applying the final output limit.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate prints a coordinator credential unknown to the worker, followed by enough output that the 6,000-character tail starts in the middle of that credential. The credential suffix is sent to and stored by the coordinator.

verification.evidence: src/gates/run.ts:126 stores `combined.slice(-OUTPUT_TAIL)`, with `OUTPUT_TAIL = 6_000` at :74. src/workers/client.ts:233 sends `redactGateData({ run, sha })`. Coordinator redaction in src/util/proc.ts:684 uses `text.split(secret).join("[redacted]")`; src/util/private-output.ts:23 invokes `privacy(field)` without truncation information. src/db/workers.ts:291 persists `JSON.stringify(this.sanitize(run))`. A suffix alone matches neither full-secret filter.
verification.trigger: A gate prints a coordinator-only credential followed by output placing the tail boundary inside that credential. Worker redaction does not know it; coordinator redaction receives only its suffix and stores it unredacted.

findings.title: A failed check from a lost lease can become a pass
findings.detail: The request says infrastructure retries must “never turn a failing check into a pass.” Check events from an attempt are streamed to hooks, but after that attempt loses its lease the final verdict uses only the later worker's GateRun. A failed check already reported by the first worker is therefore discarded for verdict purposes.
findings.suggestion: Retain completed check failures across infrastructure attempts and ensure a later passing result cannot erase them.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a failing check event, disconnects before posting its GateRun, and the replacement worker reports that check as passing. The returned GateRun marks it as passing.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:275–277 calls `this.fail(j.id, "Worker disconnected")` or `this.fail(j.id, "Lease expired")`; src/db/workers.ts:260 requeues eligible attempts with `j.attempt < 2 ? "queued" : "failed"`. A replacement result is stored independently at src/db/workers.ts:290–291: `UPDATE gate_jobs SET state='done',result=?,updated_at=? WHERE id=? AND state=?`. src/gates/lan.ts:72 returns that result directly: `return JSON.parse(job.result) as GateRun`, without merging failed check events.
verification.trigger: A leased worker reports a failed check and loses its lease before submitting the final result. A replacement worker reports the check as passing, and the returned GateRun marks it passing despite the recorded failure.

findings.title: Restart discards leased retry and timeout jobs
findings.detail: The request says `attach` waits for the stored result so “a coordinator restart re-attaches without enqueueing again.” Resume is restricted to baseline, initial and rebase purposes. A persisted timeout or retry job is cancelled and replaced when its stage resumes, even if the worker is still running or has completed it.
findings.suggestion: Provide durable resume handling for every LAN gate execution purpose, preserving the original job identity and any state needed to consume its result.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a LAN timeout rerun or regression retry is leased. On resume the pending handle fails the purpose whitelist, is cancelled, and a new job is enqueued.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29-37 requires matching purpose plus `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`; otherwise it calls `await cancelGateExecution(pending.handle, ctx.deps.gateExecutor)`. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1215 restarts the gates stage with purpose `"initial"`, while :1237 uses `"timeout"` and :1265 uses `"regression-retry-targeted"` or `"regression-retry"`. src/gates/executor.ts:60 invokes `executor.discard?.(handle)` after restart; src/gates/lan.ts:25-26 calls `workers.cancel(handle.id)`. src/gates/executor.ts:188 starts a replacement when no stored handle remains: `stored ?? (await executor.start(req, signal))`.
verification.trigger: Restart the coordinator while a LAN timeout rerun or regression retry is leased. Resuming the stage calls the initial execution, rejects and cancels the persisted retry handle, and enqueues a fresh initial job instead of reattaching, losing and repeating work.

findings.title: Home-relative paths and file URLs bypass sanitization
findings.detail:
The sanitizer compares link destinations only against literal filesystem roots. A home-relative link such as the one in the request is left broken, and a file URL containing the absolute worktree path is published unchanged, including the owner's username. The direct check below returned both inputs unchanged.

Command: bun -e 'let s=await Bun.file("src/gates/publication.ts").text(); let f=new Function(s.slice(s.indexOf("export function sanitizePublication"),s.indexOf("/** Check both")).replace("export function","function").replace(/: string( \| undefined)?/g,"")+";return sanitizePublication")(); for(let x of ["[file](~/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)","[file](file:///Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)","[/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)"]) console.log(f(x,"/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run","/Users/alice/.limitless"))'
Output:
[file](~/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)
[file](file:///Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)
[/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)
findings.suggestion: Recognize home-relative paths and local file URLs before comparing them with the configured roots, and add cases for both forms.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains [file](file:///Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts) or [file](~/.limitless/work/run/a.ts).

verification.trigger: `[/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)` has an ordinary relative destination, so the entire link is retained with the absolute private path visible in its label.

findings.title: File URI links retain the absolute local path
findings.detail: The link matcher captures the whole file URI, but rewrite only recognizes destinations beginning directly with a configured filesystem root. A file URI therefore passes through unchanged and can publish the owner's username and data layout. An isolated probe of the sanitizer returned `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local file URI destinations and rewrite their decoded filesystem paths, while preserving ordinary remote URLs.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` and the configured worktree is `/factory/data/work/run`.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 requires the destination to start with a configured root, and line 24 says `if (result === path) return match;`. A destination beginning `file://` fails that root comparison.
verification.trigger: With worktree `/factory/data/work/run`, `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` remains unchanged and retains the absolute local path. This duplicates the file-URL case in C1.

findings.title: Bare paths immediately after a colon are skipped
findings.detail: The negative lookbehind excludes a colon, so a common `path:/absolute/path` form is left untouched. An isolated probe returned `path:/factory/data/work/run/a.ts` unchanged, allowing the local path to reach publication when the private-string list does not already block it.
findings.suggestion: Recognize bare local paths following punctuation such as a colon without rewriting paths embedded in remote URLs.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer report contains `path:/factory/data/work/run/a.ts` with that directory configured as the worktree.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:17 places `(?<![\\w/.:~%-])` immediately before the configured root alternatives, explicitly excluding matches preceded by a colon.
verification.trigger: `path:/factory/data/work/run/a.ts` remains unchanged because the colon prevents the bare-path match, leaving the absolute factory path in outgoing text.

findings.title: Dot segments classify paths outside the worktree as inside it
findings.detail: Classification uses a string prefix without resolving dot segments. The sanitizer turns `[file](/factory/data/work/run/../other/log)` into `[../other/log](../other/log)`, although the destination is outside the worktree and should be rendered as a data-directory placeholder.
findings.suggestion: Normalize path segments before deciding which root contains a local destination.
findings.failure_scenario: A report links to a data-directory file using an absolute path containing `work/run/../other/log`.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 classifies paths using lexical `path.startsWith(`${root}/`)`; lines 10-11 then strip the worktree prefix with `suffix.slice(1)` without normalizing dot segments.
verification.trigger: With worktree `/factory/data/work/run`, `[log](/factory/data/work/run/../other/log)` becomes `[../other/log](../other/log)`. The file is outside the worktree and should instead become plain `<data>/...` text; the generated repository link points somewhere else.

findings.title: File-URL links retain the absolute local path
findings.detail: The link destination is compared directly with the filesystem roots, so a file:// URL never matches. The fallback bare-path matcher also excludes a path preceded by a slash. The publication therefore retains the username and factory layout, or is blocked when those strings are configured as private.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local file URLs and normalize their filesystem path before applying the same root checks.
findings.failure_scenario: [file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts) remains unchanged when the worktree is /factory/data/work/run.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 matches only `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)`; :24 returns unchanged links with `if (result === path) return match;`. A direct probe confirmed file URLs remain unchanged.
verification.trigger: With worktree `/factory/data/work/run`, `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` retains its absolute local destination. Publication can expose that path when no private-string entry blocks it.

findings.title: Nested parentheses prevent data-directory links from becoming plain text
findings.detail: The Markdown link expression accepts only one level of parentheses in a destination. For a destination with nested parentheses, the bare-path alternative rewrites only part of the destination and leaves the surrounding link intact, contrary to the requested plain-text output.
findings.suggestion: Handle valid Markdown destinations with nested parentheses before applying the bare-path replacement.
findings.failure_scenario: [log](/factory/data/runs/a(b(c)).log) becomes [log](<data>/runs/a(b(c)).log) instead of plain text.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:13 recognizes only one parenthesis nesting level through `\([^()\n]*\)`. The fallback path expression at :17 excludes parentheses. A direct probe produced `[log](<data>/runs/a(b(c)).log)`.
verification.trigger: A data-directory link containing nested parentheses has its prefix replaced but retains Markdown link syntax instead of becoming plain text.

findings.title: Publication tests omit file URLs and nested-parenthesis destinations
findings.detail: The sanitizer tests cover absolute path links but do not exercise local file URLs or valid destinations with nested parentheses. Consequently, they miss both the retained private path and the data-directory link that remains Markdown.
findings.suggestion: Add independent expected-output cases for a file:// worktree link and a data-directory link whose destination contains nested parentheses.
findings.failure_scenario: The existing tests pass without detecting that [file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts) retains the absolute path or that a nested-parenthesis log link remains a link.

verification.evidence: test/publication-text.test.ts:8–16 covers plain paths, HTTP URLs and angle-bracket destinations, but neither claimed case. src/gates/publication.ts:8 matches only `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)`; line 24 returns unchanged links when no root matches. Line 13 supports only one parenthesis nesting level via `\([^()\n]*\)`. Executing the extracted function confirmed both outputs described below.
verification.trigger: With worktree=/factory/data/work/run and dataDirectory=/factory/data, `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` remains unchanged, retaining the absolute path; `[logs](/factory/data/runs/run/log(a(b)).txt)` becomes `[logs](<data>/runs/run/log(a(b)).txt)`, retaining link markup instead of becoming plain text. Neither input is covered by the tests.

findings.title: Paths in Markdown link labels and titles bypass sanitization
findings.detail: The link alternative consumes the entire Markdown link, but the callback examines only its destination. If the destination is relative or remote, it returns the entire match unchanged, including any absolute local path in the label or title. That path can therefore be published or cause delivery to be blocked once the username is added to private-strings.txt.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path-bearing link labels and titles as well as destinations, without leaving the consumed text unchecked.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains `[See /Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)`. The destination is unchanged, so the absolute path in the visible label is published unchanged.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:21 selects only the destination with `const path = angle ?? bare`; :24 returns the entire original match when that destination is unchanged: `if (result === path) return match;`.
verification.trigger: `[See /Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)` preserves the absolute path in its label. Absolute paths in titles of unchanged links are likewise preserved, potentially publishing local layout or blocking delivery once denylisted.

findings.title: Encoded local link destinations are not recognized
findings.detail: The root comparison operates on the literal Markdown destination. A valid link whose path uses percent-encoded separators or HTML character references does not start with the literal worktree or data-directory root, so it is returned unchanged. The subsequent private-text check decodes HTML entities but not URL percent encoding, allowing an encoded username and data path to leave the factory.
findings.suggestion: Decode and classify local link destinations before comparing them with the configured roots, then emit a sanitized destination.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains `[file](%2FUsers%2Falice%2F.limitless%2Fwork%2Frun%2Fa.ts)`. The sanitizer preserves the link, and the private-text check does not recognize the percent-encoded username.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 compares raw destinations against roots, and :24 preserves unmatched links. However, src/gates/private.ts:49 decodes percent sequences and :70 checks decoded layers with `layer.includes(protectedText)`, disproving the claimed private-text bypass.
verification.trigger: A percent-encoded worktree destination remains encoded instead of becoming repo-relative. If the username is denylisted, publication is blocked; the candidate's assertion that the private-text check misses it is false.

findings.title: Sanitizing after clipping can publish a partial private path
findings.detail: Blocked-round evidence is clipped to 300 characters and the complete comment is clipped to 60,000 characters before publicationText sees it. If either cut falls within the data-directory prefix, the sanitizer cannot match the full root, leaving the beginning of the absolute path in the published comment. The report renderer also clips text before the new publication sanitizer runs.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path-bearing source text before truncation at each publication path, while preserving any full-source privacy checks.
findings.failure_scenario: Blocked evidence consists of 290 characters followed by `/Users/alice/.limitless/runs/log`. The 300-character cut retains `/Users/ali`, which no longer matches the configured data-directory root and can be published.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:2129–2131: `const evidence = redactGateOutput(redactHoldoutText(...)).slice(0, 300);`; :2139–2141: `text = publicationText(ctx, text); ... await gh(["pr", "comment", prUrl, "--body-file", "-"], ctx.signal, text);`. src/gates/publication.ts:8 requires `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)`, so an incomplete root survives. src/gates/private.ts:94 calls `privateMatches(text, entries)` without fragment matching.
verification.trigger: Blocked evidence has 290 characters followed by `/Users/alice/.limitless/runs/log`. Clipping leaves `/Users/ali`, which matches neither publication root nor a denylisted full username/root, and the comment publishes it. A cutoff later in the root can expose the complete username.

findings.title: Parent-directory segments are classified under the wrong root
findings.detail: The sanitizer classifies paths by lexical prefix without resolving `..` segments. A path that starts in the worktree but resolves into the factory data directory is emitted as a repository-relative path rather than a `<data>` placeholder.
findings.suggestion: Normalize local path segments before deciding which configured root contains the destination.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree `/factory/data/work/run`, `/factory/data/work/run/../../runs/log` becomes `../../runs/log` instead of `<data>/runs/log`.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 classifies paths using a lexical prefix; :10–11 uses `path.slice(roots[index]?.length)` and returns `suffix.slice(1)` without normalizing parent-directory segments.
verification.trigger: With worktree `/factory/data/work/run`, `/factory/data/work/run/../../runs/log` becomes `../../runs/log`, although its normalized location is outside the worktree under the data directory and should become `<data>/runs/log`.

findings.title: Paths in Markdown link labels bypass rewriting
findings.detail: The request requires rewriting “links and bare paths that point into the run's worktree.” The link alternative consumes the entire Markdown link, but the callback only examines its destination. Consequently, an absolute path in the visible label survives whenever the destination is relative or otherwise unchanged. Once the username is in private-strings.txt, the privacy check can block delivery; until then, the path can be published.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path occurrences in link labels as well as destinations while preserving ordinary link targets.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree /factory/data/work/run, the input [`/factory/data/work/run/a.ts`](docs/a.md) is returned unchanged. A standalone invocation of sanitizePublication produced that exact unchanged output.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:13 matches the entire Markdown link, including its label. Lines 21–24 inspect only the destination: `const path = angle ?? bare; ... const result = rewrite(path); if (result === path) return match;`. Executing the extracted sanitizer confirmed the candidate input remains unchanged.
verification.trigger: With worktree /factory/data/work/run, [`/factory/data/work/run/a.ts`](docs/a.md) preserves the absolute path in its label because docs/a.md requires no rewrite. Publication can expose private directory information or be blocked by the private-text check.

findings.title: File URI links retain absolute local paths
findings.detail: The request covers links pointing into the worktree and factory data directory, but rewrite only recognizes destinations beginning directly with a configured filesystem root. A file:// destination is consumed as a Markdown link and returned unchanged, exposing the local path or causing the private-strings check to block delivery.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local file URI destinations, decode them as appropriate, and apply the same worktree and data-directory rewriting.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree /factory/data/work/run, [file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts) is returned unchanged. A standalone invocation of sanitizePublication produced that exact unchanged output.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8–9 requires `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)` and otherwise returns the original path. Lines 23–24 then return the entire unchanged link. Executing the extracted sanitizer confirmed [file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts) remains unchanged.
verification.trigger: A report uses a file:/// link into the worktree. The URI scheme prevents the destination from matching either filesystem root, retaining the absolute local path in published text or causing the private-text check to block delivery.

findings.title: Appending a round section rewrites the existing PR body
findings.detail: The request lists “Rewriting already published PR bodies” as out of scope. Sanitizing pr.body together with the new section changes existing published text, including text a user may have edited, whenever it contains a matching path.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize the newly generated round section before appending it, without transforming the existing body.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing PR body contains a worktree path and a new review round is appended; the edit replaces the path in the previously published body as well as adding the round section.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:2146 sanitizes the new section: `const text = publicationText(ctx, section);`. Then :2148 sanitizes the existing body too: `const body = publicationText(ctx, pr.body + text);`; :2151 publishes that replacement with `gh(["pr", "edit", prUrl, "--body-file", "-"], ctx.signal, body)`.
verification.trigger: An existing PR body contains a path under the current worktree or factory data directory, and the new round marker is absent. Appending the round rewrites that previously published text as well.

findings.title: Recheck ownership inside the merge helper before each merge command
findings.detail: The ownership check precedes mergePullRequest, but that helper awaits a GitHub PR lookup before issuing gh pr merge and can repeat that sequence on retry. A reclaim during the lookup is invisible until the heartbeat, so the old worker can still issue a merge after losing its claim.
findings.suggestion: Pass an ownership guard into the helper and check it immediately before each merge command, including retries.
findings.failure_scenario: The old worker enters mergePullRequest, its PR view request is deferred, another owner reclaims the entry, and the view returns before the old heartbeat fires. The old worker then runs gh pr merge.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:701 awaits `mergePullRequest(...)`; ownership is checked afterward at :715: `this.assertClaim(entry.id)`. Inside src/git/repos.ts:1447, the helper awaits `sh(view, { cwd, signal })`, then executes :1462 `return sh(cmd, { cwd, signal, stdin: body })` without checking claim ownership.
verification.trigger: Reclaim the entry while the helper's PR view is pending, then return an OPEN PR with the expected SHA before the heartbeat aborts. The displaced worker issues gh pr merge.

findings.title: Guard the actual push after its preparation awaits

findings.title: Do not discard a checkout reused by the new claimant
findings.detail: All attempts for an entry use the same land-<id> worktree path. After a reclaim, the old worker reaches this unconditional cleanup even when a new worker has already recreated and started using that path. It can remove the new worker's worktree and cause its checks or merge to fail.
findings.suggestion: Isolate checkout paths by claim or otherwise ensure cleanup cannot remove a newer claimant's checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: A CI response is deferred, the entry is reclaimed and the new worker creates its checkout, then the old response returns. The old worker detects the lost claim but its finally block removes the new worker's checkout.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:548-549 performs `await this.observe(...)` followed by `this.assertClaim(entry.id)`, but :396-397 unconditionally runs `finally { await this.discard(repo, cwd); }`. The path is shared across claimants: :812 `return join(this.deps.paths.work, `land-${entry.id}`)`. Discard ends at :842 with `rmSync(cwd, { recursive: true, force: true })`.
verification.trigger: A replacement worker in another process recreates the same entry checkout while the old worker awaits CI. Releasing the old response throws on lost ownership, and its cleanup deletes the replacement checkout.

findings.title: CI inspection can still write after the claim is reclaimed

candidates.suggestion: Add a deferred race test that starts the replacement worker, waits until its checkout exists, releases the stale worker, and verifies that the replacement checkout and attempt remain usable.
candidates.failure_scenario: A reclaimed worker creates the entry’s shared worktree before the stale worker exits; the stale worker deletes it, while the current tests pass because no replacement checkout exists.

candidates.title: Recheck ownership immediately before the merge command
candidates.detail: The ownership check precedes the call to mergePullRequest, but that helper awaits a GitHub PR lookup and can retry before issuing `gh pr merge`. A reclaim during one of those waits leaves the old signal live until its next heartbeat, so the old worker can still issue a merge. The check after mergePullRequest returns is too late to prevent it.
candidates.suggestion: Pass an ownership guard into the merge helper and check it immediately before each merge command, including retries.
candidates.failure_scenario: The old worker enters mergePullRequest, another owner reclaims the entry while `gh pr view` is pending, and the view returns before the old heartbeat fires. The old worker then invokes `gh pr merge`.

candidates.title: Recheck ownership immediately before the push command
candidates.detail: pushExistingBranch awaits commit resolution, remote inspection and ancestry checks after the new ownership check and before invoking git push. A reclaim during those operations therefore still permits the old worker to push before its heartbeat detects the loss.
candidates.suggestion: Make the push helper validate the claim immediately before issuing the push.
candidates.failure_scenario: The entry is reclaimed while pushExistingBranch is waiting for `git ls-remote`; the command returns before the heartbeat and the old worker pushes its merge commit.

candidates.title: Do not discard a reclaimed worker's shared checkout
candidates.detail: The finally block discards the checkout even when an ownership check throws LandClaimLost. Both attempts use the same `land-<entry id>` path, so the old worker can remove the newer owner's checkout after it has been created, interrupting its checks or publication.
candidates.suggestion: Give attempts distinct checkout paths or otherwise ensure cleanup cannot remove a checkout belonging to a newer claim.
candidates.failure_scenario: A new owner reclaims an entry and creates its checkout while the old worker is awaiting a CI response. When that response returns, the old worker detects the lost claim and its finally block removes the new owner's checkout.

candidates.title: Recheck ownership immediately before issuing the merge
candidates.detail: The request says that after every await preceding a side effect, a worker that lost its claim issues no merge. The ownership check occurs before calling mergePullRequest, but that helper awaits a GitHub PR lookup before issuing `gh pr merge`, and can also await reconciliation during retries. A reclaim during one of those awaits leaves the old signal live until its heartbeat, so the old worker can still issue the merge.
candidates.suggestion: Make the merge helper validate claim ownership after its asynchronous preparation and immediately before each merge attempt.
candidates.failure_scenario: The old worker enters mergePullRequest and waits for `gh pr view`; another owner reclaims the entry, then the lookup returns before the old heartbeat. The old worker invokes `gh pr merge` despite having lost its claim.

candidates.title: Recheck ownership inside push preparation
candidates.detail: The request says a worker that lost its claim issues no push. The guarded checkpoint precedes pushExistingBranch, but that helper awaits commit resolution, transport setup, a remote lookup and an ancestry check before invoking the push. A reclaim during any of those awaits can therefore be followed by a push from the old worker.
candidates.suggestion: Pass an ownership guard into the push helper and invoke it immediately before the push command.
candidates.failure_scenario: The old worker passes the guarded checkpoint and waits for `ls-remote`; a new owner reclaims the entry and the lookup returns before the heartbeat. The old worker then pushes its merge commit.

candidates.title: Do not discard a reclaimed worker's checkout
candidates.detail: The request says a worker that lost its claim writes nothing. The unconditional finally block still removes the checkout after claim loss. Checkout paths are keyed only by entry ID, so a new owner can already have recreated that same path when the old worker's cleanup runs.
candidates.suggestion: Give each claim its own checkout path, or otherwise ensure cleanup cannot remove a checkout belonging to a newer claim.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CI response is deferred, the entry is reclaimed and the new worker recreates `land-<entry id>`. When the old response returns, the old worker detects claim loss but its finally block removes the new worker's checkout.

Verifier: 7 candidates, 7 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: A rejected rerun can remain pending forever after claim loss
findings.detail: The rerun claim is persisted before the POST. If ownership changes while the POST is in flight, the new guard discards its response, including an explicit rejection. The replacement worker sees the existing rerun_requested record, but only resolves it when GitHub reports a later workflow attempt. A rejected request creates no later attempt, so CI remains pending and the land cannot complete or report the failure.
findings.suggestion: Provide a recovery path for an unconfirmed rerun request that lets the current owner resolve a rejected or absent rerun without allowing the old owner to write after losing its claim.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker claims a CI rerun, GitHub returns HTTP 422 after another worker reclaims the land entry, and the old worker discards the response. The replacement repeatedly observes the original workflow attempt and retains rerun_requested indefinitely.

verification.evidence: src/db/store.ts:2900 persists "outcome = 'rerun_requested'" before the POST. src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts:236-243 executes "const res = await call(...)" then "allowed();" before handling HTTP 4xx with "reject(f, excerpt)"; allowed() throws when ownership is lost (97-98). Replacement inspections skip unchanged attempts: "if (run.run_attempt <= origin.attempt) continue;" (293), and skip pending failures without recorded refusal metadata: "if (!refused) continue;" (438-440).
verification.trigger: Reclaim the land entry while its rerun POST is pending, then return HTTP 422 without starting another attempt. The ownership guard discards the rejection, leaving rerun_requested unresolved indefinitely. The replacement waits until its land CI deadline and blocks instead of recognizing the rejected rerun.

findings.title: Recheck ownership before every push retry
findings.detail: The guard runs once before remoteSh, but remoteSh retries transient failures internally. A reclaim during the first push or its retry delay does not prevent the next push attempt if the old worker's heartbeat has not yet aborted its signal. This violates the requirement that a worker that lost its claim issue no push.
findings.suggestion: Run the ownership guard inside the retry callback immediately before each push attempt.
findings.failure_scenario: The first push fails transiently, another worker reclaims the entry during the retry delay, and the old worker issues a second push before its next heartbeat.

verification.evidence: src/git/repos.ts:1324 calls `guard?.()` once before `await remoteSh(...)` at line 1325. However, src/git/repos.ts:115-116 defines `remoteSh` as `withGitHubRetry(() => (cmd[0] === "git" ? cacheGit(cmd, opts) : sh(cmd, opts)), opts)`, so retries execute the push without the guard. The retry loop checks only `opts.signal?.throwIfAborted()` (line 91), invokes `charged(call)` (line 97), and awaits `pause(delay, opts.signal)` after a transient failure (line 103). Ownership loss aborts the signal only when detected, including by the periodic heartbeat in src/land/queue.ts:303-313.
verification.trigger: The first push fails transiently; another worker reclaims the entry during the retry delay; the delay expires before the old worker's next heartbeat. Its signal remains un-aborted, so the retry issues another push without checking ownership, potentially publishing after losing its claim.

findings.title: Reconcile rejected reruns after ownership changes
findings.detail: The rerun claim is recorded as rerun_requested before the POST. If ownership changes while the POST is pending, the new guard discards even a definitive rejection response. Subsequent inspections wait for a later workflow attempt, which will never exist after a rejected request, leaving the failure pending until the land times out.
findings.suggestion: Provide a durable reconciliation path for an interrupted rerun request that resolves rejected or otherwise unconfirmed requests without allowing the old owner to write.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub returns HTTP 422 for a rerun POST after another worker reclaims the land entry. The recorded failure remains rerun_requested, so the replacement worker waits for a workflow attempt GitHub never started.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts:236-243 places "allowed();" immediately after the awaited rerun POST and before "reject(f, excerpt)" for HTTP 4xx. Ownership loss throws (97-98), preserving the previously persisted "outcome = 'rerun_requested'" (src/db/store.ts:2900). Reconciliation requires a newer attempt (ci-classifier.ts:293), while existing pending failures without rerunRetryAt are skipped (438-440).
verification.trigger: GitHub rejects an in-flight rerun POST with HTTP 422 after another worker reclaims the entry. The rejection is discarded and never recorded; subsequent inspections wait for an attempt GitHub never started, eventually blocking the replacement land worker at its CI deadline.

findings.title: A stale worker can still write into the replacement attempt’s gate log
findings.detail: Gate result callbacks append to a log shared by all attempts without checking claim ownership. If a claim is reclaimed while a gate is running, the old worker can append its result before its next heartbeat aborts it, including after the replacement worker has truncated or begun writing the same log. The stored log can therefore mix results from different attempts, contrary to the requirement that a worker that lost its claim writes nothing.
findings.suggestion: Give each attempt its own log and guard gate-result and retry writes against claim loss, including callbacks invoked while a gate is running.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A is awaiting a gate; worker B reclaims the entry and starts checks using the same land log. Before A’s next heartbeat, A’s gate completes and its onResult callback appends output to B’s log.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:435 uses the shared path `land-${entry.id}.log`; line 441 truncates it with `writeFileSync(log, ...)`. Lines 454–458 define `onResult: (r: GateResult) => appendFileSync(log, ...)` without checking ownership. src/gates/executor.ts:216–217 invokes `hooks.onResult` for arriving check events. The ownership check at queue.ts:462 occurs only after `await executeGate(...)`.
verification.trigger: B reclaims A's entry and initializes the same log; A's pending gate emits a result before its heartbeat detects claim loss. A appends stale output into B's log.
