Verifier: 18 candidates, 18 checked, 0 refuted.

findings.title: Rollback to the previous release does not notify the executor
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the database setting written by this new daemon. The previous release never writes that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release SHA in place. A running new executor continues its job and can continue leasing queued jobs even though the active daemon is now the older release.
findings.suggestion: Use release ownership that the previous release can invalidate or otherwise ensure that a rollback stops the executor before the old daemon resumes work.
findings.failure_scenario: Start an in-place gate on this release, then roll back and start the base-commit daemon. The setting still names this release, so the executor does not cancel the gate as required.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:50 adds `factory.store.setSetting("executor.daemonRelease", factory.bootSha);`; at base 1b8a176, src/cli/daemon.ts:49-50 instead proceeds directly from `try {` to `detachSlots = await attachSlotPools(...)`, leaving that setting unchanged. src/gates/inplace.ts:39 detects release changes solely through `store.getSetting("executor.daemonRelease", "") !== releaseSha`; otherwise lines 53-57 renew the lease. src/db/workers.ts:388 uses the same setting to authorize leasing.
verification.trigger: Roll back to the base daemon while a new-release executor runs a gate, with no LAN worker polling to invalidate its lease. The persisted setting retains the new release SHA, so the executor continues the gate and can lease queued new-release jobs despite the daemon running another release.

findings.title: Process existence is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat timestamp. An executor whose event loop is stalled remains eligible indefinitely. Once its lease expires, the daemon marks the job failed, but waitStopped waits indefinitely while that process exists, so it cannot fall back or proceed with the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, safe path for confirming that an unresponsive executor's gate processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor is alive but paused or blocked while running a gate. Its lease expires; the daemon enters waitStopped and never completes the gate or starts the fallback.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 identifies availability solely with `return processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth;`. Lease expiry fails the job at src/db/workers.ts:671–672, but src/db/workers.ts:366–384 loops while `stopped === 0`, performs recovery only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`, and otherwise sleeps. src/gates/lan.ts:131 awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)` before fallback.
verification.trigger: An executor remains alive but stops making progress during a leased gate. Its lease expires, but its process identity still matches, so fallback waits indefinitely for the unresponsive executor to confirm stopping.

findings.title: Targeted and timeout retry jobs cannot reattach
findings.detail: The resume predicate explicitly accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A restart during an in-place targeted or timeout retry therefore cancels the still-running job and repeats work instead of attaching to its matching handle.
findings.suggestion: Persist and restore the retry context needed to validate and reattach matching retry jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is leased by the executor. On resume, the purpose fails this allowlist and the retry is cancelled or started again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 requires '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)'; lines 35–43 cancel and clear rejected handles. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 resumes with '"initial"', while lines 1566 and 1595 create '"timeout"' and '"regression-retry-targeted"' jobs. src/gates/lan.ts:46 executes 'workers.cancel(handle.id)'.
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts during a leased targeted or timeout retry. Stage resume rejects its persisted purpose, cancels the surviving job, and repeats gate work.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback
findings.detail: When the gate executor is configured as LAN, this factory always returns the LAN executor, even when the in-place executor is enabled. Its local path for repositories outside the LAN list runs directly in the daemon, so those local gates cannot survive a daemon restart.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local path through the in-place executor when it is enabled and available.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the executor, configure LAN gates for one repository, and run a gate in another repository. The gate runs in the daemon and is lost on restart despite a live in-place executor.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:77–81 applies the enabled flag only in the local branch: `return inplace && workers ? lanExecutor(workers, [], true) : localExecutor();`; the LAN branch returns `lanExecutor(workers, repos)`. src/gates/lan.ts:16 defaults `inplace = false`, and src/gates/lan.ts:71 routes repositories outside that list directly to `local.start(req, signal)`. src/gates/lan.ts:79 attaches those handles through `local.attach(...)`, bypassing durable in-place jobs.
verification.trigger: Set gates.executor to "lan", enable the executor, and run gates for a repository outside workers.repos while an in-place executor is alive. Gates run inside the daemon, so a daemon restart interrupts them and requires repeated work.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into local retries
findings.detail: The executor catches every error from executeGate and records an ordinary failed job. The attaching daemon then reruns every failed in-place job locally. This loses the distinction between an infrastructure failure and a ConfinementError, so a failed isolation check can be followed by a successful gate instead of failing closed.
findings.suggestion: Persist a failure classification and propagate confinement and inspection failures to the daemon without retrying them.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor's confinement preflight throws ConfinementError, but the daemon's subsequent local preflight succeeds; the gate passes despite the original security check failing.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:70–71 catches every error: `catch (error) { workers.fail(job.id, redactCredentials(String(error))); }`. src/gates/lan.ts:130–139 handles any `job.state === "failed"` by calling `local.start(request, controller.signal)` and `local.attach(...)`. No confinement-error classification survives to prevent fallback.
verification.trigger: The executor's confinement preflight throws ConfinementError; after cleanup, the daemon retries locally. If its preflight and checks succeed, the gate passes despite the original confinement failure.

findings.title: A cleanup failure can leave the run waiting indefinitely
findings.detail: waitStopped only attempts recovery or reports an error after the executor process disappears. If a job finishes with process discovery or cleanup records remaining, the executor deliberately leaves stopped=0 but continues running. waitStopped then polls forever because the executor is still alive, even though that executor will never revisit the completed job.
findings.suggestion: Make the executor publish a terminal cleanup failure, or have waitStopped detect that the job is no longer being cleaned up and fail closed with a clear error.
findings.failure_scenario: A cancelled gate leaves a cleanup record after process cleanup fails; the executor continues polling for other jobs, while the daemon waits forever to start the replacement gate.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:75–80 sets `stopped=1` only when both `!store.listProcessDiscoveries(undefined, req.cwd).length` and `!store.listProcessCleanups(undefined, req.cwd).length`; execution then returns to the polling loop at lines 29–30. src/db/workers.ts:370 runs recovery only if `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`; otherwise line 384 only sleeps.
verification.trigger: Cleanup fails and leaves a discovery or cleanup record. The executor finishes handling that job and remains alive polling, leaving stopped=0. The daemon neither retries recovery nor reports the unresolved cleanup while that executor lives, indefinitely blocking replacement work.

findings.title: Worktree exclusion is not atomic across concurrent starts
findings.detail: The query for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations. Two daemon-side starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue independently. With two executor processes, each can lease one job and run both gates in the same worktree.
findings.suggestion: Enforce worktree exclusivity atomically in the database when creating or leasing an in-place job.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concurrent gate starts for the same cwd pass the existing-job query before either enqueues, and two executors lease their jobs concurrently.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:54-59 queries existing jobs by cwd and waits only for those returned. It then yields at line 72: `await releaseGateSlotScope()`. The new job is inserted later, at lines 80-81: `if (inplace && starts.has(handle.id) && req && !workers.job(handle.id)) workers.enqueue(req, handle.id, true);`. src/db/workers.ts:390-400 selects queued jobs by release and leases with `WHERE id=? AND state='queued'`, without checking for another active job in the same cwd.
verification.trigger: Two concurrent starts for the same cwd both observe no existing job before either attaches and enqueues. Both jobs are inserted; two executor processes can lease different jobs and run checks concurrently in that worktree when gate capacity permits, violating worktree exclusion.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after a restart
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A durable in-place handle for a targeted retry is therefore cancelled even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and lease all match. The retry is restarted instead of receiving the surviving job's result.
findings.suggestion: Provide a resume path for targeted retry purposes and preserve the state needed to resume them.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is running; resume rejects its matching handle, cancels the executor job, and runs the retry again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 assigns targeted retries purpose '"regression-retry-targeted"'. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 only accepts '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"]'; lines 35–43 cancel and clear rejected handles. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 resumes the stage with '"initial"'.
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts while a targeted retry runs in the executor. The resumed stage cancels that retry and starts gate work again instead of attaching.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness check
findings.detail: Executor availability is based only on PID and birth identity; the executors table has no heartbeat timestamp. A live but stalled executor is treated as available indefinitely. New gates are enqueued instead of immediately using the requested in-process fallback, and a leased job is not considered disconnected until its lease expires.
findings.suggestion: Record and renew an executor heartbeat and require it to be fresh when selecting an executor and sweeping its jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops making progress; the daemon treats it as available and waits for pickup or lease expiry rather than recognizing that no fresh executor is available.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:354–359 reads executor identities and checks `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`, without checking a heartbeat timestamp. src/gates/lan.ts:65 uses `if (!workers.executor())` to select immediate local fallback. src/db/workers.ts:656–657 instead waits for the pickup timer: `this.fail(j.id, "No worker picked up job")`.
verification.trigger: An executor process remains alive while its event loop is unresponsive. The daemon incorrectly selects it as available, enqueues work and waits for pickup timeout instead of immediately using the required fallback for an executor without a fresh heartbeat.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs are cancelled on restart instead of reattached
findings.detail: Resume accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A recorded `baseline-retry-targeted` or `regression-retry-targeted` handle therefore fails the resume check even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and executor lease match. The live job is cancelled and the stage starts over, contrary to the requested restart behavior for targeted retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry state to resume the targeted retry and accept its matching handle during stage recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running a long targeted regression retry; the new engine cancels that job and repeats gate work instead of receiving its result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 records '"regression-retry-targeted"' for targeted retries, but src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 requires '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)'. Lines 35–43 call 'cancelGateExecution' and clear the handle; src/gates/lan.ts:46 calls 'workers.cancel(handle.id)'.
verification.trigger: A restart interrupts daemon attachment to a running targeted regression retry. Resume rejects and cancels the surviving job, causing repeated gate work.

findings.title: Restart coverage omits targeted retries
findings.detail: The engine restart cases cover baseline, initial, and rebase gates, but none interrupts a targeted baseline or regression retry. Consequently the tests do not catch the resume-purpose restriction that cancels those jobs.
findings.suggestion: Add a restart test that pauses a targeted retry, resumes the engine, and asserts that the same job completes and its command ran once.
findings.failure_scenario: A targeted retry is running when the daemon stops; the current suite passes without checking whether the resumed engine reattaches to it.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:487–494 enumerates only "baseline", "initial", and "rebase" restart cases. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 likewise permits resume only for `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`, excluding targeted retries.
verification.trigger: Daemon stops during a targeted retry; the restart tests never exercise that purpose or assert attachment to its existing job, leaving repeated retry work undetected.

findings.title: Pickup timeout test never verifies in-process fallback
findings.detail: The pickup test stops after asserting that the queued job becomes failed. It does not attach a daemon-side execution or assert that the check subsequently runs locally and returns its result, so a regression in the failed-job fallback path would pass.
findings.suggestion: Exercise an attached in-place job that is never leased, sweep it past pickup timeout, and assert that the local check runs and its result reaches the caller.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor remains alive but does not pick up a queued job, and the daemon fails to start the local fallback after the sweep marks it failed.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:319–324 enqueues `missed`, calls `later.sweep()`, and asserts only `state` is "failed" and `attempt` is 1. It never attaches to the job or checks a local command/result.
verification.trigger: A live executor misses pickup and sweep fails the queued job; a regression preventing subsequent in-process fallback would still pass this test. This establishes missing coverage, not a proven runtime fallback failure.

findings.title: Gate result comparison discards most of the result shape
findings.detail: The purported in-process comparison projects each result down to name, ok, and exitCode, while the event assertion checks only names. It would still pass if executor results or events lost output, command, timing, failure metadata, or other fields required by consumers. The test also does not compare the produced gate artifacts.
findings.suggestion: Compare representative complete result and event structures, excluding only nondeterministic values, and verify the corresponding artifact contents.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor drops a check's output or failure metadata while preserving its name and exit code; this test still passes although the reported gate data changed.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:114–115 projects results with `.map(({ name, ok, exitCode }) => ({ name, ok, exitCode }))`; line 144 compares only those projections. Lines 145–146 check event names and only the environment check's output.
verification.trigger: Executor results lose another check's output or failure metadata while retaining name, ok, and exitCode; the comparison still passes despite the changed result shape.

findings.title: Executor stores gate output without the daemon’s dynamic credential registrations
findings.detail: Credential registrations are process-local. The executor loads configured provider credentials, but it does not receive credentials registered dynamically by the daemon, such as GitHub installation tokens and worker tokens. It redacts and persists check events and results using its own incomplete registry before the daemon sees them, so the daemon’s later redaction cannot remove the copies already stored in gate_jobs.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the executor has the daemon’s complete current redaction set before processing output, or defer persistence of output to a boundary that has that set while preserving restart-safe event handling.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon registers a GitHub installation token during operation, and a gate prints that token. An in-place executor that never registered the token stores it unredacted in the job’s events or result.

verification.evidence: src/util/proc.ts:1216–1224 keeps registrations in process-local sets: `const credentialValues = new Set<string>()`. src/integrations/github-token.ts:18 registers dynamically obtained tokens with `registerCredential("GH_TOKEN", token)`. src/gates/inplace.ts:65,69 sends results directly to `workers.event(...)` and `workers.complete(...)`; src/db/workers.ts:129–132 sanitizes using `redactGateData(data)`, and :612–613 persists those events. The executor receives no daemon credential registrations.
verification.trigger: A gate prints a token registered only in the daemon process. The executor's matcher does not know that value, so it persists the token unredacted in gate_jobs events and results, even if later daemon-side rendering redacts it.

findings.title: Confinement derives credential paths from the executor environment
findings.detail: The gate receives the daemon’s saved environment, but the executor constructs its read policy from its own process environment. The policy uses environment variables such as AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, GH_CONFIG_DIR, and CARGO_HOME to deny credential paths. When those variables differ between the daemon and executor, a credential path known to the daemon can be omitted from the executor’s deny list, weakening the confinement applied to untrusted gate commands.
findings.suggestion: Build the gate’s confinement policy from the same trusted environment used by the daemon, including its credential-path variables, and refuse execution if that policy cannot be reconstructed.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon has AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE pointing to a credential file under an otherwise allowed toolchain path, while the executor lacks that variable. A gate can read the file through the in-place executor even though the daemon’s local confinement would deny it.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:27 uses `readPolicyScope.run(cfg.readPolicy, ...)`, while :64 forwards the request environment only to execution. src/config.ts:455 constructs that policy through `configureReadPolicy(raw.sandbox, configDir)`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:51,62 snapshots `AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE` from `process.env`; :144 uses `options.environment ?? process.env`, and :169 includes `env.AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE` among credential denies. src/harness/sandbox.ts:351 builds confinement with `writeRoots(opts.cwd, scratch, true)`, without passing the request environment.
verification.trigger: The daemon names a credential file through AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, but the executor lacks that variable. If the file lies in an executor-readable toolchain path, the executor omits its credential protection and a gate can read it; the daemon's policy would refuse the overlapping allowance.

findings.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after restart
findings.detail: The request says the local executor covers “the targeted retry” and that a resumed stage with the same stage, round, purpose and SHA attaches to its job. The purpose whitelist excludes both regression retry purposes and baseline retry purposes. On resume, the surrounding stage first asks to resume its initial gate, so it cancels the still-running retry and starts the stage's gate work again.

candidates.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the database setting written by this new daemon. A running new executor continues its job and can continue leasing queued jobs even though the active daemon is now the older release.

candidates.title: Process existence is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
candidates.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat timestamp. An executor whose event loop is stalled remains eligible indefinitely. Once its lease expires, the daemon marks the job failed, but waitStopped waits indefinitely while that process exists, so it cannot fall back or proceed with the worktree.

candidates.failure_scenario: An executor is alive but paused or blocked while running a gate. Its lease expires; the daemon enters waitStopped and never completes the gate or starts the fallback.

candidates.title: Targeted and timeout retry jobs cannot reattach
candidates.detail: The resume predicate explicitly accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A restart during an in-place targeted or timeout retry therefore cancels the still-running job and repeats work instead of attaching to its matching handle.

candidates.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback

candidates.title: Confinement failures are converted into local retries

candidates.title: A cleanup failure can leave the run waiting indefinitely

On stage resume, src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 calls `resumeGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", cwd, env)`. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires `pending.purpose === purpose && ["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`; failure invokes `await cancelGateExecution(...)` at line 36 and clears the handle at line 42.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor can block a worktree indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor freshness is determined solely by whether its PID and birth time still match; there is no heartbeat. If the executor is alive but no longer making progress, the sweep eventually fails its lease, but `waitStopped` continues waiting for that same live process to set `stopped`. Consequently the daemon never reaches the in-process fallback or starts another gate in the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a bounded, confirmed process-stop or recovery path before falling back.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor becomes stuck while running a gate but remains alive. Its lease expires, and the daemon waits indefinitely in `waitStopped`.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 checks only `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. At :366–384, `while (this.job(id)?.stopped === 0)` performs recovery only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`; otherwise it sleeps without a deadline. src/gates/lan.ts:131 awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)` before fallback.
verification.trigger: A leased executor stalls indefinitely while its process identity remains valid. Lease expiry fails the job, but waitStopped never finishes, blocking fallback and subsequent gates in that worktree.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into a local retry
findings.detail: The executor catches every error from `executeGate`, including `ConfinementError`, and marks the job failed. The daemon treats every failed in-place job as eligible for local fallback in `lan.ts`. A confinement inspection failure can therefore be replaced by a passing second execution, hiding the failed security check and allowing the gate to pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the failure classification across the job boundary and propagate confinement failures without retrying them as local gates.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor cannot verify its Seatbelt confinement, but the daemon's subsequent local confinement check succeeds; the local retry passes and the original security failure is lost.

verification.evidence: src/harness/sandbox.ts:282 awaits `backend.verify(roots, opts, run)`, allowing verification errors to propagate. src/gates/inplace.ts:70–71 catches every error and calls `workers.fail(job.id, redactCredentials(String(error)))`. src/gates/lan.ts:130–150 handles any failed job by running `local.start(request, controller.signal)` and returning `workers.sanitize(run)`, without preserving a confinement verdict.
verification.trigger: Executor confinement verification throws, then daemon-local verification succeeds. The failed job is retried locally and can return a passing GateRun; the original confinement failure remains only as failure metadata, rather than blocking or affecting the returned verdict.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth time; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor remains alive but stops making progress, new jobs are sent to it and previously leased jobs eventually enter `waitStopped`, which continues waiting as long as that process exists. Lease expiry therefore does not produce a bounded fallback or a completed cancellation.
findings.suggestion: Track executor freshness and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for an unresponsive owner while confirming its gate processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor hangs while running a gate and stops renewing its lease. The sweep marks the job failed, but `waitStopped` waits indefinitely because the executor PID still exists, so the run never falls back or finishes.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:671–672 calls `this.fail(j.id, "Lease expired")`, but :630 updates only `state='failed',failure_reason=?,updated_at=?`. At :370, recovery requires `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`, while :359 defines executor liveness solely as `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. src/gates/lan.ts:131 waits for stopped before fallback.
verification.trigger: An executor stops renewing a running job but remains alive. The sweep fails the expired lease, yet stopped remains zero and the daemon waits indefinitely instead of falling back.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after restart
findings.detail: The resume whitelist excludes targeted and other retry purposes. When a daemon restarts during a targeted retry, the resumed stage rejects the recorded handle and cancels the surviving job instead of attaching to it. This leaves the requested restart protection incomplete for a gate purpose explicitly named in the request.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage state to resume the matching retry job and attach to it after restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A long `regression-retry-targeted` job is running when the daemon restarts; the resumed gate stage cancels that job and reruns earlier gate work rather than receiving its result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 uses purpose `"regression-retry-targeted"`. Resume enters through `resumeGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", cwd, env)` at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires `pending.purpose === purpose` and restricts purposes to `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"]`; lines 35–42 cancel and clear a rejected handle.
verification.trigger: A restart interrupts attachment to a running targeted retry. Despite matching SHA and a live executor lease, the resumed stage rejects its purpose, cancels it, and reruns initial gates.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after a restart
findings.detail: Resume is restricted to baseline, initial and rebase purposes. Targeted retries use baseline-retry-targeted or regression-retry-targeted, so a restart rejects their matching durable handle, cancels the running job and starts the stage over. The new restart tests cover only baseline, initial and rebase, leaving this requested behavior untested.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the matching targeted job, and add a restart test that verifies the same job completes and its command runs once.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running a regression-retry-targeted check at the same SHA; the resumed stage cancels that job instead of attaching to it.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires `pending.purpose === purpose && ["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`, excluding `regression-retry-targeted`. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 resumes with purpose `"initial"`, while line 1595 assigns targeted retries purpose `"regression-retry-targeted"`. Rejection calls `await cancelGateExecution(...)` at src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:36.
verification.trigger: The daemon restarts while an executor runs a targeted retry at the same SHA. Resume rejects and cancels that job rather than receiving its result, repeating gate work.

findings.title: Executor liveness has no heartbeat freshness check
findings.detail: Executor availability is determined only by whether the recorded PID and birth time still match. The executor table has no heartbeat timestamp, so a live but stalled executor remains available indefinitely. New jobs are sent to it until pickup timeout, and waitStopped can wait indefinitely for a stalled owner after cancellation. The tests cover a dead PID and a release mismatch but never a live executor whose heartbeat stops.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and test a live but unresponsive executor for both fallback and cancellation behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops servicing jobs; the daemon treats it as fresh and a cancellation can remain blocked waiting for its acknowledgement.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:354–359 reads executor identity and release, then returns `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`, without checking heartbeat freshness. src/gates/lan.ts:105 cancellation awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id)`; src/db/workers.ts:370–384 keeps sleeping while that executor identity exists.
verification.trigger: A running executor's event loop hangs while its PID and birth remain valid. Cancellation changes the job state but cannot obtain acknowledgement, leaving cancellation blocked indefinitely.

findings.title: Pickup timeout test does not exercise in-process fallback
findings.detail: The pickup test stops after asserting that sweep marks an unclaimed job failed. It never attaches through the gate executor or verifies that the check subsequently runs locally and returns its result, so a regression in the failed-job fallback path would pass.
findings.suggestion: Add a test that leaves an in-place job unclaimed, advances through pickup expiry, and asserts the local check executes and its GateRun is returned.
findings.failure_scenario: The sweep marks the job failed, but the attach loop fails to launch or return the in-process fallback; the existing test still passes.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:319–323 only enqueues, sweeps and asserts `state` is `"failed"` and `attempt` is `1`. It never attaches or awaits a GateRun. The fallback it leaves untested is src/gates/lan.ts:138–139: `await local.start(request, controller.signal)` and `local.attach(...)`, followed at line 152 by `return start ? start.context(fallback) : fallback();`.
verification.trigger: An unpicked in-place job times out, but pickup-timeout attachment fails to launch or return the local fallback; this test still passes. This is a coverage gap, not proof that fallback currently fails.

findings.title: Executor tests replace the confinement they need to verify
findings.detail: The subprocess explicitly installs a no-op confinement wrapper, and the parent uses fakeConfinement. Consequently the test can pass even if executor gates run without the daemon's required confinement. Existing output and environment assertions do not exercise this boundary.
findings.suggestion: Add a platform-gated real confinement probe through the executor that checks both an allowed worktree operation and a denied out-of-scope write.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor launches a gate without its required confinement; every new executor test still passes because the test fixture disables confinement.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:86 wraps every executor subprocess in `confinementScope.run({ verify: async () => {}, wrap: cmd => cmd }, ...)`. src/gates/inplace.ts:28 selects `confinementScope.getStore() ?? seatbeltForPort(cfg.port)`, so these tests replace the production confinement backend with a no-op.
verification.trigger: Executor confinement setup regresses or is omitted; the new executor tests can continue passing because their backend neither verifies confinement nor wraps commands, and they assert no denied operation.

findings.title: Executor output is redacted with an incomplete credential registry
findings.detail: Credential registration is process-local. The executor loads configuration, but it does not register credentials acquired by the daemon at runtime, such as its API token, GitHub token, or worker tokens. Gate output is redacted and truncated in the executor and then written to job events and results using that executor's registry. A credential known only to the daemon can therefore be persisted unredacted, and truncation can prevent the daemon from recognizing it later.
findings.suggestion: Make the executor's redaction policy cover the daemon's dynamically registered credentials before it captures, truncates, or persists gate output.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate prints a daemon-registered API or GitHub token that is absent from the executor's credential registry; the token appears in the stored gate event or result.

verification.evidence: src/util/proc.ts:1216–1218 keeps credentials in process-local sets. Daemon-only registration includes src/server/api-token.ts:10, `registerCredential("LIMITLESS_API_TOKEN", token)`, and src/integrations/github-token.ts:18, `registerCredential("GH_TOKEN", token)`. The executor entry point at src/cli/main.ts:426 calls `runInplaceExecutor(loadConfig(), sha, controller.signal)`; config registration at src/config.ts:264–267 covers provider keys. src/gates/inplace.ts:65 sends results directly to `workers.event`; src/db/workers.ts:612–613 persists `this.sanitize(event)`, whose filters use that process's registry.
verification.trigger: A check prints a daemon-registered token absent from the executor's registry and private-string policy. Executor redaction does not recognize it and stores it in gate_jobs events/result before any daemon-side redaction.

findings.title: A live but stalled executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only the PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor process remains alive but stops polling or renewing, the daemon continues to consider it available. For a leased job, waitStopped also waits indefinitely for that same process instead of reaching a confirmed-stop recovery path.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for a stale owner.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process stalls while running a gate and remains alive. Its lease expires, but the daemon waits indefinitely for stopped to become 1 and cannot fall back or start the next gate.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:671–672 fails an expired in-place lease. However, :366 loops while `stopped === 0`, and :370 permits recovery only if the executor is absent; :359 tests only process birth identity. src/gates/lan.ts:131 awaits this loop before running the fallback.
verification.trigger: An executor stalls permanently during a gate without exiting. Its lease expires, but the still-existing process prevents recovery and stopped remains zero, blocking fallback and the next gate.

findings.title: Worktree exclusivity check races with job creation
findings.detail: The scan for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations with awaits between them. Two concurrent starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue distinct jobs, which separate executor processes can lease simultaneously. This defeats the required one-job-per-worktree guarantee.
findings.suggestion: Serialize reservation and enqueue for a worktree with an atomic database constraint or transaction, retaining the reservation until process cleanup is confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: Two gate starts for the same cwd run concurrently while two executors are available. Both pass the empty-job scan, enqueue, and execute checks in the same worktree at once.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:54-60 scans existing jobs with "workers.jobs(...)" and waits for them; line 72 then yields at "await releaseGateSlotScope()". The new row is created later at lines 80-81: "workers.enqueue(req, handle.id, true)". src/db/workers.ts:390-402 leases queued jobs using "WHERE id=? AND state='queued'", without checking other jobs' worktrees.
verification.trigger: Two concurrent starts for the same cwd both finish the empty-job scan before either attaches and enqueues. Two executors can then lease the distinct jobs and run checks simultaneously in that worktree, violating exclusivity and risking incorrect gate results.

findings.title: Restart discards running retry jobs
findings.detail: The request says that a resumed stage whose handle matches its stage, round, purpose, and SHA attaches to it, and explicitly includes the targeted retry. This allowlist rejects timeout and regression retry purposes even when all of those fields match. The stage’s initial resume check also cancels a recorded retry before it can be attached.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage state to resume the recorded retry, and validate its matching handle without restricting resumption to the first execution.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor runs `regression-retry-targeted`; the resumed stage cancels that job and repeats earlier gates instead of receiving the retry result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 calls `resumeGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", cwd, env)` before initial gates run at line 1547. Targeted retries use `"regression-retry-targeted"` at line 1595. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 rejects the purpose mismatch; lines 36–43 cancel the job and persist removal of its handle.
verification.trigger: A restart occurs during a long targeted retry. The resumed stage cancels the surviving retry and repeats initial gates rather than attaching to the existing job.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness
findings.detail: The request requires a fresh executor heartbeat and says the sweep applies freshness timers against it. Executor records contain only process identity and release, so a live but stalled executor remains available indefinitely. After a leased job expires, `waitStopped` also waits indefinitely while that process remains alive, preventing fallback.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a safe way to confirm its job processes have stopped when the executor stops responding.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops responding while a gate is running. The lease expires, yet the daemon waits indefinitely for `stopped=1` rather than completing the gate or safely failing over.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 accepts an executor when `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`; there is no freshness timestamp check. At :366–384, waitStopped has no deadline and does not recover while that identity exists. src/gates/lan.ts:130–138 waits for stopped before starting local fallback.
verification.trigger: An executor remains alive but ceases servicing its running job and lease renewals. Although the sweep marks the lease failed, the daemon cannot finish or fall back while waiting indefinitely for stopped=1.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local repositories
findings.detail: The request says that when the executor is enabled and alive, the daemon’s local gate path creates an in-place job. With `[gates] executor = "lan"`, this branch always selects the LAN executor, whose fallback for repositories outside `workers.repos` runs directly in the daemon regardless of `[executor] enabled`.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor’s local fallback through the enabled in-place executor while retaining LAN dispatch for configured repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator uses LAN gates for one repository and enables the local executor; a different repository’s local gate still runs in the daemon and is lost on restart.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:77-81 applies the opt-in only under `case "local": return inplace && workers ? lanExecutor(workers, [], true) : localExecutor();`; `case "lan"` always returns `lanExecutor(workers, repos)`. src/gates/lan.ts:71 then routes repositories outside the LAN allowlist directly in-process: `else if (!repos.includes(req.repo)) return local.start(req, signal);`.
verification.trigger: Set `[gates] executor = "lan"`, allowlist repository A in workers.repos, and enable `[executor] enabled` with a healthy executor. Gates for repository B, outside the allowlist, run in the daemon instead of the in-place executor; a daemon restart interrupts them and repeats the work.

findings.title: Resume accepts jobs without a held lease
findings.detail: The request states, “A job is only re-attached while the executor still holds its lease.” `canResume` also accepts queued jobs and completed jobs without checking a held lease. This deviates from the requested restart boundary.
findings.suggestion: Require a current executor-held lease for reattachment, or explicitly define and implement a separate completed-result recovery rule.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after saving a handle while the job is still queued; the resumed stage reattaches to that unleased job instead of starting fresh.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:35-40 explicitly accepts "j.state === 'queued' ? !!workers.executor()", requiring a held, unexpired lease only in the alternative leased branch. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:26-34 preserves a matching handle when "executor?.canResume?.(pending.handle, env)" succeeds.
verification.trigger: The daemon restarts after enqueueing a job but before an executor leases it. With a same-release executor alive and matching stage, round, purpose, environment and SHA, resume retains and attaches to the queued job despite its having no held lease. This violates the requested lease-only resume condition; additional harm is not demonstrated.

candidates.title: Rollback to an older daemon does not stop the executor
candidates.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the persistent `executor.daemonRelease` setting. candidates.suggestion: Use a coordinator release and liveness mechanism that also detects replacement by a daemon that does not write this setting, and stop the executor's jobs before the older daemon can resume them.
candidates.failure_scenario: A new-release in-place gate is running when the daemon is rolled back to the base release. The old daemon leaves the setting unchanged and starts its own recovery or gate while the executor continues.

With `[gates] executor = "lan"`, this branch always selects the LAN executor, whose fallback for repositories outside `workers.repos` runs directly in the daemon regardless of `[executor] enabled`.
candidates.suggestion: Route the LAN executor’s local fallback through the enabled in-place executor while retaining LAN dispatch for configured repositories.
candidates.failure_scenario: A coordinator uses LAN gates for one repository and enables the local executor; a different repository’s local gate still runs in the daemon and is lost on restart.

candidates.title: Resume accepts jobs without a held lease
candidates.detail: The request states, “A job is only re-attached while the executor still holds its lease.” `canResume` also accepts queued jobs and completed jobs without checking a held lease. This deviates from the requested restart boundary.
candidates.suggestion: Require a current executor-held lease for reattachment, or explicitly define and implement a separate completed-result recovery rule.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after saving a handle while the job is still queued; the resumed stage reattaches to that unleased job instead of starting fresh.

verdicts.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:39 checks only `store.getSetting("executor.daemonRelease", "") !== releaseSha`; lines 52–57 otherwise renew the lease. The setting is written by the newly added src/cli/daemon.ts:50: `factory.store.setSetting("executor.daemonRelease", factory.bootSha)`. At base, src/cli/daemon.ts:49 instead proceeds directly to `detachSlots = await attachSlotPools(...)`, with no release-setting update.
verdicts.trigger: Roll back to the base daemon while an executor gate runs. The persisted setting still names the executor's release, so the executor continues renewing and running despite the daemon release changing.

verdicts.evidence: src/harness/sandbox.ts:282 awaits `backend.verify(roots, opts, run)`, allowing verification errors to propagate. src/gates/inplace.ts:70–71 catches every error and calls `workers.fail(job.id, redactCredentials(String(error)))`. src/gates/lan.ts:130–150 handles any failed job by running `local.start(request, controller.signal)` and returning `workers.sanitize(run)`, without preserving a confinement verdict.
verdicts.trigger: Executor confinement verification throws, then daemon-local verification succeeds. The failed job is retried locally and can return a passing GateRun; the original confinement failure remains only as failure metadata, rather than blocking or affecting the returned verdict.

verdicts.evidence: src/util/proc.ts:1216–1218 keeps credentials in process-local sets. Daemon-only registration includes src/server/api-token.ts:10, `registerCredential("LIMITLESS_API_TOKEN", token)`, and src/integrations/github-token.ts:18, `registerCredential("GH_TOKEN", token)`. The executor entry point at src/cli/main.ts:426 calls `runInplaceExecutor(loadConfig(), sha, controller.signal)`; config registration at src/config.ts:264–267 covers provider keys. src/gates/inplace.ts:65 sends results directly to `workers.event`; src/db/workers.ts:612–613 persists `this.sanitize(event)`, whose filters use that process's registry.
verdicts.trigger: A check prints a daemon-registered token absent from the executor's registry and private-string policy. Executor redaction does not recognize it and stores it in gate_jobs events/result before any daemon-side redaction.

verdicts.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 names the retry purpose `options?.targeted ? "regression-retry-targeted" : "regression-retry"`. On stage resume, src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 calls `resumeGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", cwd, env)`. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires `pending.purpose === purpose && ["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`; failure invokes `await cancelGateExecution(...)` at line 36 and clears the handle at line 42.
verdicts.trigger: The daemon restarts during a running in-place targeted retry, with unchanged stage, round, SHA and release. The resumed gate stage requests purpose `initial`, cancels the saved targeted job, and repeats earlier gate work instead of attaching.

verdicts.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 uses purpose `"regression-retry-targeted"`. Resume enters through `resumeGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", cwd, env)` at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires `pending.purpose === purpose` and restricts purposes to `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"]`; lines 35–42 cancel and clear a rejected handle.
verdicts.trigger: A restart interrupts attachment to a running targeted retry. Despite matching SHA and a live executor lease, the resumed stage rejects its purpose, cancels it, and reruns initial gates.

verdicts.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires `pending.purpose === purpose && ["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`, excluding `regression-retry-targeted`. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 resumes with purpose `"initial"`, while line 1595 assigns targeted retries purpose `"regression-retry-targeted"`. Rejection calls `await cancelGateExecution(...)` at src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:36.
verdicts.trigger: The daemon restarts while an executor runs a targeted retry at the same SHA. Resume rejects and cancels that job rather than receiving its result, repeating gate work.

verdicts.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 calls `resumeGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", cwd, env)` before initial gates run at line 1547. Targeted retries use `"regression-retry-targeted"` at line 1595. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 rejects the purpose mismatch; lines 36–43 cancel the job and persist removal of its handle.
verdicts.trigger: A restart occurs during a long targeted retry. The resumed stage cancels the surviving retry and repeats initial gates rather than attaching to the existing job.

verdicts.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 checks only `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. At :366–384, `while (this.job(id)?.stopped === 0)` performs recovery only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`; otherwise it sleeps without a deadline. src/gates/lan.ts:131 awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)` before fallback.
verdicts.trigger: A leased executor stalls indefinitely while its process identity remains valid. Lease expiry fails the job, but waitStopped never finishes, blocking fallback and subsequent gates in that worktree.

verdicts.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:671–672 calls `this.fail(j.id, "Lease expired")`, but :630 updates only `state='failed',failure_reason=?,updated_at=?`. At :370, recovery requires `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`, while :359 defines executor liveness solely as `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. src/gates/lan.ts:131 waits for stopped before fallback.
verdicts.trigger: An executor stops renewing a running job but remains alive. The sweep fails the expired lease, yet stopped remains zero and the daemon waits indefinitely instead of falling back.

verdicts.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:354–359 reads executor identity and release, then returns `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`, without checking heartbeat freshness. src/gates/lan.ts:105 cancellation awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id)`; src/db/workers.ts:370–384 keeps sleeping while that executor identity exists.
verdicts.trigger: A running executor's event loop hangs while its PID and birth remain valid. Cancellation changes the job state but cannot obtain acknowledgement, leaving cancellation blocked indefinitely.

verdicts.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:671–672 fails an expired in-place lease. However, :366 loops while `stopped === 0`, and :370 permits recovery only if the executor is absent; :359 tests only process birth identity. src/gates/lan.ts:131 awaits this loop before running the fallback.
verdicts.trigger: An executor stalls permanently during a gate without exiting. Its lease expires, but the still-existing process prevents recovery and stopped remains zero, blocking fallback and the next gate.

verdicts.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 accepts an executor when `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`; there is no freshness timestamp check. At :366–384, waitStopped has no deadline and does not recover while that identity exists. src/gates/lan.ts:130–138 waits for stopped before starting local fallback.
verdicts.trigger: An executor remains alive but ceases servicing its running job and lease renewals. Although the sweep marks the lease failed, the daemon cannot finish or fall back while waiting indefinitely for stopped=1.

verdicts.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:319–323 only enqueues, sweeps and asserts `state` is `"failed"` and `attempt` is `1`. It never attaches or awaits a GateRun. The fallback it leaves untested is src/gates/lan.ts:138–139: `await local.start(request, controller.signal)` and `local.attach(...)`, followed at line 152 by `return start ? start.context(fallback) : fallback();`.
verdicts.trigger: An unpicked in-place job times out, but pickup-timeout attachment fails to launch or return the local fallback; this test still passes. This is a coverage gap, not proof that fallback currently fails.

verdicts.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:86 wraps every executor subprocess in `confinementScope.run({ verify: async () => {}, wrap: cmd => cmd }, ...)`. src/gates/inplace.ts:28 selects `confinementScope.getStore() ?? seatbeltForPort(cfg.port)`, so these tests replace the production confinement backend with a no-op.
verdicts.trigger: Executor confinement setup regresses or is omitted; the new executor tests can continue passing because their backend neither verifies confinement nor wraps commands, and they assert no denied operation.

verdicts.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:54-60 scans existing jobs with "workers.jobs(...)" and waits for them; line 72 then yields at "await releaseGateSlotScope()". The new row is created later at lines 80-81: "workers.enqueue(req, handle.id, true)". src/db/workers.ts:390-402 leases queued jobs using "WHERE id=? AND state='queued'", without checking other jobs' worktrees.
verdicts.trigger: Two concurrent starts for the same cwd both finish the empty-job scan before either attaches and enqueues. Two executors can then lease the distinct jobs and run checks simultaneously in that worktree, violating exclusivity and risking incorrect gate results.

verdicts.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:35-40 explicitly accepts "j.state === 'queued' ? !!workers.executor()", requiring a held, unexpired lease only in the alternative leased branch. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:26-34 preserves a matching handle when "executor?.canResume?.(pending.handle, env)" succeeds.
verdicts.trigger: The daemon restarts after enqueueing a job but before an executor leases it. With a same-release executor alive and matching stage, round, purpose, environment and SHA, resume retains and attaches to the queued job despite its having no held lease. This violates the requested lease-only resume condition; additional harm is not demonstrated.

verdicts.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:77-81 applies the opt-in only under `case "local": return inplace && workers ? lanExecutor(workers, [], true) : localExecutor();`; `case "lan"` always returns `lanExecutor(workers, repos)`. src/gates/lan.ts:71 then routes repositories outside the LAN allowlist directly in-process: `else if (!repos.includes(req.repo)) return local.start(req, signal);`.
verdicts.trigger: Set `[gates] executor = "lan"`, allowlist repository A in workers.repos, and enable `[executor] enabled` with a healthy executor. Gates for repository B, outside the allowlist, run in the daemon instead of the in-place executor; a daemon restart interrupts them and repeats the work.

findings.title: Key validation does not enforce the required owner and mode
findings.detail: The startup check accepts any regular file with the owner-read bit set and no group or world permission bits. It does not check the file's owner, and it accepts modes such as 0700 and 0400 despite requiring mode 0600. A file owned by another user can therefore pass the metadata check even when the daemon cannot read it, deferring failure until a configured repository first needs a token.
findings.suggestion: Check the file owner and enforce the requested mode and readability during configuration loading, with a clear startup error.
findings.failure_scenario: A key file owned by another user has mode 0600. Its metadata passes this check, but the daemon cannot read it and App-authenticated GitHub calls fail later.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:390 uses only `key = statSync(privateKeyPath)`; src/config.ts:394 checks `!key.isFile() || (key.mode & 0o077) !== 0 || !(key.mode & 0o400)`, without checking effective readability. src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64 later calls `readFileSync(app.privateKeyPath)` and :67 reports `cannot read or sign with private key`.
verification.trigger: A stat-accessible mode-0600 key owned by another user passes startup validation, but an unprivileged daemon cannot read it; subsequent App GitHub calls fail.

findings.title: Verify the key is readable by the factory at startup
findings.detail: The permission check inspects mode bits but does not check the file owner or whether the daemon can actually read the file. A mode-0600 key owned by another user passes configuration loading, then fails only when the first App operation tries to read it. The check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 despite requiring mode 0600.
findings.suggestion: Verify the file belongs to the running user, is readable, and has the required mode before accepting the configuration.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured key is a regular mode-0600 file owned by another user. Startup succeeds, but every GitHub operation for an App repository later fails with `cannot read or sign with private key`.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:390 performs `statSync(privateKeyPath)` and :394 validates metadata only. The first key read is `readFileSync(app.privateKeyPath)` at src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64, whose failure produces `cannot read or sign with private key` at :67.
verification.trigger: Configure a regular mode-0600 key that the daemon can stat but cannot read. Startup accepts it instead of refusing, and App GitHub operations fail later.

findings.title: Key validation does not enforce the required mode or ownership
findings.detail: The mode check accepts owner execute bits, so a key with mode 0700 passes despite the required mode 0600. It also never checks that the file belongs to the process owner, so a mode-0600 file owned by another user can pass startup validation even when the daemon cannot read it. The failure then occurs later during token acquisition instead of at startup.
findings.suggestion: Validate the required file mode and ownership, and confirm the file is readable during startup.
findings.failure_scenario: Configure a regular private-key file with mode 0700, or a mode-0600 file owned by another user. Configuration loads instead of refusing with the key-file reason.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:394 checks `(key.mode & 0o077) !== 0` and `!(key.mode & 0o400)`, allowing mode 0700 and never checking `key.uid` or actual readability. src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64 defers reading the key until authentication.
verification.trigger: Mode 0700 passes despite the stated mode requirement. More materially, another user's unreadable mode-0600 key passes startup and causes subsequent App authentication failures.

findings.title: Key validation tests omit owner-only executable mode and ownership
findings.detail: The permission cases cover group and world bits but do not exercise a mode such as 0700 or a file owned by another user. Consequently they pass with the incomplete startup validation and do not catch the underlying key-file defect.
findings.suggestion: Add a regression case for mode 0700 and a controlled ownership or stat fixture for a key owned by another user, asserting startup refusal.
findings.failure_scenario: A change that checks only group and world permission bits while ignoring owner execute bits and file ownership passes the current key permission tests.

verification.evidence: test/github-app.test.ts:102–104 tests only `test.each([0o644, 0o640, 0o601])`, followed by an expectation that config throws. Fixtures use `writeFileSync(keyPath, pem, { mode: 0o600 })` (line 43), with no ownership variation. src/config.ts:394 validates `!key.isFile() || (key.mode & 0o077) !== 0 || !(key.mode & 0o400)`; this ignores owner execute permission and file ownership.
verification.trigger: Validation accepts an owner-executable key such as mode 0700, or ignores file ownership, while all existing key-permission tests still pass because they exercise only group/world permission violations on a fixture owned by the test process.

findings.title: An App key outside the config directory can be exposed to agents
findings.detail: The configuration accepts any absolute key path, but the agent read policy automatically denies the config directory, not the configured key file. A key placed in a repository checkout or another agent-readable location can therefore be read by an agent or gate despite the requirement that the key never reach them.
findings.suggestion: Restrict the key to a protected location or add its canonical path to every agent and gate read-deny policy, including aliases.
findings.failure_scenario: The operator configures `private_key_path` to a mode-0600 file in a checkout. An agent running as the same user can read that file through its permitted checkout access.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:387 accepts `resolve(configDir, a.private_key_path)`, including absolute checkout paths. src/harness/read-policy.ts:42 adds `denyRead: Object.freeze([...paths("deny_read"), configDir])`, without adding the App key. src/harness/codex.ts:321 grants `["/", "read"]`, with exclusions supplied through `denyRead` at :324.
verification.trigger: Configure a mode-0600 key in an agent-accessible checkout outside existing denied paths. Startup accepts it and the same-user agent can read the private key; its configured path receives no automatic protection.

findings.title: Key validation does not verify the file owner or required mode
findings.detail: The check accepts any owner-readable file with no group or world permission, including mode 0400 or 0700, and never checks its UID. It therefore does not enforce the requested owner-owned, mode-0600 key file; in particular, a file owned by another account can pass validation where the daemon has elevated access.
findings.suggestion: Check the file's owner against the daemon's effective UID and enforce the requested permission bits, with a clear startup error.
findings.failure_scenario: A regular key file owned by a different UID with mode 0600 is readable by an elevated daemon; startup accepts it even though the daemon does not own the file.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:390 obtains file metadata, but :394 checks only `key.isFile()` and permission bits; no UID comparison occurs before the configuration is accepted at :409: `githubApp = { appId, installationId, privateKeyPath, repos: ... }`.
verification.trigger: An elevated daemon accepts a regular mode-0600 key owned by another UID. The alleged daemon-ownership restriction is unenforced, although this scenario does not itself demonstrate unreadability or secret disclosure.

findings.title: Manual landing bypasses the configured App identity
findings.detail: The request requires “one implementation used by every factory gh invocation for a repository” and says configured repositories use the App without fallback. The manual landing script invokes this checker for its merge, but the checker calls sh directly and never loads or configures the identity provider. Its merge therefore uses the owner's gh login even when the repository is configured for the App; its PR reads and the direct gh calls in land-pr.sh have the same gap.
findings.suggestion: Load the configured identity in the manual landing path and route its repository-scoped gh calls through the shared provider, including the calls made directly by land-pr.sh.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator runs scripts/land-pr.sh for an App-configured repository: the PR is merged as the owner, and an App token exchange failure cannot stop that merge.

verification.evidence: scripts/land-pr.sh:153 invokes `check_private "$pr" "$repo" --merge "$sha"`. That path in scripts/check-private-strings.ts:55–56 constructs `["gh", "pr", "merge", pr, "-R", repo, "--squash", "--delete-branch"]` and executes it with `await sh([...merge, "--subject", title, "--body", data.body, "--match-head-commit", sha], opts)`. It neither loads App configuration nor uses `githubSh`. src/util/proc.ts:1184 supplies `env: opts.env ?? (process.env as Record<string, string>)`, so the merge uses the inherited owner's authentication.
verification.trigger: With the repository configured for the App and the operator authenticated as the owner, running scripts/land-pr.sh merges as the owner. No App token exchange occurs, so an exchange failure cannot block the merge.

findings.title: Startup accepts a key file that the daemon cannot read
findings.detail: The request says the key must be “a regular file readable only by its owner (mode 0600), or startup refuses.” This check examines permission bits but neither verifies the file's owner nor checks actual readability. A mode-0600 file owned by another user passes configuration validation even though the daemon cannot read it; startup succeeds and GitHub operations fail later. It also accepts owner-executable modes such as 0700 despite the stated mode requirement.
findings.suggestion: Validate ownership and actual readability at startup, and enforce the requested permission mode.
findings.failure_scenario: private_key_path points to a regular mode-0600 file owned by another user: loadConfig succeeds, then the first App operation fails while reading the key.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:390 calls `key = statSync(privateKeyPath)`, and src/config.ts:394 checks only `!key.isFile() || (key.mode & 0o077) !== 0 || !(key.mode & 0o400)`. Neither verifies ownership or actual readability. The first read occurs in src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64: `readFileSync(app.privateKeyPath)`, whose failure becomes `cannot read or sign with private key` at lines 65–68.
verification.trigger: Configure a stat-accessible regular file with mode 0600 owned by another user and unreadable by the daemon. Configuration accepts it instead of refusing startup; the first App operation fails when reading the key.

findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next poll; reconciliation sees the resumed status and never posts the required reason. Similarly, a failed started-comment write can delay processing until after needs_human has ended.

findings.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint

The code does not verify the comment author or exact body, although issue comments are untrusted data. A third party can therefore make the reconciler mark a failed write as done without the factory ever posting the required comment.

findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101-102 constructs the event only from current status: `if (run.status === "needs_human") events.set("needs_human", ...)`. findings.title: Restart-between-effects coverage exercises only the start event
findings.detail: The restart test interrupts the initial in-progress label and started comment. Consequently, regressions in recovery between a needs-you, failed, cancellation, or merge label change and its associated comment are not covered as requested.
findings.suggestion: Exercise interruption during each applicable lifecycle transition, then restart and assert the final label set and exactly one corresponding comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change loses a failed comment after the failed label is written and the daemon restarts; the existing restart test still passes because it covers only the started event.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1275 parameterizes only interruption point: `test.each(["after label", "after comment"])`; its assertions at :1295–1298 require `limitless:in-progress` and `comment:started`. findings.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments

The private-string check detects encoded private-string entries, but registered credentials are not necessarily entries in that list. A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
findings.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
findings.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:134-148 applies `redactCredentials(...)` directly to the encoded body, then checks only `loadPrivateStrings(...)`; line 163 posts that body. src/util/proc.ts:1234-1236 registers literal and JSON-escaped credential variants, without percent decoding. src/gates/publication.ts:76 checks `publicationMatches(text, entries)[0]`, whose entries here come exclusively from private-strings.txt.
verification.trigger: A failure reason contains a percent-encoded registered token whose literal form is absent from private-strings.txt. Literal credential redaction misses it, the private-string check passes, and the public comment exposes the recoverable token.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint

findings.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 builds the predictable marker `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:${run.id}:${event} -->`. candidates.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to configured queue repositories
candidates.detail: The lifecycle reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and it is not started when the issue queue is disabled. The request requires updates for runs started through CLI, MCP, label, and comment paths as well as the queue; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue selection.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover all repositories for which linked runs can be created.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #123` targets a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos; it receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
candidates.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority application, even when that label is no longer present. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label that predates the failure, so the two checks together do not establish that a current priority label was re-applied after failure.
candidates.suggestion: Require the post-failure event to be the latest trusted application of a currently present approved priority label.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:2 from before failure. A trusted user applies and then removes priority:1 after failure; the historical priority:1 event permits the issue to be picked using the stale priority:2 label.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-configured repositories
candidates.detail: The request covers “any start path: queue, `limitless run` with `Closes #n`, MCP, label or comment trigger.” Reconciliation skips repositories outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. Consequently, runs started through those other paths receive no lifecycle labels or the required comments unless their repository also happens to be configured for the issue queue.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and apply it to linked issues from all supported start paths.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #7` starts in a repository with no issue-queue configuration; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

candidates.title: Transient lifecycle events are lost between polls
candidates.detail: The request requires each label change and comment to be a recorded side effect with a durable checkpoint. Here needs-human, failed, and cancelled events are discovered only from the current status. If a run enters and leaves one of those states before a poll observes it, no effect is recorded and its comment is permanently lost. The initial in-progress label can likewise be skipped if the run reaches a later state before its first poll.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the corresponding transitions occur, then reconcile each recorded effect independently of the current status.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the reconciler never posts the needs-you reason or applies its label.

candidates.title: Repeated needs-human episodes share one comment checkpoint
candidates.detail: The comment effect is keyed only by run and event name. Once `comment:needs_human` is done, a later needs-human transition in the same resumed run is suppressed, including its new reason. The request requires a comment when a run reaches needs_human, and the second episode is a distinct transition.
candidates.suggestion: Key lifecycle effects by a durable transition or status-episode identifier.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run asks for human help, resumes after an answer, then needs human help again for a different reason; only the first reason is posted.

candidates.title: A failed label write can allow a failed CLI issue to be picked
candidates.detail: A lifecycle write failure is caught and queue selection continues, but `latestIssueRun` only finds runs with an issue source reference. A failed CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` has no such reference. Until the failed label is successfully written, the queue therefore sees neither the failure label nor that latest failed run and can select the issue without re-approval.
candidates.suggestion: Include all linked-issue runs in the existing eligibility/admission evidence, including runs linked through their prompt.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails, the GitHub failed-label write errors, and the issue still has its previously approved priority label; the same poll can create a queue run for it.

candidates.title: Re-approval in the same timestamp second is rejected
candidates.detail: The requirement specifies the labeled events' order and actor. Comparing parsed timestamps with strict greater-than rejects a trusted priority event that follows the failure event but has the same timestamp precision, even though the timeline preserves their order.
candidates.suggestion: Use the ordered timeline events to determine whether a trusted priority application follows the failure event, including ties in timestamps.
candidates.failure_scenario: GitHub records the failure label and a subsequent trusted priority label with the same second in `createdAt`; the issue remains ineligible.
