findings.title: Admission can re-pick a failed issue before its failure label is written
findings.detail: If the failure-label write fails or is deferred, the issue has no current failed label. Eligibility then falls back to accepting any trusted priority application after finishedAt, even though the required failure-label application has not happened. Reconciliation errors are nonfatal and admission proceeds in the same poll.
findings.suggestion: Keep a failed run ineligible until its failure label is confirmed and a trusted priority application follows that label.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, its label write encounters a GitHub error, and a trusted user reapplies priority before the next poll. The queue can start another run without any approval after the failure label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:117–123 uses `context.latest.status === "failed" && failed ? reapprovedAfterFailure ... : events.some(...)`, allowing approval after finishedAt when the failure label is absent. Admission reuses this same logic at src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:265–269. Label-write errors are logged without stopping selection (src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:227–234; src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:203–204).
verification.trigger: A failed run has no remaining in-progress label, its failure-label write fails, and a trusted user reapplies priority after completion. If the failure label remains unwritten through reconciliation, admission permits another run despite no approval after the failure label.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies use fixed text and never include the run's reason, although the request requires a comment with the reason. The tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent, so they encode the defect rather than catch it.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, and test both safe and sensitive reasons.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a safe error such as "typecheck failed"; the issue comment only says "failed: see" and links to the UI.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 constructs only `needs you: see ${link}.` and `failed: see ${link}.`; line 95 wraps that fixed text with the run id. Neither comment includes the run's reason.
verification.trigger: A run fails with a safe reason such as "typecheck failed", or reaches needs_human with an actionable reason; its issue notification omits that reason.

findings.title: A blocked publication is marked done without posting the required fallback
findings.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done and no comment is posted. The request requires a fixed safe message in this case. The test at test/issue-queue.test.ts:1559 explicitly expects suppression, so it asserts the wrong behavior.
findings.suggestion: Construct and validate a fixed fallback message, post it when the original text is blocked, and test that it is posted exactly once.
findings.failure_scenario: A lifecycle comment contains a configured private string; its checkpoint becomes done and the issue never receives the corresponding notification.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:98–100 handles a blocked body by calling `save(effect, "done")` and logging. Line 87 prevents later regeneration: `if (effects.has(effect)) continue;`. No fallback body is queued.
verification.trigger: A configured private string matches a lifecycle comment; the checkpoint becomes done and the issue receives no corresponding notification. This duplicates C7.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled for runs outside the issue queue configuration
findings.detail: Lifecycle management requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos and the queue to have trusted accounts. findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` for a repository that is not enabled in the issue queue; no label or comment is written.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:11–13 defines lifecycleManaged as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; lines 109–110 call `observe(run, repo, number)` only when lifecycleManaged is true, and line 116 applies the same filter to delivery. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:156 returns immediately without queue configuration: `if (!q?.repos.length || !q.trusted.length) return () => {};`.

findings.title: Transitions between polls can be lost

findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you label or comment.

findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a non-sensitive error such as a failed build. The issue comment says only that the run failed and does not tell the watcher why.

findings.title: Polling snapshots lose lifecycle transitions between polls

This branch immediately marks confirmed ownership lost and clears the intent, bypassing the malformed-record and generation checks used for the initial read. findings.title: Release-intent replay bypasses lease-time validation
findings.detail: Reconciliation delegates a pending release to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which can replay the release with `client.write` without a GitHub-time sample or `beforeSend` predicate. Both startup recovery and ordinary operations use that path, so an expired generation can mutate the claim after its lease window has closed.
findings.suggestion: Ensure release replay uses the same fresh time decision and send-time revalidation as other same-generation writes.
findings.failure_scenario: A release intent is journaled, the process stops before sending it, and recovery runs more than ten minutes later while the old tip remains current. Recovery writes the expired generation's release without checking whether it is renewable.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:65 calls `await recoverLeases({ client, store })`; line 89 calls `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)`. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113–121 replays a release when the old tip matches confirmed ownership using `client.write(repo, ref, read.tip, intent.record, { signal, onCommit: ... })`, with no time check or `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206 makes that guard optional: `const allowed = opts.beforeSend?.();`.
verification.trigger: Restart with a journaled release whose before SHA still matches the confirmed tip, after that generation has expired. Recovery sends the release without establishing renewability or validating time before send.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
findings.detail: The loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes applied in this manager instance. Confirmed held rows loaded at startup, and acquisitions confirmed by intent reconciliation, never enter that map. Even if `active` would accept their handles, the loop never renews them.
findings.suggestion: Enumerate confirmed held rows when starting or reconciling and make their handles available to the renewal loop.
findings.failure_scenario: A manager restarts with a confirmed held lease and starts the loop. Every tick skips that lease; it expires even though the associated run is active.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 initializes `const handles = new Map<string, LeaseHandle>()`. Recovery at line 65 never populates it. Its only insertion is line 192, `handles.set(key(repo, ref), held)`, following a direct applied write. The renewal loop at line 242 iterates only `handles.values()`.
verification.trigger: Create a manager over a store containing a confirmed held lease, then start it with an active run. Without another successful acquisition or mutation, every tick skips the persisted lease and it expires.

findings.title: A different run cannot reconcile an earlier pending acquisition
findings.detail: The cross-run check returns `refused` before reconciliation whenever the existing row has an intent. This violates the requirement to reconcile pending intents before every operation, and prevents the caller from clearing a dropped first acquisition unless a separate loop happens to run.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the existing intent under the mutex before deciding whether the row blocks the requested run.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent on an absent ref and ends. Run B calls `acquire` before the renewal loop is started; it receives `refused` indefinitely even though reconciliation would drop A's intent and allow B to acquire generation 1.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns early: `if (row && row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")) return refused;`. Reconciliation occurs afterward at line 108. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113–116 would drop an acquisition intent when the ref remains absent; leases.ts:91 would then forget the never-confirmed row.
verification.trigger: Run A leaves an unresolved acquisition intent while GitHub still has no ref. Run B repeatedly acquires before the loop starts. Each call returns refused before reconciliation can drop A's intent and unblock B.

findings.title: Reconciled and recovered leases are never registered for renewal
findings.detail: The renewal loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated solely by an immediately applied write. Recovery or later reconciliation can confirm a held acquisition without adding a handle to that map. Confirmed held rows already present when the manager starts are likewise omitted. Those leases therefore receive no periodic renewal even when the active hook would return true.
findings.suggestion: Register confirmed held handles after recovery and successful reconciliation, and ensure the loop can discover existing confirmed held rows.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition returns `unconfirmed`, then the next tick reconciles its intent as applied. The row is held, but no handle is in `handles`, so subsequent ticks never renew it and the lease expires.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:186 returns immediately for `unconfirmed`; handle registration occurs only at line 192 in the direct `applied` branch. The reconciliation wrapper at lines 87–92 never registers a handle. Lines 240–242 reconcile pending rows, then renew only `handles.values()`.
verification.trigger: An initial acquisition applies remotely but returns unconfirmed. A later tick reconciles it as applied, leaving a confirmed held row without a registered handle. Subsequent ticks skip renewal even when the active hook would accept that lease.

findings.title: A different run bypasses reconciliation of a pending intent
findings.detail: The cross-run early return occurs before reconciliation. The request requires every operation to reconcile pending intents first and return `wait` while an intent remains unresolved. Here a failed first acquisition by run A can leave an intent that run B never attempts to settle, so B is refused even when reconciliation would drop the intent and permit acquisition.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the row before applying the cross-run ownership check, then re-read the row and decide whether it can be forgotten or must be refused.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A has a pending acquisition intent on an absent ref and ends. Run B calls acquire before the renewal loop has reconciled it; the manager returns `refused: live` without checking GitHub or dropping A's abandoned intent.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 checks `row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")` and returns `refused` before line 108's `await reconcile(repo, ref, signal)`. Thus a different run's pending intent prevents any GitHub reconciliation on this path.
verification.trigger: Run B acquires a ref with run A's pending acquisition intent before the loop reconciles it. B receives refused: live, even when reconciliation would discover an absent ref, drop A's intent, and permit acquisition.

findings.title: A second moved result marks ownership lost without checking for supersession
findings.detail: After two moved outcomes that are not classified as same-holder writes, the code marks any confirmed row lost regardless of the moved tip's generation or identity. The invariant permits loss only when a moved record supersedes confirmed ownership. A malformed tip or an older-generation tip does not establish that the confirmed generation was superseded.
findings.suggestion: Classify the second moved tip against the confirmed generation and identity before marking the row lost; preserve ownership when supersession is not established.
findings.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation 2 write encounters two moved responses whose tips are malformed or generation 1. The manager marks generation 2 lost and calls `onLost` despite having no superseding record.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:201–208 checks only same-holder equality before counting moves: `if (mine) continue; if (++moved < 2) continue; if (row?.confirmed && row.runId === want.run) { lose(row, result.tip);`. Lines 60–62 persist loss and invoke `onLost`, without validating that this tip supersedes the confirmed generation.
verification.trigger: Two writes encounter non-same-holder moved tips, with a valid ownership read between attempts. Even if the second tip is malformed or an older generation, confirmed ownership is marked lost.

findings.title: An exception in one renewal tick rejects the timer callback
findings.detail: The async interval callback has no error handling. A thrown clock, store, client, or hook error rejects the callback without an observer and skips the remaining leases for that tick. Depending on runtime unhandled-rejection behavior, this can terminate the process; otherwise other active leases silently miss renewal.
findings.suggestion: Observe and report tick failures and isolate per-ref work so one failed operation does not prevent other leases from being processed.
findings.failure_scenario: One lease's `active` hook or clock sample throws during a tick while another active lease also needs renewal. The callback rejects and the second lease is skipped.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:239–243 installs an async interval callback containing `for (const h of handles.values()) if (current(h) && next.active(h)) await manager.update(h, {});` with no exception handler. src/util/claim-clock.ts:47 explicitly throws when `clockGettime` fails.
verification.trigger: An active hook or clock sample throws while processing the first lease. The interval callback rejects, and subsequent leases receive no renewal during that tick.

findings.title: Release intent replay bypasses send-time lease validation
findings.detail: `reconcileLeaseIntent` can replay a pending release with `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook. Calling it here permits a release of an expired generation after an outage or restart, without the fresh renewable decision and immediate send-time revalidation required for same-generation writes.
findings.suggestion: Provide reconciliation with a time-validating send hook for release replay, and re-decide when validation fails.
findings.failure_scenario: A release intent is persisted before its write, the process stops for longer than the lease duration, and recovery finds the old tip unchanged. Reconciliation sends the release without checking whether the generation is still renewable.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:65 calls `recoverLeases({ client, store })`; line 89 likewise delegates reconciliation without time validation. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:114–121 replays a release using `client.write(..., { signal, onCommit: ... })`, omitting `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206–208 aborts only when the optional hook returns false.
verification.trigger: Restart after lease expiry with an unsent release intent and an unchanged confirmed tip. Recovery sends and confirms the release despite the generation no longer being renewable.

findings.title: Cross-run requests bypass pending-intent reconciliation
findings.detail: A row belonging to another run is refused before its pending intent is reconciled. An unresolved intent must instead be reconciled first and return wait while pending; if it resolves as a dropped, never-confirmed acquisition, the next run must be able to acquire. The test at test/leases.test.ts:169 explicitly expects the premature refusal and unchanged intent, thereby asserting the defect.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile pending intents before deciding whether another run can acquire, and test both unresolved and dropped intents from the next run.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent and run B attempts the same ref. B receives refused without a GitHub read, even if reconciliation would drop A's intent and permit B to acquire.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns immediately for a different run when `row.intent` exists: `if (row && row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")) return refused;`. The reconciliation call follows at line 108, so it is bypassed.
verification.trigger: Run A leaves an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent. Run B requests the same ref and receives refused without reconciliation, even when the unchanged ref would allow A's intent and row to be dropped and B to acquire.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
findings.detail: The loop enumerates only the in-memory handles map, which is populated by successful writes in this manager instance. Confirmed held rows present after startup or created by reconciliation of an unconfirmed acquisition are never added to that map, so the loop never renews them. The tests cover reconciliation of an update after an already successful acquisition, but do not cover a recovered held row or an acquisition first confirmed by reconciliation.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive loop handles from confirmed held rows, and add tests for startup recovery and an unconfirmed acquisition resolved by a tick.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition reaches GitHub but its response is lost; a later tick reconciles the intent to held. Subsequent ticks never renew that lease, so it expires despite the active hook returning true.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 initializes `const handles = new Map<string, LeaseHandle>();`. Only the direct applied-write path registers a handle at :192: `handles.set(key(repo, ref), held)`. Reconciliation at :89–92 never registers one, while :242 renews only `for (const h of handles.values())`.
verification.trigger: An initial acquisition returns unconfirmed after GitHub applies it. A tick reconciles the intent to confirmed held, but no handle enters the renewal map. Subsequent ticks skip the lease regardless of the active hook, allowing expiry.

findings.title: Replayed releases bypass lease-time revalidation
findings.detail: Reconciliation can replay a pending release through `reconcileLeaseIntent`, whose replay write has no time sample or before-send predicate. Calling it before every operation and on every tick therefore permits a same-generation release after the lease window and renewable period have expired. The release expiry test exercises only a newly initiated release, not a pending release replay.
findings.suggestion: Ensure replayed releases use the same fresh time decision and before-send guard as other same-generation writes, and test expiry before replay and while its commit is in flight.
findings.failure_scenario: A release intent is persisted before its ref update, the process pauses beyond lease expiry, and a later tick reconciles it while the ref still points to the old tip. The replay sends the expired generation's release without checking GitHub time.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:89 delegates to `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)` without time validation. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113–121 replays a release against its confirmed predecessor using `client.write(..., { signal, onCommit: ... })`, with no `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206–208 aborts only when `opts.beforeSend?.()` returns false.
verification.trigger: A persisted release remains unsent while the process pauses beyond expiry. A later tick finds the old confirmed tip and replays the release for the expired generation without checking GitHub time.

findings.title: Mutant cases explicitly accept two winners
findings.detail: The concurrent-create and takeover tests change their expected winner count to two when the unconditional-ref-write mutant is enabled. Consequently those mutant cases pass while exhibiting the violation, contrary to the requested mutation check that these tests fail against the mutant.
findings.suggestion: Keep the one-winner assertion identical under the mutant and demonstrate separately that running the contract tests with that mutant fails.
findings.failure_scenario: An unconditional ref-write implementation lets both coordinators report held for the same generation, yet the mutant test passes because it expects two winners.

verification.evidence: test/leases.test.ts:138 explicitly accepts two winners: `expect(winners).toHaveLength(unconditional ? 2 : 1)`. Lines 143–147 run both create and takeover with `race(mode !== "CAS", ...)`. test/claim-github-fake.ts:125–129 bypasses both CAS and fast-forward checks when `unconditional` is true, then calls `this.apply(request)`. Targeted execution was blocked during imports by `floors.prefault is not a function`.
verification.trigger: Concurrent create or takeover using the unconditional-ref-write mutant produces two held results at the same generation; the mutant test accepts this instead of failing the one-winner assertion required by the request.

findings.title: Release replay bypasses send-time lease validation
findings.detail: The manager delegates pending intents to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which replays a release through `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a fresh GitHub-time decision. A release interrupted before its ref update can therefore be sent after its generation has expired, violating the requirement that every same-generation mutation be revalidated immediately before the ref update. Startup recovery uses the same replay path.
findings.suggestion: Make release reconciliation perform the same fresh time decision and send-time validation as an ordinary release, including during startup recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: A release creates its commit but stops before updating the ref; the manager restarts after the lease has expired while the old tip is still present. Recovery writes the released record for the expired generation without checking GitHub time.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:65 calls `await recoverLeases({ client, store })`. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:153 invokes `reconcileLeaseIntent`; :113–121 replays a release when the ref equals its confirmed predecessor, passing only `signal` and `onCommit` to `client.write`, without a time predicate or `beforeSend`.
verification.trigger: The process stops after journaling a release commit but before updating the ref, then restarts after lease expiry. Startup recovery writes the expired generation's release while the old tip remains present.

findings.title: A different run cannot reconcile a pending acquisition
findings.detail: The different-run check returns `refused` before reconciling an existing intent. If the prior run's first acquisition was unconfirmed and is later known to have left the ref unchanged, subsequent acquisitions by another run cannot drop and forget that row through this operation. Until a running renewal loop happens to reconcile it, the next run is incorrectly blocked; while the intent remains unresolved, the required result is `wait`, not `refused`.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile pending intents before applying the different-run ownership check, then inspect the resulting row.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent on an absent ref and ends. Run B calls `acquire` before the loop runs, after GitHub is readable and confirms the ref is still absent; it receives `refused` instead of resolving A's intent and acquiring.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns early: `if (row && row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")) return refused;`. Reconciliation occurs afterward at :108. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113–116 would drop an acquisition intent when the ref is still absent; leases.ts:91 would then forget its never-confirmed row.
verification.trigger: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent and ends. Before a loop tick, run B acquires the same ref after GitHub becomes readable and confirms absence. The early cross-run guard returns refused without reconciling and clearing A's failed intent.

findings.title: Recovered held leases are absent from the renewal loop
findings.detail: The loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated after a write returns `applied` in this manager instance. Recovery and later intent reconciliation can confirm a held lease without adding its handle to that map. Such a lease is never presented to `active` or renewed by the loop, even though it is confirmed in the store.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, while preserving generation checks.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition's ref update succeeds but returns `unconfirmed`; a later loop tick reconciles it as applied. No handle is added to `handles`, so subsequent ticks never renew the confirmed lease and it expires.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:186 returns immediately for `unconfirmed`, before handle registration at :192. The reconciliation helper at :87–92 does not populate `handles`. The loop reconciles intents at :240–241 but renews only `handles.values()` at :242.
verification.trigger: An acquisition succeeds remotely but returns unconfirmed. A later tick confirms it as held and clears the intent, yet subsequent ticks omit it from renewal because its handle was never registered, allowing expiry.

duplicates.title: Recovered confirmed leases are absent from the renewal loop
duplicates.detail: The request requires the loop to update each confirmed held handle. The loop visits only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by an immediately applied write. Recovery and tick-time reconciliation can confirm a held acquisition without adding its handle, and existing confirmed rows are not loaded on manager creation. Those leases therefore receive no periodic renewal.
duplicates.suggestion: Populate or derive the loop's handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, as well as after writes.

findings.detail: `toTarget` now throws for an excluded model, but this call occurs before the trial's error handler. findings.title: The stop assertion still depends on a fixed scheduling window
findings.detail: After releasing the gate, the test waits 800 ms and assumes any surviving check has written `end`. On a sufficiently loaded runner, a check that survived `stop()` can remain unscheduled until after the assertion, allowing the test to pass even though interruption failed. The restart test likewise can finish its log assertion before a surviving old check gets scheduled. This leaves the requested failure detection dependent on timing.
findings.suggestion: Use an observable process or completion handshake that establishes the original check has terminated before asserting its log, without relying on a fixed delay.
findings.failure_scenario: If `stop()` returns while the gate subprocess survives, and that subprocess is delayed for more than 800 ms after the release file is created, the first test observes only `start` and passes.

verification.evidence: test/land-queue.test.ts:687–692 creates the release file with `writeFileSync(gateReleasePath(), "")`, waits `await Bun.sleep(800)`, runs 20 `settleIdle()` calls, then asserts `expect(gateLog()).toEqual(["start"])`. test/land-queue.test.ts:80 writes `end` only when the gate subprocess resumes and observes the release. These checks provide no synchronization proving a surviving subprocess had time to run.
verification.trigger: If a regression lets stop() return with the gate subprocess alive, and that process remains unscheduled through the 800 ms wait and subsequent settling, the assertion passes despite failed interruption.

findings.failure_scenario: Stop returns without interrupting the gate, but the gate process is not scheduled until after the 800 ms wait and assertion; the test passes despite the gate later writing `end`.

findings.detail: Skipped draft triggers are no longer returned by pendingConflictTriggers, and the only code that reactivates them is in the GitHub poller. candidates.title: A head change can be missed while a draft lookup is in flight
candidates.detail: The request says to recheck a draft deferral when the poller observes “a new head.” This guard compares the snapshot only with the poller's previous snapshot. If the poller saves the new head before an in-flight live lookup marks an older-head trigger as draft, subsequent polls see the same head and never call recheckDraftConflictTriggers, even though that method would detect the mismatch against the trigger's observed SHA. The deferred trigger remains stale until another qualifying change occurs.
candidates.suggestion: Check deferred triggers against each observed snapshot, or otherwise make recording the deferral and observing the head change race-safe.

findings.title: A saved head change can be lost before the draft deferral is rechecked
findings.detail: The poller saves the new snapshot before reactivating draft triggers, and uses the saved snapshot on the next pass to decide whether the head changed. If the process stops between those operations, the next pass sees the same head and an open draft, so it never rechecks the deferred trigger. The same ordering can occur when a live lookup finishes after the poller has saved the newer head and marks the trigger as draft. The trigger remains skipped despite the poller having observed a new head.
findings.suggestion: Make recording the observation and reactivating eligible draft triggers durable together, or compare each deferred trigger's recorded head with the current observation on every poll.
findings.failure_scenario: A trigger is skipped as draft at head A. The poller observes draft head B and saves it, then the daemon restarts before rechecking triggers. Subsequent observations of draft head B do not reactivate the trigger.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/github-poller.ts:345 computes `const same = prev?.headRefOid === head`; lines 372–374 call `save(...)` before `if (!same || snap.isDraft === false || snap.state !== "OPEN") store.recheckDraftConflictTriggers(pr.url, snap)`. src/db/store.ts:2665 persists `pr.data` in a transaction committed at line 2675. src/db/store.ts:1114 selects only `WHERE state = 'pending'`, excluding the stranded draft deferral.
verification.trigger: A crash in the narrow synchronous window after saving draft head B but before reactivating the draft-skipped trigger for head A leaves B persisted. After restart, unchanged OPEN/draft observations of B make the recheck condition false, so that trigger stays skipped until another qualifying PR change. Severity is medium because the crash must hit a millisecond-scale window.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict
findings.detail: A land trigger is immediately evaluated against any saved poller snapshot, even if that snapshot predates the approved head. `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped when the saved head differs, and a later poll cannot reconsider it. The queue has already blocked the entry, so the requested conflict round never starts.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation before rejecting a land trigger for a stale head, or retain the trigger pending until a current observation can decide it.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A; a review round pushes head B and B is approved before the next poll. Landing B conflicts with the base, but the saved snapshot still says A, so the B trigger is permanently skipped as `PR head moved`.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:16–21 reads saved githubPrData and executes `if (snapshot) store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snapshot, now());` without refreshing it. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 compares `seen.headRefOid !== trigger.head` and assigns `"PR head moved"`; src/db/store.ts:1139 permanently sets `state = 'skipped'`. A later poll can independently recover by creating another trigger.
verification.trigger: Saved head A, approved and conflicting head B -> B's durable land trigger is permanently skipped using stale A, rather than starting the requested round.

findings.title: A conflict observed during another round is lost permanently
findings.detail: An active review or conflict round causes the trigger to be marked skipped. The poller emits `pr.conflicting` only on entry into the conflicting state, so if the active round fails or ends without changing the head, subsequent polls do not create another trigger. The unresolved conflict therefore never gets its own round.
findings.suggestion: Keep the trigger pending while another round is active and reconsider it when that round terminates, subject to a fresh PR observation and the daily cap.
findings.failure_scenario: A review round is in flight when the poller first observes the PR as CONFLICTING. The trigger is skipped; the review round later fails without pushing, and every subsequent poll still sees CONFLICTING, so no conflict round starts.

verification.evidence: src/db/store.ts:1130–1141 checks `rounds.some((r) => !TERMINAL_STATUSES.includes(r.status))`, assigns `"round in flight"`, then executes `UPDATE conflict_triggers SET state = 'skipped', reason = ? WHERE id = ?`. Only triggers `WHERE state = 'pending'` are retried (src/db/store.ts:1071). New poller triggers require `item.kind === "pr.conflicting"` (src/db/store.ts:2610–2612), but that event is emitted only when `next.mergeable === "CONFLICTING" && prev?.mergeable !== "CONFLICTING"` (src/integrations/github-poller.ts:206).
verification.trigger: An open factory PR first becomes CONFLICTING while a review round is active. Its conflict trigger is permanently skipped. If the review round fails without pushing and subsequent polls continue reporting CONFLICTING, no replacement trigger is emitted and no conflict round starts, including after restart.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land trigger
findings.detail: The land path uses any stored GitHub snapshot without refreshing it. `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped when that snapshot's head differs from the land entry's approved head, even if the snapshot is simply older than the approval. The trigger is then no longer pending, so this landing-queue trigger cannot recover on restart.
findings.suggestion: Refresh or otherwise establish the snapshot's freshness before permanently skipping a land trigger; retain it pending when the observation cannot establish the current head.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller saved head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved before the next poll, and the land queue detects a conflict at B. Processing compares B with the saved A and skips the trigger instead of starting a round.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 uses the saved snapshot directly: `if (snapshot) store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snapshot, now());`. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 maps its head mismatch to `"PR head moved"`; src/db/store.ts:1139 executes `UPDATE conflict_triggers SET state = 'skipped', reason = ? WHERE id = ?`. Later polling may create a replacement trigger, but this land trigger is discarded.
verification.trigger: The poller stores A; B is approved and conflicts during landing before another poll -> the B land trigger is permanently skipped.

findings.title: Retrying comment creation can post duplicate resolution comments
findings.detail: The `gh` wrapper retries transient failures around the entire comment command. If GitHub creates the comment but its response is lost, the retry creates another comment without checking the marker again. The preflight marker lookup only protects a later delivery attempt, not retries within this call.
findings.suggestion: Recheck for the marker after an uncertain comment outcome before issuing another creation request.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts `pr comment`, but the client receives a timeout or connection reset; the retry posts a second comment with the same conflict-round marker.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1894 checks `comments?.some((comment) => comment.body?.includes(marker))` before the call at :1899: `await gh(["pr", "comment", prUrl, "--body-file", "-"], ctx.signal, text)`. The wrapper at :1922 applies `withGitHubRetry` to each individual command. src/git/repos.ts:91 retries `charged(call)` after transient errors (:93–97), without repeating the comment lookup.
verification.trigger: GitHub creates the comment but its response is lost with a retryable error and retry budget remains. The command retries directly and creates a duplicate resolution comment.

findings.title: Auto-merge is disabled before validating the PR delivery grant
findings.detail: The new auto-merge mutation occurs before `stored()` and `assertFactoryBranchPush` verify that the PR is still open, belongs to the expected branch and repository, and matches the round's current grant. A stale or invalid round can therefore modify the PR even though delivery is subsequently refused.
findings.suggestion: Validate the current grant and PR identity before disabling auto-merge, and revalidate after the mutation before pushing.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR head branch changes while a conflict round runs and auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge, then rejects the changed branch.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1865–1866 executes `if (review.kind === "conflict" && pr.autoMerge) await gh(["pr", "merge", prUrl, "--disable-auto"], ctx.signal);` before `stored()` (:1869) and `assertFactoryBranchPush(...)` (:1870). src/core/delivery.ts:88 rejects a changed branch: `if (pr.headBranch !== branch) return ...`.
verification.trigger: The PR branch changes during the round while auto-merge remains enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge before rejecting the changed branch, leaving an unrelated current PR state modified.

findings.title: Restart tests do not cover a stale saved observation
findings.detail: The restart tests use either no saved observation or one matching the trigger. They therefore pass while a saved observation for an older head causes a durable land trigger to be skipped permanently, and while an outdated open, non-draft observation can start an ineligible round.
findings.suggestion: Add restart and land-trigger cases with an older saved head and with a PR that became draft or closed after the saved observation. Assert that a current observation governs whether the trigger starts.
findings.failure_scenario: A pending trigger for head B is recovered while the database still contains an open CONFLICTING snapshot for head A; the existing tests never exercise this state.

verification.evidence: test/conflict-rounds.test.ts:331–337 records a trigger and reopens the database without saving an observation. The other startup test uses the same head for both: line 517 calls `recordConflictTrigger(url, await remoteHead(), ...)` and line 525 saves `headRefOid: await remoteHead()`. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 consumes any saved snapshot directly: `if (snapshot) store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snapshot, now());`. src/db/store.ts:1126–1140 classifies a mismatched snapshot as `"PR head moved"` and persists `state = 'skipped'`.
verification.trigger: Recover a pending trigger for head B while the saved open CONFLICTING observation still names head A. Recovery skips the trigger; neither restart test exercises this mismatch.

findings.title: The non-factory polling case bypasses the poller
findings.detail: The non-factory branch inserts a trigger and calls the store consumer directly, so it does not test whether polling a non-factory PR creates a round. A regression in tracking, event generation, or poller consumption for that case would still pass the test.
findings.suggestion: Exercise a tracked non-factory PR through the same fake GitHub poller path as the other eligibility cases and assert that no conflict round starts.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller erroneously starts a conflict round for a non-factory PR, but the test bypasses the poller and continues to pass.

verification.evidence: test/conflict-rounds.test.ts:365–371 handles `eligibility === "non-factory"` by directly calling `recordConflictTrigger(...)` and `startConflictTrigger(...)`. The actual `startGitHubPoller(...)` call at lines 372–373 is confined to the `else` branch. Line 393 then asserts zero rounds.

findings.title: Cached first attempts lose the workspace needed by retries after restart
findings.detail: A completed first attempt is reused from state after restart, but the resumed stage cleans the checkout before reaching this line. A pending or newly started retry therefore runs without the build output or other files produced by that first attempt. Previously, a resumed gate stage reran the first attempt and recreated those files before retrying.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the workspace required by a pending retry, or replay the local first attempt before performing the retry after restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate setup creates an ignored build directory, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts before or during its retry. On resume, checkoutCommitted removes the directory, the cached initial result is reused, and the retry fails because its build output is missing.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1157 calls `await checkoutCommitted(cwd, undefined, Boolean(ctx.state.implementerIssue))` before the initial execution. src/git/repos.ts:476 cleans with `["git", "clean", "-ffdxq"]`, removing ignored artifacts. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:23 then returns cached attempts: `if (results[purpose]) return results[purpose];`. src/gates/run.ts:280 runs regression retries with `{ ...cfg, setup: [], checks: selected }`.
verification.trigger: Setup generates an ignored build directory, the initial check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts before the retry completes. Resume removes the directory, skips the cached initial execution including setup, and runs the retry without its required build output, producing a false gate failure.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed
findings.detail: The shared execution path awaits only `result` and never reads `execution.events`. Gate reporting and landing logs currently work only because the local executor calls hooks directly; an executor implementing the advertised interface has no way to deliver its streamed check events to those consumers.
findings.suggestion: Consume the event stream in the shared execution path and forward events to the appropriate gate and landing reporting hooks, coordinating stream completion and errors with the result.
findings.failure_scenario: An injected executor yields check events and returns a valid GateRun. The stage verdict is computed, but no per-check pipeline events or landing check output are recorded.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:139–150 attaches execution and only awaits its result: `const execution = executor.attach(handle, signal)`; `return await execution.result`. It never consumes `execution.events`. Pipeline recording depends on `onResult` (src/pipeline/engine.ts:357–364), invoked directly only by the local implementation: `hooks.onResult?.(r, phase)` (src/gates/executor.ts:87).
verification.trigger: An injected executor supplies check events through its iterable without invoking local hooks. Its GateRun decides the verdict, but streamed per-check pipeline events and landing output are omitted. Default local execution retains its hooks.

The retry therefore runs without files created by the initial attempt, despite the existing requirement that retries see the same build output. Prepare likewise discards changes before resuming its baseline retry.
findings.suggestion: Preserve or reconstruct the first attempt's required workspace state before resuming a local retry, with restart coverage for checks that depend on generated files.

findings.title: A checkpoint failure leaves started work uncancelled
findings.detail: The executor starts work before persisting its handle, but if persistence rejects, execution exits without attaching or cancelling. An executor whose start actually launches work can continue indefinitely without a durable handle, and a subsequent attempt can start duplicate work.
findings.suggestion: On persistence failure, attach to the returned handle and cancel the execution before propagating the failure, while preserving the original error.
findings.failure_scenario: A remote executor starts a gate suite and the state save fails because the database write fails; the run fails while the untracked suite continues.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:137–139 executes `await executor.start(req, signal)`, then `await persist(handle)`, then `executor.attach(handle, signal)`. Cancellation is installed only afterwards at lines 140–145. The checkpoint calls `await ctx.save("gate-started")` (src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:46); its catch only rethrows (lines 54–56).
verification.trigger: An injected executor starts independent work and returns a handle; persistence then rejects. executeGate exits before attaching or installing cancellation, leaving that work running without a durable handle. The shipped local executor starts actual checks only during attach, so this requires an injected backend.

findings.title: Redacting the local handle changes the request replayed after restart
findings.detail: The local handle contains the gate request, including commands and paths, but the persisted copy is transformed by `redactGateData`. On restart, local attach executes that transformed request rather than the trusted gate configuration. Credential redaction or terminal-control stripping can change a valid command or path, so the resumed run can check different behavior or fail unexpectedly.
findings.suggestion: Keep sensitive request data out of the persisted handle and reconstruct the local request from trusted run state when reattaching, without transforming executable input.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured gate command contains a registered credential or a terminal control character; after a restart, the local executor runs the redacted or stripped command.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:44 persists `handle: redactGateData(handle)`. src/gates/output.ts:31 sanitizes every string via `redactGateOutput(v)`, which at :23 applies `redactCredentials(stripVTControlCharacters(output))`. src/gates/executor.ts:60 reads `const req = handle.request` and :77-81 runs `runLocalGates` using `req.cwd` and `req.gates`.
verification.trigger: A gate command contains a credential value eligible for redaction or a terminal formatting sequence. Restart while its handle is pending causes local attachment to execute the sanitized persisted command, changing its behavior.

findings.title: Executor event streams are never consumed

findings.failure_scenario: An executor yields check events and returns a GateRun without invoking local hooks. The gate completes but its check events and landing log output are silently missing.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:147 returns `await execution.result` without iterating events. findings.title: Persisting a sanitized local request can change the command replayed after restart

findings.failure_scenario: A base gate command contains a string registered for credential redaction. The daemon stops after saving the handle; on resume, local attachment executes the command with that string replaced by the redaction marker.

findings.title: Resumed retries reuse results after their build output has been removed
findings.detail: The request says regression retries and baseline retries do not change, and the surrounding code requires retries to see the first attempt's build output. findings.suggestion: Restore the first attempt's required workspace state on local resume, or rerun the initial local execution before retrying while preserving the stored handle semantics for executors that can reattach.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command generates an untracked build artifact, an initial check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts during its retry. On resume the artifact is cleaned, the saved initial result is reused, and the retry fails because the artifact is missing.

findings.title: Landing checks discard the execution handle

findings.failure_scenario: A landing check is running on an executor whose work survives daemon restart. The daemon restarts before the result arrives; the queue starts a second execution because the first handle was never stored.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed

findings.suggestion: Consume the execution event stream in the shared path and translate its events into the existing hooks, including setup and status events as needed.
findings.failure_scenario: An injected executor emits check results through its events iterable while its result is pending. The pipeline displays no check progress, and landing writes only the log header despite the executor providing output.

findings.title: Restarting a retry discards the files produced by its first attempt
findings.detail: The stage cleans the checkout before consulting the persisted initial result. After a restart during a regression retry, that initial result is reused, but the setup and first check are not rerun to recreate their build output. The resumed local retry therefore runs against a different tree from the one it is supposed to retry. The prepare path similarly discards changes before reusing its persisted baseline result.
findings.suggestion: Restore the required working state before replaying a local retry, or rerun the preceding local gate execution when its working state cannot survive a restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command creates an ignored build artifact, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts during its retry. On resume, checkoutCommitted deletes the artifact and the retry fails because setup is skipped, changing the gate verdict.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1157 unconditionally calls `await checkoutCommitted(cwd, undefined, Boolean(ctx.state.implementerIssue))` before resuming gates. src/git/repos.ts:476 executes `["git", "clean", "-ffdxq"]`, deleting ignored artifacts. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:23 skips the completed initial attempt with `if (results[purpose]) return results[purpose];`. src/gates/run.ts:280 constructs the regression retry with `await runner({ ...cfg, setup: [], checks: selected })`. src/gates/executor.ts:77 replays the stored request through `runLocalGates`.
verification.trigger: Setup creates an ignored artifact needed by checks; an eligible transient failure starts a regression retry, and the daemon restarts before its result is persisted. Resume deletes the artifact, reuses the initial result without rerunning setup, and replays the retry without setup. The missing artifact makes the retry fail, retaining a blocking regression instead of a flaky pass.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed
findings.detail: executeGate awaits only the result and never iterates execution.events. The local executor bypasses this omission by invoking hooks directly, but an injected executor has no access to those hooks. Its check events never reach the pipeline event store or the landing log, so the shared executor interface does not preserve gate event behavior for another implementation.
findings.suggestion: Consume the event stream while awaiting the result and route its events to the existing pipeline and landing reporting paths; avoid duplicating local events.
findings.failure_scenario: An injected executor yields a check event and then returns a successful GateRun. The stage completes, but no check event is recorded and a landing log contains no check output.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:139 attaches the execution, but :147 only does `return await execution.result`; nothing consumes `execution.events`. Hooks reach only the local executor (:135), which calls `hooks.onResult?.(r, phase)` at :87. Landing output depends on `onResult` in src/land/queue.ts:397-398.
verification.trigger: An injected executor emits a check through events and resolves its result. The result decides the stage, but the emitted check never reaches the run event stream or landing log.

findings.title: A checkpoint failure leaves started work without a handle or cancellation
findings.detail: If start succeeds and persisting the handle throws, executeGate exits before attach and before registering cancellation. An executor that actually starts work in start can continue running with no durable handle by which the daemon can reattach or cancel it.
findings.suggestion: Define and implement cleanup for a started execution when handle persistence fails, and cover that failure path with an executor that starts work before returning its handle.
findings.failure_scenario: A remote-style injected executor starts a gate job, then the run-state save fails. The stage fails while the job continues, and a resumed run starts another job because no handle was stored.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:137-139 executes `await executor.start(req, signal)`, then `await persist(handle)`, then `executor.attach(handle, signal)`. Cancellation is installed only at :140-145. The persistence callback awaits `ctx.save("gate-started")` in src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:46; its catch at :54-56 only rethrows.
verification.trigger: An injected executor starts external work and checkpoint persistence rejects. executeGate exits before attaching or installing cancellation, leaving the work unmanaged; if no subsequent save succeeds, restart has no durable handle and can start duplicate work. The shipped local executor starts work only during attach, so this requires an injected executor.

findings.title: Resuming a retry removes the first attempt’s build output
findings.detail: On restart, the stage cleans the checkout before consulting the saved initial result. The saved result then prevents the initial execution, including setup, from running again, while the pending retry runs only its selected checks. This breaks the existing guarantee that a retry sees the build output from its first attempt.
findings.suggestion: Restore the retry’s required workspace state on resume, or rerun the local initial execution and setup before retrying without reusing a result whose workspace has been discarded.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command installs dependencies, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts while its regression retry is pending. checkoutCommitted removes the dependencies, the cached initial result skips setup, and the resumed retry fails because its dependencies are absent.

verification.evidence: src/git/repos.ts:465 explicitly documents that checkout cleanup removes dependencies: '`-x` removes ignored payloads ... along with dependencies, which gate setup installs again.' src/pipeline/engine.ts:1157 calls that cleanup on resume. However, src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:23 returns the persisted initial result via `if (results[purpose]) return results[purpose];`, while src/gates/run.ts:280 runs retries with `setup: []`. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:26-27 selects the pending retry's stored handle for reattachment.
verification.trigger: The daemon restarts during a local regression retry after setup installed ignored dependencies. Resume removes those dependencies, skips the completed initial execution, and reattaches the setup-free retry. Checks fail because dependencies are absent, producing an incorrect blocking verdict. This is the same defect as C1.

findings.title: A failed checkpoint leaves started executor work unmanaged
findings.detail: If persisting the handle throws after start succeeds, executeGate exits without attaching to or cancelling the execution. A non-local executor can already be running work at that point, and the handle is not durable, so neither cancellation nor restart can recover it.
findings.suggestion: On a checkpoint failure, attach using the returned handle and cancel the started execution before propagating the persistence error, with cleanup failures reported.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor starts a remote gate suite, then the run-state save fails because the database write fails. The run fails while the gate suite continues without a persisted handle or cancellation path.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:137-139 places `await persist(handle)` between start and attach, outside the try/finally at :146-151. The only `execution.cancel()` call is at :142, after persistence. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:44-46 assigns the handle in memory and then awaits the database checkpoint.
verification.trigger: An injected executor starts a remote suite, then the database checkpoint fails. The helper propagates the failure without attaching or cancelling that suite. This does not strand local gate processes because local start merely creates a handle (src/gates/executor.ts:40-44).

findings.title: Redacting the persisted local request changes what is replayed
findings.detail: The local handle embeds its executable request, but redactGateData rewrites every string in that request before persistence. On restart, localExecutor executes the rewritten cwd and gate commands. Credential redaction or terminal-control normalization can therefore change a command or path and cause a different check to run.
findings.suggestion: Persist a replayable local handle without rewriting executable inputs, while keeping secrets out of persisted state through an appropriate request reconstruction or secure reference.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential appears in a gate command or checkout path. The first execution uses the original value, but after a restart the stored handle contains the redaction marker and the replay runs a changed command or fails to find its directory.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:44 stores `handle: redactGateData(handle)`. src/gates/output.ts:31 applies redaction to every string. src/gates/executor.ts:137 selects `stored ?? (await executor.start(req, signal))`; attachment reads `const req = handle.request` (line 60) and executes `req.cwd` and `req.gates` (lines 77–81).
verification.trigger: A gate command or checkout path contains a registered credential matching redaction rules. After restart, local attachment executes the redacted stored request, changing the command or directory.

Its check and status events are therefore lost from pipeline events and landing logs.
findings.suggestion: Consume the execution event stream and forward its events to the appropriate daemon hooks, while preserving completion and cancellation behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor emits a check result while its gate suite is running; the suite completes, but the run's gate event stream and landing log omit that check.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:139 obtains an Execution, and :147 awaits its result without iterating its events. findings.title: Fake executor tests do not exercise event forwarding
findings.detail: Every fake execution exposes an empty event stream, so the pipeline and landing tests pass even though the shared executor path never consumes events. The local streaming test reads the stream directly and likewise cannot detect this integration defect.
findings.suggestion: Have the injected executor emit check and status events, then assert that pipeline events and landing logs receive the relevant output before or after the result completes.
findings.failure_scenario: A non-local executor emits a failing check event, but no test fails when the daemon discards it.

verification.evidence: test/gate-executor.test.ts:72 returns an empty event stream: `events: { async *[Symbol.asyncIterator]() {} }`. The event assertions at lines 230–231 and 331–332 exercise local executions directly. src/gates/executor.ts:146–147 only awaits `return await execution.result;`, without consuming `execution.events`, so the fake-executor tests do not detect discarded events.
verification.trigger: An injected non-local executor emits a failing check event. The daemon discards the event, and the fake-executor tests cannot detect this because their event streams are empty.

findings.title: Redacting the local handle changes the commands replayed after restart
findings.detail: The local handle contains the full executable request, but the persisted handle is passed through `redactGateData`, which replaces registered credential strings and strips terminal control characters from every string. On restart, `localExecutor.attach` executes that altered request instead of the trusted gate configuration supplied by the caller. A command or path containing a registered credential substring can therefore run differently or fail after restart.
findings.suggestion: Persist an opaque local handle and reconstruct its request from trusted run state on resume, without storing or executing a redacted copy of executable input.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted base gate command contains a value that is also registered for credential redaction. The daemon restarts after the handle checkpoint; the resumed local executor runs the command with that value replaced by the redaction marker.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:44 persists `handle: redactGateData(handle)`. src/gates/output.ts:31 redacts every string. On resume, src/gates/executor.ts:137–139 attaches the stored handle, and lines 60 and 77–81 execute its stored request.
verification.trigger: A trusted gate command contains a registered credential matching redaction rules. Restart after the handle checkpoint causes local replay to execute the command with `[redacted]` substituted.

findings.title: A resumed local retry loses the initial run’s build output
findings.detail: The request says local attachment after restart must re-run the check as a resumed gate stage did before, and that regression and baseline retries do not change. Returning the persisted initial result skips its setup and checks after restart. The prepare and gates stage resume paths clean or check out the worktree before reaching the pending retry, so files produced by the initial run are gone. The retry then runs against a different environment and can give a different baseline or regression verdict.
findings.suggestion: For local work, restore the pre-change resume behavior by re-running the initial suite before retrying, or otherwise restore the initial suite’s required build state.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command creates an untracked build artifact, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts during its retry. On resume the persisted initial result is reused after the worktree is cleaned; the retry fails because the artifact is missing.

verification.evidence: Preparation calls `await discardChanges(wt.path)` (src/pipeline/engine.ts:433), which runs `git clean -fdq` for a dirty worktree (src/git/repos.ts:484–487). src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:23 returns the saved initial result: `if (results[purpose]) return results[purpose]`. Baseline retry explicitly uses `runner({ ...cfg, setup: [], checks: selected })` (src/gates/run.ts:188).
verification.trigger: Setup creates an ordinary untracked artifact and a check fails transiently. Restart during baseline retry cleans that artifact, reuses the initial result, and reattaches the setup-free retry. findings.detail: The catch path recomputes preparationMs whenever roundsUsed is absent. findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the initial TLS connection
findings.detail: The initial connection accepts any certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that connection. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request to the real coordinator, return its code and secret to the worker, and present its own certificate. The owner sees the same code on both sides and approves it; the attacker then observes the claim and issued token. Pinning the attacker's certificate on subsequent requests does not prevent this. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is never authenticated or used to bind the exchange.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to both endpoints' certificate fingerprints and the pairing exchange, so relaying through a different TLS certificate changes the code or causes verification to fail.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies the real coordinator's pairing response, and forwards the approved claim while terminating both TLS connections.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23–27 calls the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`. src/db/workers.ts:54–55 generates independent random `secret` and `code` values. src/workers/client.ts:39 then pins `first.fingerprint`, and :47 persists it.
verification.trigger: An interceptor terminates the initial TLS connection and relays the coordinator's pairing response and subsequent claim. Both sides display the same code, but the interceptor learns the approved token and the worker pins the interceptor's certificate.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: Private read protection is an in-memory registry. Pairing releases the token and fingerprint registrations on return, and `runWorker` registers them only in the worker CLI process. A daemon running gates or agents in a separate process therefore does not include those files in its sandbox deny paths. The coordinator TLS key has the same lifetime problem when its listener is disabled after the key has been created. Mode 0600 does not protect files from another process running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the configured worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that constructs agent or gate sandboxes, independent of whether a worker or listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, then run a factory daemon and a gate on the same machine; the daemon's sandbox is built without the worker token path registered, allowing a gate with access to that path to read the token.

verification.evidence: src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores protection in a process-local `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()`; :30 returns only that map's keys. src/workers/client.ts:47–48 registers the credential files, then :55–57 releases both registrations. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 builds denies from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`; neither discovers persisted worker files.
verification.trigger: A separately started daemon has no worker-file registrations. A gate whose read allowances otherwise cover the credential location can read the same user's mode-0600 worker token. The general home deny protects ordinary gate layouts, but does not supply the missing specific deny for otherwise-readable locations.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate creation permanently blocks restart
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before invoking OpenSSL. If generation fails, times out, or the process stops before both files are complete, the next start either rejects the incomplete pair or tries to parse invalid material. No cleanup or recovery occurs, so the worker listener or pairing command continues to fail on every subsequent start.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names, validate them, and publish them only after successful generation; clean up incomplete temporary material on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped after creating the empty key file but before OpenSSL creates the certificate; every later listener start throws `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates `writeFileSync(keyPath, "", { flag: "wx", mode: 0o600 })` before awaiting OpenSSL. Lines 16–17 throw `new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material")` when only one file exists; the catch at lines 45–47 only calls `release()` and rethrows. src/cli/daemon.ts:30 awaits listener startup before starting the factory and rethrows failures at lines 44–46.
verification.trigger: With the worker listener enabled, interruption after key.pem creation but before cert.pem creation leaves persistent partial TLS material. Every subsequent daemon startup fails until that material is manually repaired.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. The displayed code comes from the coordinator but is not bound to that certificate or to an authenticated exchange. An intermediary can relay the pairing request and code unchanged, obtain the pairing secret and issued token, and leave the worker pinned to the intermediary's certificate even though the owner compared matching codes.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange so a relaying intermediary cannot obtain a usable token or substitute its certificate.

findings.title: Permanent TLS and configuration errors are retried silently forever
findings.detail: The heartbeat loop catches every request exception and retries without a deadline or diagnostic. This includes a changed coordinator fingerprint and malformed coordinator URL, neither of which can be repaired by retrying. The worker remains running but never sends another heartbeat, and the owner receives no explanation.

findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing. Every heartbeat fails fingerprint validation, but the worker silently retries indefinitely instead of reporting that it must be paired again.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:114–115 rejects with `"Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed"`. src/workers/client.ts:99–102 catches every request rejection and returns `undefined`; :93 loops forever, sleeping at :106 and capping only the delay at :107.
verification.trigger: The coordinator certificate changes, or the coordinator URL is invalid. Each heartbeat request rejects, but the worker silently retries indefinitely without reporting the permanent error or need to pair again.

findings.title: Existing TLS key loses sandbox protection when the listener is disabled
findings.detail: The TLS key is registered with the sandbox deny list only when the listener starts. After a listener has created the key, restarting the daemon with workers.listen unset skips registration even though the key remains on disk. Agent sandboxes that can read that data directory can then read the coordinator's private key, contrary to the requirement that it be denied in every agent sandbox.

findings.failure_scenario: Enable the listener once, then disable it and restart the daemon with the data directory outside the default home deny paths. A subsequent agent can read worker-tls/key.pem.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15–16: `if (!listen) return undefined;` precedes `const tls = await certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"));`. The key's protection is registered only inside certificate: src/workers/tls.ts:12–14: `const keyPath = join(home, "key.pem")` and `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 builds sandbox denies from `...privateReadPaths()`.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup

findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before openssl writes cert.pem. Subsequent starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates the empty key before `await sh(...)` at line 19. Lines 16–17 reject existing key.pem with missing cert.pem as `"Incomplete worker TLS material"`; lines 45–47 rethrow without removing the partial files. src/cli/daemon.ts:30,44–46 propagates this failure out of daemon startup.

findings.title: Credential read protection ends with the pairing process

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:55–57 executes `cert.release()` and `for (const release of held) release()` after pairing. src/util/private-reads.ts:21 deletes released entries, and :4 defines a process-local map. src/cli/daemon.ts:15 registers the API token and :30 starts the worker listener, without registering stored worker-client credentials. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 derives credential denies from the built-in list and that process-local registry.

findings.title: Privacy probe masks the cross-process credential protection gap
findings.detail: The real-Seatbelt test creates the TLS material and registers both worker files in the same process that starts the gate, retaining all registrations throughout the probe. findings.failure_scenario: The current implementation releases the registrations after pairing, yet this test retains them and reports all three files denied.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:262–266 creates live registrations with `certificate(...)` and `privateFile(...)`, retaining them until lines 294–296: `for (const p of protectedFiles) p.release(); tls.release();`. Production pairing instead releases them before returning: src/workers/client.ts:55–57: `finally { cert.release(); for (const release of held) release(); }`. Registrations are process-local (src/util/private-reads.ts:4: `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>();`) and release deletes them (line 21: `else privatePaths.delete(p);`). src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 builds protection from `policySpellings([...credentials, ...privateReadPaths()], true, fs)`; its built-in credential list does not include the worker data directory.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that untrusted connection. An active intermediary can forward the request to the real coordinator, relay its code to the worker, and retain the returned pairing secret. findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies `/worker/pair` to the coordinator, and relays the real code. After the owner approves it, the attacker claims the worker token.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 makes the first pairing request with only `{ signal }`; src/workers/tls.ts:103 uses `rejectUnauthorized: false`. src/workers/client.ts:33 prints the returned code and :39 pins `first.fingerprint`. src/db/workers.ts:83-89 issues the approved token solely on possession of the pairing secret: `return w.state === "approved" ? { token: this.issued(w) } : { pending: true };`.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: `protectPrivateFile` maintains an in-memory registry. Pairing releases its registrations before exiting, and `runWorker` registers the files only in the worker process. findings.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a worker and a factory daemon under the same user. An agent launched by the daemon reads `<data>/worker/token` and impersonates that worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:87-88 registers token protection only inside `runWorker` through `privateFile`. src/workers/tls.ts:52 calls `protectPrivateFile(path)`, whose registry is process-local: src/util/private-reads.ts:4 `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>();`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 builds denies from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`; :151-161 contains no worker data directory, and :217 applies the home-wide deny only to gates.
verification.trigger: A paired worker and a separate factory daemon run as the same user with the default data directory. The daemon never registers the worker token path, so an editing agent can read the same-user 0600 token and impersonate the worker.

findings.title: Disabling the listener leaves its existing TLS key unprotected from agents
findings.detail: The TLS key is added to the process-local private-read registry only when the listener is enabled. findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator previously enabled workers, then starts with the listener disabled. A tool-enabled agent reads `<data>/worker-tls/key.pem` before the listener is enabled again.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15–16 returns on `!listen` before calling `certificate(...)`; src/workers/tls.ts:14 registers the key with `protectPrivateFile(keyPath)` only when that function runs. src/cli/daemon.ts:30–31 starts the optional listener and then mounts integrations, without separately protecting an existing key.

findings.title: Store untrusted heartbeat fields only after redaction
findings.detail: Heartbeat capabilities are serialized directly into SQLite. Several worker-controlled strings can contain coordinator credentials or private strings, but sanitization occurs only when listing workers. findings.failure_scenario: A paired worker sends a coordinator credential or private string in `osVersion`; the value is written verbatim to the workers table.

verification.evidence: src/workers/protocol.ts:8 accepts `osVersion: z.string().max(128)`. src/server/workers.ts:43–46 passes `Heartbeat.parse(await req.json())` directly to `workers.heartbeat(current, capabilities)`. src/db/workers.ts:143–144 executes `UPDATE workers SET last_heartbeat_at=?,capabilities=? WHERE name=? AND state='approved'` with `.run(this.now(), JSON.stringify(c), w.name)`. Redaction occurs only when listing, through `return this.sanitize({` at src/db/workers.ts:124, after persistence.
verification.trigger: An approved worker submits an otherwise valid heartbeat containing a registered coordinator credential or private string of at most 128 characters in osVersion. The coordinator stores that value verbatim in workers.capabilities.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied in the daemon's agent sandboxes
findings.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates.
