findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator. An agent launched by its daemon reads the token under the worker data directory and uses it to impersonate the worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:55-57 releases pairing protections on return: `for (const release of held) release();`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores protection in a process-local Map. src/cli/daemon.ts:30 starts the worker listener, which protects only its TLS key through src/server/workers.ts:16 `certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"))`; it does not register `<data>/worker/token`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:217 reserves the home-wide deny for gates.

findings.title: Disabling the listener removes protection for an existing TLS key
findings.detail: The request says the TLS key is read-denied in every agent sandbox. findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables workers after having enabled them, then starts a run. An editor agent can read the retained coordinator TLS private key.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15: `if (!listen) return undefined;` skips src/workers/tls.ts:14: `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190: `const denyRead = policySpellings([...credentials, ...privateReadPaths()], true, fs);` therefore receives no worker-key deny on the disabled startup.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup

findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped or openssl fails after the empty key file is created but before the certificate is written; every subsequent daemon start fails with "Incomplete worker TLS material".

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 writes an empty key.pem before invoking OpenSSL at lines 19–38. Its catch at lines 45–47 performs only `release(); throw error;`. findings.title: Initial pairing permits a relay to steal the worker token
findings.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate and receives both the comparison code and the claim secret. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the initial request and response, so the owner and worker see matching codes, while the attacker learns the secret and can claim the approved token. Pinning the attacker's certificate for subsequent requests does not prevent this.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and the claim secret, or use an authenticated pairing exchange that does not expose the claim credential to an unverified intermediary.
findings.failure_scenario: A network attacker proxies the initial pairing exchange, forwards the genuine code to the worker, and claims the token after the owner approves that code.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 sends the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`, and :114 checks the certificate only `if (options.pin !== undefined ...)`. src/db/workers.ts:83-89 looks up `tokenHash(secret)` and returns `{ token: this.issued(w) }` when approved, without proof of possession of the worker certificate.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory private-path map only in the pairing or worker CLI process, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A daemon running on the same machine has a separate map and does not register these persisted files when constructing its agent sandboxes. Thus an agent reader in that daemon can read the worker token and fingerprint; file mode 0600 does not protect against another process running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that creates agent sandboxes, including when the worker command is not running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a paired worker and a Limitless daemon; an agent launched by the daemon reads the worker token from the data directory and impersonates the worker.

verification.evidence: src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores protections in `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()`; :30 returns only that process's keys. src/workers/tls.ts:52 registers token protection through `protectPrivateFile(path)`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 constructs denies from `[...credentials, ...privateReadPaths()]`; src/harness/codex.ts:302 grants `["/", "read"]`. findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
findings.detail: The key file is created before the asynchronous OpenSSL command completes. If generation fails or the process stops before the certificate is written, the next startup encounters the incomplete pair and always throws. Normal restarts cannot recover without manually deleting the leftover material.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names and publish them only after successful generation, or safely clean up an incomplete first-generation attempt.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before OpenSSL writes cert.pem; every subsequent worker-listener startup fails with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates key.pem before awaiting OpenSSL: `writeFileSync(keyPath, "", { flag: "wx", mode: 0o600 });`. On subsequent startup, src/workers/tls.ts:16–17 rejects a partial pair: `if (!existsSync(keyPath) || !existsSync(certPath))` followed by `if (existsSync(keyPath) || existsSync(certPath)) throw new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material");`. The catch at lines 45–47 only calls `release(); throw error;`, leaving files intact. src/cli/daemon.ts:30 awaits the listener before starting integrations and the owner API, and lines 44–46 propagate its failure.
verification.trigger: With the worker listener configured, interruption after key.pem creation but before cert.pem creation leaves persistent partial TLS material. Every subsequent daemon startup fails until the files are manually repaired or removed.

findings.title: Certificate replacement prevents the documented re-pairing flow
findings.detail: The guide says a worker must pair again after the coordinator certificate changes, but an approved worker's existing name is always rejected by the pairing route. Re-running the documented pairing command with the default name therefore cannot recover unless the owner first revokes the existing record or chooses another name.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection

Comparing the displayed codes does not detect the intermediary because the code is not bound to the TLS connection.

findings.title: Credential read protection ends when pairing exits

A separate daemon on the worker machine therefore does not register those files in its agent sandbox deny rules; running the worker in another process does not share its registrations either. The same lifecycle problem affects an existing coordinator TLS key when its listener is disabled.

findings.title: Permanent TLS and configuration failures retry forever
findings.detail: The catch treats every request error as transient and retries indefinitely without logging the original error. A changed certificate fingerprint, malformed coordinator URL, or invalid stored pin therefore leaves the worker silently looping instead of reporting the failure and requiring corrective action.

findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the key path before invoking OpenSSL, but failures leave generated or partial files in place. The next start either rejects the incomplete pair or reads invalid material, so a transient interruption permanently blocks the worker listener until the files are manually removed.

findings.failure_scenario: OpenSSL times out or the process stops after creating key.pem but before writing cert.pem; subsequent daemon starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

Thus disabling the listener skips registration for the persisted key.

An editor agent running as the same user can read the persisted worker-tls/key.pem because its sandbox lacks the key deny; mode 0600 does not prevent same-user reads. The leaked key enables impersonating the pinned coordinator.

findings.title: An approved pairing that fails before token storage cannot be retried
findings.detail: An approved name is always rejected by `pair`, even if the worker never received or saved its token. A transient failure after approval therefore leaves the worker unable to pair again until the owner explicitly revokes it.
findings.suggestion: Provide a safe recovery path for an approved but unclaimed pairing, or report the required revoke-and-repair action clearly.
findings.failure_scenario: The owner approves a request, but the worker process exits before its next claim; restarting `limitless worker pair` with the same name receives a refusal.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:78 persists `state='approved',token_hash=?` during approval. src/workers/client.ts:30–38 keeps `pending.secret` only in memory; credential files are written only after receiving a token at lines 45–48. On restart, src/db/workers.ts:43–46 rejects the same name because `existing.state === "approved"`, without checking pairing expiry.
verification.trigger: The owner approves pairing, then the worker exits before claiming and storing its token. Restarting the pair command loses the claim secret and is refused for the same name, even after expiry; owner revocation or another name is required to recover.

candidates.title: Initial pairing permits a relay to steal the worker token
candidates.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate and receives both the comparison code and the claim secret. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the initial request and response, so the owner and worker see matching codes, while the attacker learns the secret and can claim the approved token. Pinning the attacker's certificate for subsequent requests does not prevent this.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and the claim secret, or use an authenticated pairing exchange that does not expose the claim credential to an unverified intermediary.
candidates.failure_scenario: A network attacker proxies the initial pairing exchange, forwards the genuine code to the worker, and claims the token after the owner approves that code.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
candidates.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory private-path map only in the pairing or worker CLI process, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A daemon running on the same machine has a separate map and does not register these persisted files when constructing its agent sandboxes. Thus an agent reader in that daemon can read the worker token and fingerprint; file mode 0600 does not protect against another process running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that creates agent sandboxes, including when the worker command is not running.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a paired worker and a Limitless daemon; an agent launched by the daemon reads the worker token from the data directory and impersonates the worker.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
candidates.detail: The key file is created before the asynchronous OpenSSL command completes. If generation fails or the process stops before the certificate is written, the next startup encounters the incomplete pair and always throws. Normal restarts cannot recover without manually deleting the leftover material.
candidates.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names and publish them only after successful generation, or safely clean up an incomplete first-generation attempt.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before OpenSSL writes cert.pem; every subsequent worker-listener startup fails with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Certificate replacement prevents the documented re-pairing flow
candidates.detail: The guide says a worker must pair again after the coordinator certificate changes, but an approved worker's existing name is always rejected by the pairing route. Re-running the documented pairing command with the default name therefore cannot recover unless the owner first revokes the existing record or chooses another name.
candidates.suggestion: Support an explicit secure re-pairing flow for an existing worker, or document the required revocation before re-pairing.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes and an existing worker runs `limitless worker pair` with its original name; the coordinator rejects the request as already paired.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
candidates.detail: The first request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. An active intermediary can forward the pairing request to the real coordinator, relay the same code to the worker, and use the observed pairing secret to claim the approved token. Comparing the displayed codes does not detect the intermediary because the code is not bound to the TLS connection.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate or otherwise authenticate the coordinator before sending the pairing secret.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the initial pairing connection, relays the request and code to the real coordinator, and claims the worker token after the owner approves the matching code.

candidates.title: Credential read protection ends when pairing exits
candidates.detail: The private-file deny registry is process-local, and pairing releases both credential paths before exiting. A separate daemon on the worker machine therefore does not register those files in its agent sandbox deny rules; running the worker in another process does not share its registrations either. The same lifecycle problem affects an existing coordinator TLS key when its listener is disabled.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of whether the worker listener or client is running.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is paired, the pairing command exits, and an agent launched by a separate local daemon reads the worker token from the data directory.

candidates.title: Permanent TLS and configuration failures retry forever
candidates.detail: The catch treats every request error as transient and retries indefinitely without logging the original error. A changed certificate fingerprint, malformed coordinator URL, or invalid stored pin therefore leaves the worker silently looping instead of reporting the failure and requiring corrective action.
candidates.suggestion: Retry only transient transport errors with an appropriate bound, and propagate certificate, pin and configuration errors with their original cause.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing; every heartbeat fails fingerprint verification, but the worker remains running indefinitely with no diagnostic.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
candidates.detail: Certificate generation creates the key path before invoking OpenSSL, but failures leave generated or partial files in place. The next start either rejects the incomplete pair or reads invalid material, so a transient interruption permanently blocks the worker listener until the files are manually removed.
candidates.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths, clean them up on failure, and publish the completed pair only after validation.
candidates.failure_scenario: OpenSSL times out or the process stops after creating key.pem but before writing cert.pem; subsequent daemon starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Worker credentials lose sandbox protection when pairing exits
candidates.detail: Protection is held in a process-local registry and released when pairing finishes. A separate daemon or agent process does not inherit that registration, even though the token and coordinator fingerprint remain on disk. The real-Seatbelt test explicitly registers synthetic files in the same process that launches the gates, so it does not exercise this lifecycle or cross-process case.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that constructs an agent sandbox, and test access from a separately started process after pairing has finished.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine pairs a worker, the pairing command exits, and a separate local factory process launches an agent sandbox that can otherwise reach the worker data directory; the persisted token and fingerprint are absent from that process's private-read registry.

candidates.title: No test covers claiming an approved pairing after coordinator restart
candidates.detail: The implementation reconstructs an issued token from the persistent TLS key so that a worker can claim it after a restart, but the pairing tests approve and claim within one listener lifetime. A regression in key reuse or token reconstruction would leave an approved worker unable to pair without being caught.
candidates.suggestion: Approve a pending request, restart the listener and store, then claim with the original secret and verify that the returned token authenticates a heartbeat.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator restarts after the owner approves a pending request but before the worker claims its token.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator certificate
candidates.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the coordinator generates a random code that is unrelated to either endpoint's certificate. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request and response unchanged, present its own certificate to the worker, and relay the subsequent claim. The owner and worker see the same code, but the worker pins the attacker's certificate and sends it the issued token.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the displayed pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange, and verify that binding on both sides before issuing or accepting credentials.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies requests to the real coordinator, and forwards the unchanged pairing code. After approval, the attacker receives the worker token while the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

candidates.title: Worker credential deny registrations do not protect other processes
candidates.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory, process-local deny list, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A separately running daemon or agent process therefore never registers the worker credential paths. Its agent sandbox can consequently lack the explicit denies required for these files, even while the worker is running in another process.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of the worker process and pairing command.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator with a tool-enabled agent. The worker runs as a separate process, so the coordinator's agent sandbox does not receive the worker token and fingerprint deny entries.

candidates.title: Pairing can be relayed through an attacker-controlled coordinator
candidates.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins that certificate after receiving the pairing response. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the pair request and the unchanged code to the real coordinator, then relay the claim request after owner approval. The codes match, but the attacker obtains the issued token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is stored but is never authenticated or used to bind the claim.
candidates.suggestion: Bind approval and token delivery to authenticated coordinator and worker identities so that relaying a matching code cannot disclose the worker token or substitute the pinned coordinator.
candidates.failure_scenario: A worker pairs over a network controlled by an attacker who proxies both pairing endpoints to the real coordinator; the owner sees the same code and approves, after which the proxy receives the worker token.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not registered for denial in the daemon's sandboxes
candidates.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. Their protection is held only in the pairing or worker CLI process's in-memory private-path registry and is released when that process exits. A separate daemon on the same machine does not register these paths when it starts, so its sandbox policy can permit access to them. The real-Seatbelt test creates and protects all files in the same process as the gate, so it does not cover this deployment.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that launches agent or gate sandboxes, independently of whether the worker CLI is running, and test across the actual process boundary.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is both a worker and a coordinator, with its data directory in a location readable by an agent sandbox; after pairing, a gate launched by the separate daemon reads the worker token and fingerprint.

candidates.title: The coordinator TLS key is unprotected when the listener is disabled
candidates.detail: The request says the TLS key must be read-denied in every agent sandbox. The key path is registered only when the worker listener starts. After a listener has generated the key, disabling `[workers] listen` and restarting leaves the private key on disk without registering it in the daemon's sandbox deny policy. Re-enabling the listener later reuses that key.
candidates.suggestion: Register the existing coordinator key path for sandbox denial independently of whether the listener is enabled.
candidates.failure_scenario: An owner disables the listener after pairing workers, then runs an agent with read access to the data directory; the agent reads the persisted key and can impersonate the coordinator when the listener is re-enabled.

candidates.failure_scenario: The owner approves a request, but the worker process exits before its next claim; restarting `limitless worker pair` with the same name receives a refusal.

findings.title: Treat a worker confinement failure as a terminal failure
findings.detail: A check reporting a confinement failure is rejected as an invalid result, which calls workers.fail. After the retry is exhausted, the LAN executor runs the gates locally and can return a pass. This converts a failed security check into a successful gate result.
findings.suggestion: Preserve confinement failures as a distinct terminal failure and propagate them through the gate result without retrying them into a pass.
findings.failure_scenario: Both worker attempts report a Seatbelt launch failure, but the local fallback executes successfully; the overall gate is reported as passing.

verification.evidence: src/workers/validation.ts:22 rejects checks with `!confinementFailed(r)`. src/server/workers.ts:131-133 handles that rejection with `workers.fail(id, ...)`. src/db/workers.ts:260 transitions exhausted attempts to `"failed"`. src/gates/lan.ts:73-89 handles that state by running locally, then `workers.complete(handle.id, run, true); return workers.sanitize(run);` without retaining a blocking confinement failure.
verification.trigger: Both worker attempts report confinement launch failures; local fallback passes. The returned GateRun contains the passing local outcome, so the confinement failures become infrastructure retries rather than terminal failures.

findings.title: Do not discard failed checks received before an infrastructure failure
findings.detail: Check events from a worker are persisted and forwarded, but the final result is replaced by the next attempt or local fallback if that worker disconnects before posting its GateRun. A later pass therefore erases an already observed failing check, contrary to the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve and account for validated failing check results across attempts when producing the final gate outcome.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a failing test check and loses its connection before posting the final result; the retry or local fallback passes, so the run receives a passing GateRun.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:68–72 reads stored events only into the event stream: "events.push(...stored.slice(index))", then returns the replacement result directly: "if (job.state === 'done' && job.result) return JSON.parse(job.result) as GateRun". The local fallback similarly uses only its new result at src/gates/lan.ts:86–89: "workers.complete(handle.id, run, true); return workers.sanitize(run)". src/db/workers.ts:288–291 stores that result without reconciling earlier failed check events.
verification.trigger: A worker posts a failed check, then disconnects before submitting its final GateRun. Infrastructure retry or local fallback passes that check; the returned GateRun reports a pass despite the recorded failure.

findings.title: Do not retry certificate pin failures indefinitely
findings.detail: The catch treats every workerRequest exception as a transient connection error. That includes an invalid coordinator URL or a changed pinned TLS fingerprint, so the worker silently retries forever instead of surfacing the security or configuration failure. The retry has no deadline.
findings.suggestion: Classify request errors and propagate certificate validation and configuration failures; bound retries for transient transport errors.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator presents a certificate whose fingerprint differs from the stored pin. The worker stays running and retries indefinitely without reporting the fingerprint mismatch.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:114-115 rejects a pin mismatch with `new Error("Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed")`. src/workers/client.ts:146-148 catches every request error and returns `undefined`; :157-158 sleeps and caps the retry delay at 10 seconds inside the unbounded loop at :139.
verification.trigger: The coordinator presents a certificate differing from the stored pin → the worker silently retries indefinitely instead of reporting the permanent fingerprint mismatch.

findings.title: The credential test does not establish worker-side redaction
findings.detail: The worker and coordinator run in the same process and share the credential registry. The test registers the secret globally and checks only the stored coordinator result and events, so coordinator-side sanitization can make it pass even if the worker sends the credential in plaintext.
findings.suggestion: Inspect the outgoing worker event and result bodies before coordinator processing, or run the worker in a separate process with a credential unknown to the coordinator.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker-side redaction is removed and a gate prints a worker-only credential; the shared coordinator registry still redacts the stored output, so this test passes while the credential crosses the connection.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:659 registers `registerCredential("WORKER_OUTPUT_TEST", secret)`; its loop invokes `runWorker(...)` in the same process (test/workers.test.ts:459). Assertions inspect only stored data: `expect(jobs[0]?.result).not.toContain(secret)` and `expect(jobs[0]?.events).not.toContain(secret)` (test/workers.test.ts:681–682). Coordinator storage independently calls `events.push(this.sanitize(event))` (src/db/workers.ts:238), and sanitize uses `redactGateData(data)` (src/db/workers.ts:59).
verification.trigger: Worker-side redaction regresses: the shared credential registry lets coordinator-side sanitization mask leaked output before these storage assertions inspect it. The test never checks the transmitted payload or isolates a worker-only credential.

findings.title: The bundle test never exercises distinct head and base commits
findings.detail: The shared request fixture assigns the same commit to headSha and baseSha. Consequently, the end-to-end bundle test cannot detect an implementation that bundles only the head, even though the request requires both commits to be available on the worker.
findings.suggestion: Create distinct base and head commits and have a worker gate verify that both requested commits are present.
findings.failure_scenario: Bundle creation omits baseSha when it differs from headSha; the existing end-to-end test still passes because its two SHAs are identical.

verification.evidence: The fixture returns `baseSha: sha, headSha: sha` (test/workers.test.ts:123–124). The end-to-end test uses `const req = await request(true)` (test/workers.test.ts:657) and checks only that output contains `req.headSha` (test/workers.test.ts:677). Production bundle creation currently includes both via `[request.headSha, request.baseSha]` (src/server/workers.ts:88).
verification.trigger: A regression drops the distinct base commit from bundle creation. Existing bundle tests continue passing because their base and head are identical and they never verify availability of a distinct base commit.

findings.title: Reconcile streamed check failures with the final result
findings.detail: The coordinator validates each check event and the final GateRun independently. It accepts a passing final result even if the same lease previously reported that check as failed. The failed event is stored, but it does not influence the returned GateRun, so an inconsistent worker response can turn an observed failure into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Validate the final run against the check events recorded for the current lease and treat inconsistent results as an infrastructure failure.

candidates.title: Verify the worker checkout SHA after gates run
candidates.detail: The worker records HEAD before running gate commands and posts that saved SHA with the result. Gate commands can change the worker checkout's HEAD. The coordinator checks its own untouched checkout after the remote execution, so it cannot detect this change and can record passing gate evidence for the requested commit even though a gate ran against another commit.
candidates.suggestion: Re-read HEAD after all gates complete and reject the job as an infrastructure failure if it differs from the requested head; add a test in which a gate changes HEAD.

candidates.title: Treat a worker confinement failure as a terminal failure

candidates.title: Do not discard failed checks received before an infrastructure failure

findings.title: Accepting a passing final result can erase an already reported failure
findings.detail: Check events and the final GateRun are validated independently. The coordinator never compares an event with the corresponding final result, so a worker can report a failed check and then submit the same check as passing. The final passing result is returned to the pipeline even though the coordinator has already received evidence of failure.
findings.suggestion: Track check results by lease attempt and reject a final result that contradicts the events for that attempt, preserving failures as infrastructure failures or explicitly represented retries.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a valid event for the requested test with ok=false, then posts a valid GateRun for the same SHA and command with ok=true and exitCode=0. The job completes successfully.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:125 validates streamed events with `validCheck(request, event.data.result, event.data.phase)`; lines 130–136 independently validate and accept the final run: `!validRun(request, result.data.run)` and `workers.complete(id, result.data.run)`. src/workers/validation.ts:25–49 never reads prior events. src/db/workers.ts:290–291 stores that run as `state='done'`; src/gates/lan.ts:72 returns it as the execution result.

findings.title: Restart discards in-flight LAN retry jobs
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial, and rebase handles are eligible for reattachment. A shutdown during a timeout rerun or a baseline or regression retry leaves its durable LAN job running, but resume treats its handle as stale, cancels it, and enqueues another execution. This repeats work that had already been leased or completed and defeats durable reattachment for these gate executions.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to reattach the matching durable handle on resume, including timeout and targeted retry purposes.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator shuts down after a worker completes a regression-retry job but before the pipeline checkpoints its result. On restart, the completed handle is discarded and the retry is run again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–37 accepts a persisted handle only when stage, round and purpose match and '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)', otherwise calling 'await cancelGateExecution(pending.handle, ctx.deps.gateExecutor)'. Regression retries use 'options?.targeted ? "regression-retry-targeted" : "regression-retry"' (src/pipeline/engine.ts:1265), and the restarted stage first calls runGateExecution with '"initial"' (src/pipeline/engine.ts:1215). With no accepted handle, src/gates/executor.ts:188 executes 'const handle = stored ?? (await executor.start(req, signal))'. Although completed LAN results are durable and attach can return them ('if (job.state === "done" && job.result) return JSON.parse(job.result) as GateRun', src/gates/lan.ts:73), this path never reattaches the retry handle.
verification.trigger: A worker completes a LAN regression-retry job, then the coordinator restarts before checkpointing the pipeline result. On resume, the initial gate invocation discards the persisted retry handle and starts fresh work; if regression retry is needed again, it also runs again instead of consuming the completed result.

findings.title: Local fallback can populate a LAN baseline cache entry
findings.detail: After infrastructure failures, the LAN executor returns a locally executed GateRun as an ordinary LAN result. The baseline cache key was selected as LAN before execution, so a passing fallback baseline is cached under that key. A later run can reuse it while its actual gates execute on a worker with a different environment, even though the cache distinguishes executors to avoid comparing results from different environments.
findings.suggestion: Do not cache a baseline produced by local fallback under the LAN executor key; propagate the actual execution environment or mark fallback results non-cacheable.
findings.failure_scenario: No worker is available for a baseline, so local fallback passes and is cached as LAN. A worker later becomes available and runs the change, while the pipeline reuses the local baseline as its worker baseline.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:551 chooses the cache identity from configuration: `executor: cfg.gateExecutor === "lan" && cfg.workers.repos.includes(ctx.repo.slug) ? "lan" : "local"`. src/gates/lan.ts:77-89 executes fallback via `local.start(request, controller.signal)` and returns `workers.sanitize(run)` without executor provenance. src/pipeline/engine.ts:577 then stores that passing result: `if (cacheableBaseline(fresh, gates)) store.putBaselineCache(key, fresh, ctx.run.id);`. Subsequent runs reuse it at src/pipeline/engine.ts:569-572: `if (cached && cacheableBaseline(cached, gates)) ... return redactGateData(cached);`.
verification.trigger: With LAN enabled for an opted-in repository and baseline caching enabled, unavailable workers cause a passing local fallback baseline to be cached under the LAN key. When workers become available, change gates run remotely while the pipeline reuses the local baseline, potentially reporting worker-environment failures as change regressions.

findings.title: Bound retries for job requests and propagate permanent failures
findings.detail: The shared request loop discards every transport error and retries indefinitely, including certificate fingerprint mismatches and other permanent errors. It also retries every server error without a deadline. Heartbeats can continue renewing a job while a bundle, event, result, or failure request is stuck in this loop, so the coordinator never expires the lease or falls back locally. Permanent connection errors also leave the worker silently retrying instead of reporting the cause.
findings.suggestion: Classify retryable transport and server errors, propagate permanent errors, and bound job-request retries so a failed job stops renewing its lease or reports its infrastructure failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator accepts heartbeats but repeatedly returns HTTP 500 for a job's result endpoint. The worker retries that result forever while heartbeats renew the lease, leaving the gate run pending indefinitely.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:139–158 retries in `for (;;)`, returning only for status 200 and throwing for `reply.status < 500`; otherwise it sleeps and caps only the delay: `delay = Math.min(delay * 2, 10_000)`. src/workers/client.ts:173 sends `jobs: heldJobs()` while the independent heartbeat loop continues at lines 250–254. src/db/workers.ts:187–189 renews each held job with `lease_expires_at=?` using `this.now() + this.times.lease`. src/gates/lan.ts:72–73 completes or falls back only when the job becomes `done` or `failed`.
verification.trigger: The result endpoint repeatedly returns HTTP 500 while heartbeats succeed. Result submission retries without a deadline, and heartbeats continually renew the held lease, leaving the gate run pending indefinitely instead of triggering infrastructure retry and local fallback.

findings.title: A failed streamed check can be replaced by a passing final result
findings.detail: The request says infrastructure failures must “never turn a failing check into a pass” and that the result is untrusted. Streamed check events are stored independently, but the final GateRun is validated only against the requested names and commands; it is never compared with the events already accepted for that lease. A worker can therefore report a failed check and then submit the same check as passing, and the coordinator accepts the passing GateRun as the authoritative outcome.

candidates.title: Accepting a passing final result can erase an already reported failure
candidates.detail: Check events and the final GateRun are validated independently. The coordinator never compares an event with the corresponding final result, so a worker can report a failed check and then submit the same check as passing. The final passing result is returned to the pipeline even though the coordinator has already received evidence of failure.
candidates.suggestion: Track check results by lease attempt and reject a final result that contradicts the events for that attempt, preserving failures as infrastructure failures or explicitly represented retries.
candidates.failure_scenario: A worker posts a valid event for the requested test with ok=false, then posts a valid GateRun for the same SHA and command with ok=true and exitCode=0. The job completes successfully.

candidates.title: Restart discards in-flight LAN retry jobs
candidates.detail: Only baseline, initial, and rebase handles are eligible for reattachment. A shutdown during a timeout rerun or a baseline or regression retry leaves its durable LAN job running, but resume treats its handle as stale, cancels it, and enqueues another execution. This repeats work that had already been leased or completed and defeats durable reattachment for these gate executions.
candidates.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to reattach the matching durable handle on resume, including timeout and targeted retry purposes.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator shuts down after a worker completes a regression-retry job but before the pipeline checkpoints its result. On restart, the completed handle is discarded and the retry is run again.

candidates.title: Local fallback can populate a LAN baseline cache entry
candidates.detail: After infrastructure failures, the LAN executor returns a locally executed GateRun as an ordinary LAN result. The baseline cache key was selected as LAN before execution, so a passing fallback baseline is cached under that key. A later run can reuse it while its actual gates execute on a worker with a different environment, even though the cache distinguishes executors to avoid comparing results from different environments.
candidates.suggestion: Do not cache a baseline produced by local fallback under the LAN executor key; propagate the actual execution environment or mark fallback results non-cacheable.
candidates.failure_scenario: No worker is available for a baseline, so local fallback passes and is cached as LAN. A worker later becomes available and runs the change, while the pipeline reuses the local baseline as its worker baseline.

candidates.title: Bound retries for job requests and propagate permanent failures
candidates.detail: The shared request loop discards every transport error and retries indefinitely, including certificate fingerprint mismatches and other permanent errors. It also retries every server error without a deadline. Heartbeats can continue renewing a job while a bundle, event, result, or failure request is stuck in this loop, so the coordinator never expires the lease or falls back locally. Permanent connection errors also leave the worker silently retrying instead of reporting the cause.
candidates.suggestion: Classify retryable transport and server errors, propagate permanent errors, and bound job-request retries so a failed job stops renewing its lease or reports its infrastructure failure.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator accepts heartbeats but repeatedly returns HTTP 500 for a job's result endpoint. The worker retries that result forever while heartbeats renew the lease, leaving the gate run pending indefinitely.

candidates.title: Reject a final result that contradicts streamed check failures
candidates.detail: Check events are validated and stored independently of the final GateRun. The final result is checked only against the requested names and commands, so a worker can first report a failing check and then submit a passing result for the same check. The coordinator accepts the pass even though it has already recorded evidence of a failure.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile the final result with the events from the current lease and reject contradictory outcomes as an infrastructure failure.
candidates.failure_scenario: A worker posts a valid check event with `ok: false`, then posts a GateRun containing the same check with `ok: true` and exit code 0. Both requests are accepted and the gate completes as passing.

candidates.title: Worker-side credential redaction is not independently tested
candidates.detail: The end-to-end test registers the credential in the same process that runs both the worker and coordinator, then checks only the stored coordinator result and events. Coordinator-side redaction can therefore make the test pass even if the worker sends the credential unredacted. That leaves the requested boundary check untested.
candidates.suggestion: Capture the worker's outgoing event and result payloads before they reach the coordinator, or run the worker in a separate process with a credential unknown to the coordinator, and assert that the credential is absent.
candidates.failure_scenario: Worker-side redaction regresses and a gate prints a worker-only credential. The credential crosses the network, but the current test still passes because the coordinator shares the credential registry and redacts it before storage.

candidates.title: Publish worker check events before validating the final result
candidates.detail: Individual check events are stored and forwarded to the run as gate results after only their name, command, and shape are checked. The worker has not yet supplied a checked SHA or a complete GateRun. If its eventual result has the wrong SHA, omits a check, or never arrives, those earlier events remain visible as pass or fail evidence even though the attempt is classified as an infrastructure failure.
candidates.suggestion: Keep worker check events provisional until the final SHA and GateRun have been validated, or clearly mark and exclude them from authoritative gate evidence until validation succeeds.
candidates.failure_scenario: A leased worker posts a passing event for a requested check, then posts a result with a different SHA. The result is rejected and retried, but the earlier passing event has already been persisted in the run's gate events.

candidates.title: A failed streamed check can be replaced by a passing final result
candidates.detail: The request says infrastructure failures must “never turn a failing check into a pass” and that the result is untrusted. Streamed check events are stored independently, but the final GateRun is validated only against the requested names and commands; it is never compared with the events already accepted for that lease. A worker can therefore report a failed check and then submit the same check as passing, and the coordinator accepts the passing GateRun as the authoritative outcome.
candidates.suggestion: Track the accepted check events for each lease attempt and reject a final result that disagrees with them, treating the mismatch as an infrastructure failure.
candidates.failure_scenario: A worker posts a valid event for the requested `test` check with `ok: false`, then posts a valid final GateRun for `test` with `ok: true` and exit code 0. The job completes as passing despite the recorded failed check.

findings.title: Recheck ownership inside the merge helper before each merge command
findings.detail: The ownership check precedes mergePullRequest, but that helper awaits a GitHub PR lookup before issuing gh pr merge and can repeat that sequence on retry. A reclaim during the lookup is invisible until the heartbeat, so the old worker can still issue a merge after losing its claim.
findings.suggestion: Pass an ownership guard into the helper and check it immediately before each merge command, including retries.
findings.failure_scenario: The old worker enters mergePullRequest, its PR view request is deferred, another owner reclaims the entry, and the view returns before the old heartbeat fires. The old worker then runs gh pr merge.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:701 calls `await mergePullRequest(...)`; ownership is checked only after it returns at :715: `this.assertClaim(entry.id)`. Inside src/git/repos.ts:1447, the helper awaits `sh(view, { cwd, signal })`, then at :1462 executes `sh(cmd, { cwd, signal, stdin: body })` without checking claim ownership.
verification.trigger: Reclaim the entry while the helper's PR view is pending, then return an OPEN PR with the expected head before the heartbeat aborts. The displaced worker issues gh pr merge.

findings.title: Guard the actual push after its preparation awaits
findings.detail: The transaction verifies the claim before calling pushExistingBranch, but that helper awaits commit resolution, transport setup, a remote lookup, and an ancestry check before issuing git push. A reclaim during any of those awaits leaves the old worker able to push before its heartbeat notices.
findings.suggestion: Check ownership inside the push helper immediately before issuing the push, using a guard supplied by the land worker.
findings.failure_scenario: The worker passes the ownership transaction, pauses in the helper's ls-remote call, and another owner reclaims the entry. When ls-remote returns, the stale worker pushes its merge commit.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:517 checks ownership with `this.owned(...)`, then :522 calls `await pushExistingBranch(...)`. In src/git/repos.ts:1313 the helper awaits `remoteSh(["git", "ls-remote", url, ref], ...)`, awaits merge-base at :1315, then pushes at :1321: `await remoteSh([...BRANCH_PUSH, ...])`. Neither continuation checks claim ownership.
verification.trigger: Reclaim after the outer ownership check while the helper's ls-remote is pending. If the remote still matches approvedSha and the signal remains active, the displaced worker pushes its merge commit.

findings.title: Do not discard a checkout reused by the new claimant
findings.detail: All attempts for an entry use the same land-<id> worktree path. After a reclaim, the old worker reaches this unconditional cleanup even when a new worker has already recreated and started using that path. It can remove the new worker's worktree and cause its checks or merge to fail.
findings.suggestion: Isolate checkout paths by claim or otherwise ensure cleanup cannot remove a newer claimant's checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: A CI response is deferred, the entry is reclaimed and the new worker creates its checkout, then the old response returns. The old worker detects the lost claim but its finally block removes the new worker's checkout.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:548-549 executes `await this.observe(...)` followed by `this.assertClaim(entry.id)`, but :396-397 unconditionally runs `finally { await this.discard(repo, cwd); }`. The checkout path at :812 is `join(this.deps.paths.work, `land-${entry.id}`)`, and discard at :842 executes `rmSync(cwd, { recursive: true, force: true })`.
verification.trigger: A new claimant creates its checkout at the same entry-specific path while the old worker awaits CI. When the old response returns, the ownership assertion throws and cleanup deletes the new claimant's checkout.

findings.title: CI inspection can still write after the claim is reclaimed
findings.detail: Passing the ownership check as `current` does not guard every write inside `ciDecision`. Its inspection awaits the default branch and check-run responses, then emits feed events and updates the `ci.main` setting before checking `current()`. A claim reclaimed during either read can therefore leave the old worker writing outcomes after ownership was lost.
findings.suggestion: Check ownership after the awaited reads and in the same transaction as each resulting durable write, including CI inspection writes.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker starts CI inspection, another owner reclaims the entry while the default-branch check response is pending, and the old response contains a failing check. The old worker emits a `ci.main_red` event and updates the CI setting after reclaim.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:584-587 defines `current` to check `this.store.ownsLandClaim(entry.id, this.owner)` and passes it to ciDecision at :631-632. However, src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts:239 awaits `checks(mainSha)`, then :259-264 emits `"ci.main_red"` and :267 executes `store.setSetting(...)` before :268 checks `if (!current()) return true`.
verification.trigger: Reclaim while the default-branch checks response is pending, then return a failing check matching the PR's failing check. The displaced inspection writes a main-red feed event and CI setting before noticing ownership loss.

findings.title: A displaced worker can delete the new owner's worktree
findings.detail: The unconditional cleanup runs after `LandClaimLost` as well as normal completion. Both attempts use the same `land-<entry id>` worktree path, so once a new owner has checked it out, the old worker's `discard` removes that checkout and its Git worktree registration. The new owner can then fail or operate on a deleted checkout.
findings.suggestion: Give each attempt an isolated worktree path or otherwise ensure cleanup cannot remove a successor's checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker is waiting for CI, its claim is reclaimed, and the new worker creates the same checkout. When the old CI response arrives, its ownership check throws and its `finally` deletes the new worker's checkout.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:397 unconditionally executes `await this.discard(repo, cwd)` on exit, including ownership-loss exceptions from :549. Both claimants use :812's `join(this.deps.paths.work, `land-${entry.id}`)`. Cleanup at :839 calls `removeWorktree(...)` and :842 calls `rmSync(cwd, { recursive: true, force: true })` without an ownership guard.
verification.trigger: The new claimant recreates the shared entry checkout before the old CI response completes. The displaced worker detects claim loss but its finally block removes the new owner's worktree. This duplicates C3.

findings.title: A worker that lost its claim can remove the new worker's checkout
findings.detail: The unconditional cleanup runs when an ownership check throws after a reclaim. Both attempts use the same `land-<entry id>` worktree path, so the old worker can remove the checkout after the new owner has created it. This violates the requirement that a worker that lost its claim write nothing and can cause the new attempt's Git commands or gates to fail.
findings.suggestion: Make checkout ownership and cleanup safe across overlapping attempts, and prevent an old attempt from removing a newer attempt's worktree.
findings.failure_scenario: The old worker waits for CI, another queue reclaims the entry and creates its checkout, then the CI response returns. The old worker detects the lost claim but its finally block removes the shared checkout.

candidates.title: Revalidate the PR base before landing
candidates.detail: The unowned request snapshots the PR's base branch, but the subsequent land and merge paths do not verify that GitHub still targets that branch. GitHub can change a PR's base without changing its head SHA, so the pinned-head check does not detect a retarget. The queue can run checks from one base and then squash-merge into another, violating the requirement that the destination base's checks govern the land.

candidates.title: Accept a PR number for an unowned land

An unowned PR supplied as a number always fails with `run not found` even when it belongs to a configured repository.

Hand-made contributions from forks therefore cannot use the confined land queue.

candidates.failure_scenario: A contributor opens a PR from their fork against a configured repository and requests landing with its full current head SHA; the request fails with "cross-repository pull requests cannot be landed".

candidates.title: Unowned PRs cannot be requested by PR number
candidates.detail: The request specifies `limitless land <pr> --sha <full sha>`, and the existing command accepts PR numbers as well as URLs. The new path accepts only a full GitHub URL, so a PR number that has no factory run is rejected as "run not found".

candidates.title: Unowned PR numbers are rejected
candidates.detail: The existing land command accepts a PR number, but the unowned path accepts only a full GitHub URL. A valid manual PR supplied as a number falls through to “run not found,” even when its repository can be determined from the configured context.
candidates.suggestion: Resolve unowned PR references through GitHub and verify the resulting repository is configured, or provide an explicit repository-qualified form when the number is ambiguous.
candidates.failure_scenario: `limitless land 77 --sha <full-sha>` for a manually opened PR returns “run not found”; the new test explicitly expects this result.

candidates.title: All fork PRs are refused
candidates.detail: The request covers open PRs on configured repositories, but this unconditional check excludes PRs whose head is in a fork. In particular, a fork PR whose head already contains the current base can be checked and squash-merged without pushing a base merge, yet it is rejected before queueing.
candidates.suggestion: Support fork PRs through the same pinned checks and merge flow, handling the case where a base merge must be pushed to the head repository.
candidates.failure_scenario: An open PR from a fork targets a configured repository and its approved head already includes the base; the request fails with “cross-repository pull requests cannot be landed.”

candidates.title: Rollback blocks active unowned lands
candidates.detail: The empty-string sentinel satisfies the old schema, but the previous release treats it as a real run ID. After a rollback, its queue resumes the active entry, cannot find run "", and marks the land blocked. Upgrading again cannot resume it automatically, including when the new release had already pushed its checked base merge.
candidates.suggestion: Provide a rollback-compatible representation and processing strategy for active unowned entries, or otherwise ensure the previous release does not claim and permanently block them.
candidates.failure_scenario: Queue an unowned PR, restart into the previous release while it is checking or waiting for CI, and the old worker blocks it with a missing-run error.

candidates.title: Unowned lands have no UI representation
candidates.detail: The new entry is persisted and exposed by the land API, but the UI has no queue view or other rendering path for entries without a run. Its existing land presentation is attached to run details, so a user cannot see the unowned entry in the UI as requested.
candidates.suggestion: Expose unowned land entries in a UI queue or equivalent view, including their state and PR link.
candidates.failure_scenario: Queue a manual PR and open the UI: there is no run detail page for it and no UI list showing its land state.

candidates.title: Blocked unowned lands disappear from the digest
candidates.detail: The new feed item has a null run ID, but the digest discards every item without a run ID before computing actionable blocked lands. Consequently a blocked manual land is omitted from the owner’s actionable feed digest.
candidates.suggestion: Resolve unowned land feed items by their PR URL or land entry ID and evaluate their current state without requiring a run.
candidates.failure_scenario: A manual PR fails its confined checks and produces a `land.blocked` feed item; the digest removes that item because `runId` is null.

candidates.title: Active unowned lands cannot survive a rollback

Verifier: 7 candidates, 7 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: Scratch warnings do not reach an implementer when the round otherwise passes
findings.detail: The warning is appended only when a later implementation stage already runs. An advisory audit finding does not itself produce feedback or schedule another round, so an approved round can proceed to publication with the scratch file still in its commit history. This leaves the reported failure mode unresolved when no gate, review or verification failure happens to trigger another round.
findings.suggestion: Arrange for an implementer to receive actionable scratch feedback before publication while keeping the finding advisory, and cover the otherwise-passing round.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer adds .tmp-gate/report.xml containing output that exceeds the publication decoding limit; gates and review pass. No second implementation runs, and publication is refused.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1124-1139 adds scratch advisories only to a subsequent implementStage prompt: `...(ctx.state.lastAudit ?? []).filter(...)`. But src/pipeline/engine.ts:962-965 immediately exits a passing round: `if (passed) { await ctx.setPhase("deliver"); return; }`. test/pipeline-audit.test.ts:96 explicitly expects `prompts.length` to be `1` when review approves.
verification.trigger: The first implementation adds oversized .tmp-gate/report.xml and gates, review and verification pass. Delivery begins without the implementer receiving the warning; publication can then fail on the decoding limit.

findings.title: Large text logs with terminal control characters are excluded from the size warning
findings.detail: Sizes are recorded only for blobs that pass reviewableText, which rejects control bytes such as ESC. Git can treat a UTF-8 log containing ANSI color sequences as text, but the size rule sees no size for it and emits no warning. Generated command and gate output commonly contains such sequences.
findings.suggestion: Measure new files classified as text independently of the stricter reviewable-content predicate.
findings.failure_scenario: A round adds a 200 KiB UTF-8 build log containing ANSI color escape sequences outside a root hidden directory. It receives no large-text-addition warning.

verification.evidence: src/git/repos.ts:560 rejects control bytes: `if (byte === 0x7f || (byte < 0x20 && ![9, 10, 12, 13].includes(byte))) return false;`. src/git/repos.ts:1150 filters sizes with `.filter((path) => contents.get(afterText.blobs.get(path) ?? "")?.reviewable)`. src/gates/audit.ts:297 requires `(diff.headTextSizes?.[f.path] ?? 0) > 102_400`.
verification.trigger: Add a 200 KiB UTF-8 log containing ANSI ESC bytes outside a root hidden directory. Its size is omitted, so no large-text-addition warning fires.

findings.title: Advisory can reach publication without an implementer seeing it
findings.detail: The warning is added only when an implementation round is already starting. If gates and review pass, the pipeline does not start another round, so the implementer never receives the feedback and the scratch file can remain in the published history. The new approve-path test explicitly expects only one implementation round.
findings.suggestion: Arrange for the implementer to receive and act on the advisory before publication while retaining the requested non-blocking treatment for intentional additions.
findings.failure_scenario: The first round adds .tmp-gate/report.xml and all gates and review pass. The run proceeds without a second implementer prompt containing the warning.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1974-1975 rejects delivery only for missing audit evidence or blocking findings: `!ctx.state.lastAudit || ctx.state.lastAudit.some((f) => f.severity === "block")`. src/pipeline/engine.ts:962-965 sends a passing round directly to delivery. Scratch advisories enter implementer feedback only when implementStage runs again (src/pipeline/engine.ts:1124-1139).
verification.trigger: A first round adds .tmp-gate/report.xml and otherwise passes. Its advisory reaches audit records and review, but no subsequent implementer prompt runs before delivery.

findings.title: Large text logs with terminal escapes are excluded from the warning
findings.detail: The size map excludes anything that fails reviewableText, which rejects escape bytes even in otherwise valid UTF-8 text. Terminal-colored gate output commonly contains ANSI escapes, so a large new log outside a hidden root directory receives no large-text warning.
findings.suggestion: Use a text classification appropriate for the size advisory that includes UTF-8 logs with terminal control sequences.
findings.failure_scenario: A new 150 KiB gate-output.txt contains normal UTF-8 output and ANSI color escapes. It is omitted from headTextSizes and the large-text-addition rule does not fire.

verification.evidence: src/git/repos.ts:560 rejects ANSI ESC (0x1b) through `byte < 0x20 && ![9, 10, 12, 13].includes(byte)`. src/git/repos.ts:1150 includes only `.reviewable` blobs in headTextSizes; src/gates/audit.ts:297 defaults missing sizes to zero.
verification.trigger: Add a 150 KiB gate-output.txt containing ANSI color escapes. The large-text-addition rule silently misses it.

findings.title: Cover large-text warnings in the next-round prompt
findings.detail: The pipeline test exercises next-round feedback only for the root-hidden-addition rule. The large-text-addition rule is tested in audit isolation and with real Git, but no test verifies that its warning reaches a subsequent implementer prompt.
findings.suggestion: Add a pipeline case that commits a new text file over the threshold, triggers a second round, and asserts that the next implementer prompt names the file and large-text advisory.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression removes large-text-addition from the pipeline feedback filter while leaving audit detection intact; the existing tests still pass, but the implementer does not see that advisory in the next round.

verification.evidence: test/pipeline-audit.test.ts:89 creates only a small report: `".tmp-gate/report.xml": "<report/>\n"`; line 106 checks only `expect(prompts[1]).toContain("Advisory [root-hidden-addition] .tmp-gate/report.xml")`. test/gates.test.ts:1080 checks `large-text-addition` detection without exercising pipeline prompts. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1131 independently lists both rules: `["root-hidden-addition", "large-text-addition"].includes(f.rule)`.
verification.trigger: A regression removes `large-text-addition` from the pipeline feedback filter. Detection tests and existing next-round prompt assertions still pass, while large-text advisories disappear from implementer feedback.

findings.title: Encoded credentials in filenames escape diagnostic redaction
findings.detail: The new publication diagnostic passes a Git-controlled path to `redactCredentials` without decoding it first. That function replaces only literal credential variants, so a percent-encoded credential remains recoverable in the error message. The new audit filename handling in `src/gates/audit.ts` has the same issue: `redactGateOutput` also performs literal credential redaction. findings.title: Review eval calls are attributed to one provider and counted as one invocation
findings.detail: Review systems can invoke several finders, samples, and verifiers, including models on different providers. Their trial totals combine those calls, but the fallback creates one record using the trial's primary provider and model. This assigns other providers' tokens and costs to the primary provider and undercounts invocations.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate individual stored call evidence where available, and represent unattributable combined work explicitly rather than assigning it all to the primary provider.
findings.failure_scenario: A review eval calls provider A as its primary reviewer and provider B as a verifier. The report shows one invocation and the combined spend under A, with no invocation or spend under B.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/review.ts:926 returns `result: combined(results, last, { ...decision.review, panel })`; combined sums costs and usage (src/pipeline/review.ts:541–547). src/db/stats.ts:269–275 assigns the entire trial's tokens and costs to `provider: details.provider` and `modelId: String(t.model_id)`. src/db/stats.ts:179 counts `invocations: rows.length`.
verification.trigger: A review eval invokes primary provider A and verifier B. Its combined trial becomes one execution attributed to A, including B's spend and tokens; B's work is omitted.

findings.title: Implementation evals lose stored cache token totals
findings.detail: Every eval with rounds is assigned null cache-read and cache-write tokens, even when the trial contains those accumulated measurements and has only one round. Because the summation returns null if any row is unknown, one implementation eval also makes the corresponding provider totals unknown.
findings.suggestion: Use the stored trial cache totals when they can be attributed, including single-round trials, and preserve known aggregate totals where per-round splits cannot be recovered.
findings.failure_scenario: A single-round implementation trial stores 100 cache-read tokens and 20 cache-write tokens. Its model and provider statistics report both values as null, including when it is the only eval for that provider.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:1143–1144 accumulates `trial.details.cacheReadTokens` and `trial.details.cacheWriteTokens`. Even a single implementation round is stored by `if ("hidden" in item) { ... trial.details.rounds.push(roundEvidence); }` (src/evals/runner.ts:1173–1175). src/db/stats.ts:280–281 sets `const read = rounds?.length ? null : (details.cacheReadTokens ?? null)` and likewise for write.
verification.trigger: A single-round implementation eval stores 100 cache-read and 20 cache-write tokens. Because it has a recorded round, its model and provider statistics report both cache metrics as null.

findings.title: Eval round totals attribute multiple provider calls to one model
findings.detail: A recorded eval round can include retries or panel calls, but its stored tokens and costs are the combined trial delta while its provider and model identify the round target. Treating that round as one invocation assigns all of the combined work to that target and omits the other calls from their providers and models.
findings.suggestion: Use individually attributed call records where available; otherwise expose the attribution as unknown rather than presenting combined spend as belonging to the target.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval panel calls a reviewer on provider A and a verifier on provider B. The resulting round reports both calls' cost and tokens under A and reports no work for B.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:1111–1115 selects a verifier and calls `sendTo(request, to, ...)`; src/pipeline/review.ts:926 combines panel results. src/db/stats.ts:265–275 uses recorded rounds or a single fallback record with `provider: details.provider` and whole-trial `costUsd: Number(t.cost_usd)` and tokens.
verification.trigger: A panel eval calls reviewer A and verifier B. Both calls' cost and tokens appear under A, with no work attributed to B. This duplicates C1's attribution defect; review panels use the trial fallback record rather than persisted implementation rounds.

findings.title: Discarding eval cache splits makes available totals unknown
findings.detail: When rounds exist, the code forces cache-read and cache-write values to null even though the enclosing trial stores accumulated cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens. Consequently a single ordinary multi-round trial makes its provider's aggregate cache and uncached input totals null, despite those totals being available in stored data.
findings.suggestion: Preserve trial-level cache totals for aggregates that can be attributed accurately, and mark only unavailable per-round breakdowns unknown.
findings.failure_scenario: A completed multi-round eval has cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens in its details. Its eval totals nevertheless return null for both cache metrics and inputTokens.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:1143–1144 accumulates cache splits in trial details. src/db/stats.ts:280–281 discards them whenever rounds exist: `const read = rounds?.length ? null : (details.cacheReadTokens ?? null)`. src/db/stats.ts:291 makes `inputTokens` null when either split is null; src/db/stats.ts:171–173 makes a metric's aggregate null if any row lacks it.
verification.trigger: A completed multi-round eval has stored cache-read and cache-write totals. Its round records receive null cache splits, making provider eval cache totals and uncached input totals null despite available trial totals.

findings.title: Count a running eval trial before any provider invocation exists
findings.detail: A running trial with no recorded rounds is converted into a workload record even when it is still preparing and has no invocation status or usage. This silently reports an invocation and an unsuccessful share for work that may never reach a provider.
findings.suggestion: Only count a trial fallback when persisted evidence establishes that a provider call occurred; represent in-progress preparation separately if needed.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval trial is persisted as running while its workspace is being prepared, with zero usage and no rounds or invocationStatus. The statistics report one failed eval invocation before any model call.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:931 persists `store.recordEvalTrial({ ...trial, status: "running" })` before invocation; src/evals/runner.ts:1013 subsequently calls `withScratch(cwd, (dir) => invoke(dir, request, to, log))`. src/db/stats.ts:258 excludes zero-usage records only when `(t.status === "skipped" || details.preparationFailed)`; line 271 otherwise uses `details.invocationStatus ?? String(t.status)`. Lines 179–180 count that row and treat only `status === "ok"` as successful.
verification.trigger: A first eval call is still preparing its invocation workspace after the trial becomes running, with no rounds, invocationStatus or usage. Statistics count one unsuccessful eval invocation before the provider call starts.

findings.title: Eval successful share can reflect grading failures instead of provider results
findings.detail: For implementation evals, the runner can change a round's status from `ok` to `error` or `timeout` when grading fails, even though the provider invocation succeeded. This aggregation uses that modified round status as the provider invocation status, understating the successful share.
findings.suggestion: Preserve and aggregate the provider invocation status separately from the grading outcome.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementation model returns successfully, but its grading process times out. The eval provider statistics count the invocation as unsuccessful.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:1209–1212 changes `roundEvidence.status` to `grade.implement.reason` when the provider result is `"ok"` but grading returns `"error"` or `"timeout"`. src/db/stats.ts:265–266 selects stored rounds, and line 287 uses `status: r.status`; line 180 computes success from `r.status === "ok"`. The preserved `invocationStatus: result.status` at src/evals/runner.ts:1235 is bypassed for rounds.

findings.title: Cross-origin requests can trigger unbounded historical aggregation
findings.detail: The existing GET endpoint now synchronously loads and aggregates every stored invocation and eval trial when no cutoff is supplied. GET requests are exempt from the origin check, so a web page can repeatedly trigger this work against a local daemon even though it cannot read the response. As history grows, each request consumes increasing CPU and memory and blocks the daemon's event loop.

candidates.detail: Review panels can invoke finders and verifiers on different providers and models. The runner combines their usage and costs into the trial totals, but this code assigns all of those totals to details.provider and the trial model. candidates.failure_scenario: A review trial targets provider A but also invokes a verifier on provider B. The full combined token count and cost appear under A, while B receives none.

candidates.title: Implementation evals discard stored cache token totals
candidates.detail: Every eval with round evidence forces both cache measurements to null, even though the runner accumulates cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens on the trial. candidates.suggestion: Use the stored trial cache totals where they can be attributed, and preserve them at an appropriate aggregate level when individual rounds cannot be split.

candidates.title: Recorded rounds are reported as individual invocations
candidates.detail: A round can contain multiple provider calls: the runner retries a failed resumed session within the same round and sums both calls into one round record. Counting each round as one invocation understates workload and its success share reflects only the final result, despite the API naming the field invocations.
candidates.suggestion: Count individual calls when evidence supports it, or expose round counts separately without presenting them as invocation counts or invocation success rates.
candidates.failure_scenario: An implementation round makes a failed resumed call followed by a successful fresh call. Statistics report one successful invocation instead of two calls with one failure.

candidates.title: Combined eval calls are attributed to one provider and counted as one invocation
candidates.detail: For evals without recorded implementation rounds, the fallback treats the entire trial as one provider invocation. This assigns all of that usage to the trial target and omits the other providers' calls, so provider and model workload numbers are wrong.
candidates.suggestion: Aggregate per-call evidence where it is persisted, and make unavailable attribution explicit rather than assigning combined usage to a single provider.
candidates.failure_scenario: An eval review panel calls a finder on provider A and a verifier on provider B. The report counts one invocation and assigns both calls' tokens and cost to A; B receives no workload.

candidates.title: Missing durations are reported as zero total wall time
candidates.detail: The duration aggregation silently drops unknown durations and returns the sum of the remaining values. If every duration is unknown, it reports zero milliseconds; if only some are unknown, it presents a partial sum as the total. This differs from the explicit unknown handling used for the other metrics.
candidates.suggestion: Represent total wall time as unknown when any included duration is unavailable, or expose the measured count and clearly identify the sum as partial.
candidates.failure_scenario: A provider has one unfinished invocation with no finished timestamp. Its historical totals report one invocation and zero milliseconds of total wall time even though its duration is unknown.

candidates.title: Eval rounds discard available cache-token totals
candidates.detail: Every eval trial with recorded rounds reports unknown input and cache-token totals, even when the trial stores those measurements and has only one round. The test explicitly expects null for round cache splits, so it would not catch this loss of available workload data.
candidates.suggestion: Attribute the stored cache totals when they can be assigned unambiguously, and test a single-round trial with nonzero stored cache-read and cache-write tokens.
candidates.failure_scenario: An eval trial has one recorded round and details.cacheReadTokens = 20 and details.cacheWriteTokens = 5; its provider and model report null for both cached-token metrics and uncached input.

candidates.title: Round aggregation test asserts missing cache measurements

candidates.suggestion: Add a single-round eval with nonzero trial-level cache totals and assert the provider/model input, cache-read and cache-write aggregates.
candidates.failure_scenario: A single-round eval stores cache usage in its trial details, but the statistics endpoint returns null for those metrics and the existing test still passes.
