findings.title: Long failing test names can disappear from the excerpt
findings.detail: When an assertion line is followed by a Bun failure line, the excerpt takes the end of the intervening text. If the failure line alone exceeds the remaining budget, this discards its beginning, including the `(fail)` marker and the beginning of the selected signature. The fix round then receives an excerpt that does not identify the failing test.
findings.suggestion: Reserve space for the beginning of the selected signature line before filling the remaining excerpt budget with assertion and stack context.
findings.failure_scenario: A Bun log contains `error: assertion failed` followed by a `(fail)` line whose test name is longer than 2,000 characters. The signature contains the beginning of that line, but the excerpt contains only its tail.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts:91 takes the signature from the line's beginning: `bounded(text, offset(index), offset(index + 1) - 1)`. Lines 98–99 select the excerpt's suffix when `last` is true; line 107 calls `window(..., Math.max(0, 1999 - head.length), true)`. A focused probe with a 2,200-character title returned `hasFail: false` for the excerpt.
verification.trigger: An assertion followed by a failing test title exceeding 2,000 characters produces a signature containing the title's beginning but an excerpt containing only its trailing characters.

findings.detail: The request budgets about 80 lines including tests; the diff adds 354 lines and removes 36, including a new windowed redaction API in a shared utility. This makes the change substantially larger to review and maintain than the stated scope permits.
findings.suggestion: Reduce the implementation and tests to the requested scope, or explicitly explain the necessary overrun.
findings.failure_scenario: Reviewers must assess a shared credential-redaction change and more than four times the requested line budget for a CI signature and excerpt change.

findings.title: An unrelated later test failure can replace the first error as the signature
findings.detail: When the first failure-shaped line starts with `error:`, the search advances to any later `(fail)` line unless another failure-shaped or passing line intervenes. It does not establish that the lines belong to the same Bun assertion block. For a build error followed by a test failure, the signature identifies the later test and the excerpt combines evidence from two failures, potentially discarding the later test's diagnostic. A targeted check, `bun -e 'import {ciSignature} from "./src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts"; console.log(ciSignature("test", "error: first failure\n"+"x".repeat(3000)+"\n(fail) second failure", "fallback"));'`, returned `line: "(fail) second failure"` with an excerpt starting `error: first failure`.
findings.suggestion: Associate an assertion with a following Bun test name only when the intervening output establishes that they belong to the same failure; otherwise retain the first error line.
findings.failure_scenario: A job logs `error: first failure`, then ordinary output, then `(fail) second failure`; the record and fix-round signature identify the second failure while the excerpt begins with the first.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts:88 searches forward using `findIndex((l) => failureLine.test(l) || /^\s*\(pass\)/i.test(l))`; line 89 switches to a subsequent `(fail)` line without checking its relationship to the error. A probe of the supplied input returned `line: "(fail) second failure"` and an excerpt beginning `error: first failure`.
verification.trigger: An independent error followed by ordinary output and an unrelated `(fail)` line is treated as one Bun assertion block, attributing the signature to the later failure.

findings.title: Long Bun failure lines can disappear from the excerpt
findings.detail: When an assertion block precedes a long `(fail)` line, the tail window keeps the end of that line and can discard its beginning, including the failure marker and test name. The selected signature is therefore absent from the evidence sent to the fix round. The targeted command `bun -e 'import {ciSignature} from "./src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts"; const x=ciSignature("test", "error: assertion\n"+"x".repeat(3000)+"\n(fail) important "+"y".repeat(3000), "fallback"); console.log(JSON.stringify({line:x.line.slice(0,40), excerptHasFailure:x.excerpt.includes("(fail)"), excerptLength:x.excerpt.length}));'` produced `{"line":"(fail) important yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy","excerptHasFailure":false,"excerptLength":1999}`.
findings.suggestion: Reserve space for the beginning of the selected signature line while retaining useful assertion and stack context.

findings.title: Rollback to the previous release does not notify the executor
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the database setting written by this new daemon. The previous release never writes that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release SHA in place. A running new executor continues its job and can continue leasing queued jobs even though the active daemon is now the older release.
findings.suggestion: Use release ownership that the previous release can invalidate or otherwise ensure that a rollback stops the executor before the old daemon resumes work.
findings.failure_scenario: Start an in-place gate on this release, then roll back and start the base-commit daemon. The setting still names this release, so the executor does not cancel the gate as required.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:50 adds `factory.store.setSetting("executor.daemonRelease", factory.bootSha);`; the base version's startup proceeds directly to `attachSlotPools` without updating that setting. src/gates/inplace.ts:39 checks only `store.getSetting("executor.daemonRelease", "") !== releaseSha` for release changes and :57 renews the lease when it remains equal. src/db/workers.ts:388 likewise gates leasing on this persisted setting.
verification.trigger: An executor is running a gate when the daemon rolls back to the base release. The older daemon leaves executor.daemonRelease naming the newer release, so the executor continues its gate and can lease queued jobs from that release instead of stopping for the rollback.

findings.title: Process existence is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat timestamp. An executor whose event loop is stalled remains eligible indefinitely. Once its lease expires, the daemon marks the job failed, but waitStopped waits indefinitely while that process exists, so it cannot fall back or proceed with the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, safe path for confirming that an unresponsive executor's gate processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor is alive but paused or blocked while running a gate. Its lease expires; the daemon enters waitStopped and never completes the gate or starts the fallback.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 identifies an executor solely by `return processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth;`. Lease expiry fails the job at src/db/workers.ts:671–672, but src/gates/lan.ts:131 then executes `await workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)`. In waitStopped, recovery only runs when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)` (src/db/workers.ts:370); otherwise it repeatedly sleeps (line 384).
verification.trigger: An executor stops making progress while retaining its process identity and a leased job with stopped=0. After lease expiry, the daemon waits indefinitely for that executor to acknowledge stopping, blocking completion and fallback.

findings.title: Targeted and timeout retry jobs cannot reattach
findings.detail: The resume predicate explicitly accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A restart during an in-place targeted or timeout retry therefore cancels the still-running job and repeats work instead of attaching to its matching handle.
findings.suggestion: Persist and restore the retry context needed to validate and reattach matching retry jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is leased by the executor. On resume, the purpose fails this allowlist and the retry is cancelled or started again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires `pending.purpose === purpose && ["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`; lines 35–43 cancel and clear rejected handles. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 resumes with `"initial"`, while lines 1566 and 1595 start retries with `"timeout"` and `"regression-retry-targeted"`.
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts during an in-place targeted or timeout retry. Stage recovery rejects the saved retry handle, cancels its job and repeats gate work instead of attaching.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback
findings.detail: When the gate executor is configured as LAN, this factory always returns the LAN executor, even when the in-place executor is enabled. Its local path for repositories outside the LAN list runs directly in the daemon, so those local gates cannot survive a daemon restart.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local path through the in-place executor when it is enabled and available.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the executor, configure LAN gates for one repository, and run a gate in another repository. The gate runs in the daemon and is lost on restart despite a live in-place executor.

verification.evidence: src/app.ts:186 passes `gateExecutorFor(cfg.gateExecutor, this.workers, cfg.workers.repos, cfg.executorEnabled)`. However, src/gates/executor.ts:79–81 selects `case "lan": ... return lanExecutor(workers, repos);`, omitting the enabled flag. src/gates/lan.ts:16 defaults `inplace = false`, line 17 constructs `const local = localExecutor();`, and line 71 routes unlisted repositories directly to it: `else if (!repos.includes(req.repo)) return local.start(req, signal);`.
verification.trigger: Set gates.executor to LAN, enable the in-place executor with a fresh heartbeat, and run gates for a repository outside workers.repos. The daemon runs those gates in-process instead of creating a durable in-place job; a daemon restart interrupts them and requires repeated work.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into local retries
findings.detail: The executor catches every error from executeGate and records an ordinary failed job. The attaching daemon then reruns every failed in-place job locally. This loses the distinction between an infrastructure failure and a ConfinementError, so a failed isolation check can be followed by a successful gate instead of failing closed.
findings.suggestion: Persist a failure classification and propagate confinement and inspection failures to the daemon without retrying them.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor's confinement preflight throws ConfinementError, but the daemon's subsequent local preflight succeeds; the gate passes despite the original security check failing.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:70–71 catches every error: `catch (error) { workers.fail(job.id, redactCredentials(String(error))); }`. src/db/workers.ts:626–632 marks in-place jobs `state='failed'`. src/gates/lan.ts:130–139 handles that state by calling `local.start(request, controller.signal)` and `local.attach(...)`, without distinguishing ConfinementError.
verification.trigger: Executor confinement preflight throws ConfinementError; the job becomes failed and triggers local fallback. If the daemon’s preflight succeeds, its passing gate result replaces the security failure.

findings.title: A cleanup failure can leave the run waiting indefinitely
findings.detail: waitStopped only attempts recovery or reports an error after the executor process disappears. If a job finishes with process discovery or cleanup records remaining, the executor deliberately leaves stopped=0 but continues running. waitStopped then polls forever because the executor is still alive, even though that executor will never revisit the completed job.
findings.suggestion: Make the executor publish a terminal cleanup failure, or have waitStopped detect that the job is no longer being cleaned up and fail closed with a clear error.
findings.failure_scenario: A cancelled gate leaves a cleanup record after process cleanup fails; the executor continues polling for other jobs, while the daemon waits forever to start the replacement gate.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:76–80 sets stopped=1 only when `!store.listProcessDiscoveries(undefined, req.cwd).length && !store.listProcessCleanups(undefined, req.cwd).length`, then returns to the polling loop at line 29. src/db/workers.ts:370 permits recovery only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`; with a live executor, line 384 only sleeps.
verification.trigger: Process cleanup fails and leaves a discovery or cleanup record. The executor catches the failure and continues polling, leaving stopped=0 permanently. Cancellation or replacement waits indefinitely because the daemon neither retries recovery nor reports the unconfirmed stop while that executor remains alive.

findings.title: Worktree exclusion is not atomic across concurrent starts
findings.detail: The query for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations. Two daemon-side starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue independently. With two executor processes, each can lease one job and run both gates in the same worktree.
findings.suggestion: Enforce worktree exclusivity atomically in the database when creating or leasing an in-place job.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concurrent gate starts for the same cwd pass the existing-job query before either enqueues, and two executors lease their jobs concurrently.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:54–59 checks existing jobs by cwd, then src/gates/lan.ts:72 yields at `await releaseGateSlotScope()`. Jobs are inserted later in attach: `workers.enqueue(req, handle.id, true)` (src/gates/lan.ts:80–81). Concurrent starts can therefore both pass the query. Leasing checks only the individual job: `WHERE id=? AND state='queued'` (src/db/workers.ts:400), with no worktree exclusion.
verification.trigger: Two concurrent starts for the same cwd complete their exclusion queries before either attaches. Both enqueue distinct jobs; two executor processes with available gate capacity can lease them and run checks in the same worktree simultaneously.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after a restart
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A durable in-place handle for a targeted retry is therefore cancelled even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and lease all match. The retry is restarted instead of receiving the surviving job's result.
findings.suggestion: Provide a resume path for targeted retry purposes and preserve the state needed to resume them.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is running; resume rejects its matching handle, cancels the executor job, and runs the retry again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 assigns targeted retries purpose `"regression-retry-targeted"`. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 permits only `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`; lines 35–43 cancel the rejected job and clear its handle.
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts while a targeted retry is running. Recovery rejects its saved handle and repeats gate work instead of receiving the existing job's result.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness check
findings.detail: Executor availability is based only on PID and birth identity; the executors table has no heartbeat timestamp. A live but stalled executor is treated as available indefinitely. New gates are enqueued instead of immediately using the requested in-process fallback, and a leased job is not considered disconnected until its lease expires.
findings.suggestion: Record and renew an executor heartbeat and require it to be fresh when selecting an executor and sweeping its jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops making progress; the daemon treats it as available and waits for pickup or lease expiry rather than recognizing that no fresh executor is available.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:354 reads executor identity fields `id, pid, birth, release_sha`, and line 359 checks only `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. src/gates/lan.ts:62 uses `if (!workers.executor())` to choose immediate in-process fallback. Queued jobs instead wait until the pickup timeout at src/db/workers.ts:656–657: `this.fail(j.id, "No worker picked up job")`.
verification.trigger: An executor remains alive but unresponsive. The daemon considers it available despite its lack of progress, enqueues work, and waits for pickup timeout instead of immediately using the required fallback for an executor without a fresh heartbeat.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs are cancelled on restart instead of reattached
findings.detail: Resume accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A recorded `baseline-retry-targeted` or `regression-retry-targeted` handle therefore fails the resume check even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and executor lease match. The live job is cancelled and the stage starts over, contrary to the requested restart behavior for targeted retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry state to resume the targeted retry and accept its matching handle during stage recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running a long targeted regression retry; the new engine cancels that job and repeats gate work instead of receiving its result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1536 calls `resumeGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", cwd, env)`, but line 1595 records targeted retries as `"regression-retry-targeted"`. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 rejects that purpose, and lines 35–43 cancel and clear the job.
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts during an executor's targeted regression retry. The resumed stage cancels the retry as a mismatch and starts gate work again.

findings.title: Restart coverage omits targeted retries
findings.detail: The engine restart cases cover baseline, initial, and rebase gates, but none interrupts a targeted baseline or regression retry. Consequently the tests do not catch the resume-purpose restriction that cancels those jobs.
findings.suggestion: Add a restart test that pauses a targeted retry, resumes the engine, and asserts that the same job completes and its command ran once.
findings.failure_scenario: A targeted retry is running when the daemon stops; the current suite passes without checking whether the resumed engine reattaches to it.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:487–494 enumerates only ["baseline", "matching"], ["baseline", "changed"], ["initial", "matching"], ["initial", "changed"], ["rebase", "matching"], and ["rebase", "changed"]. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 restricts resume to '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)'.
verification.trigger: A daemon restarts during a targeted retry; the restart tests never exercise that purpose or assert reattachment to its existing job.

findings.title: Pickup timeout test never verifies in-process fallback
findings.detail: The pickup test stops after asserting that the queued job becomes failed. It does not attach a daemon-side execution or assert that the check subsequently runs locally and returns its result, so a regression in the failed-job fallback path would pass.
findings.suggestion: Exercise an attached in-place job that is never leased, sweep it past pickup timeout, and assert that the local check runs and its result reaches the caller.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor remains alive but does not pick up a queued job, and the daemon fails to start the local fallback after the sweep marks it failed.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:319–324 calls 'later.sweep()' and asserts only 'state).toBe("failed")' and 'attempt).toBe(1)' before ending. The fallback requires the separate attach path in src/gates/lan.ts:130–139: 'if (job.state === "failed")' followed by 'await local.start(request, controller.signal)'.
verification.trigger: A live executor leaves a job queued until pickup timeout; this test passes after the failed-state transition even if attachment never starts the in-process fallback.

findings.title: Gate result comparison discards most of the result shape
findings.detail: The purported in-process comparison projects each result down to name, ok, and exitCode, while the event assertion checks only names. It would still pass if executor results or events lost output, command, timing, failure metadata, or other fields required by consumers. The test also does not compare the produced gate artifacts.
findings.suggestion: Compare representative complete result and event structures, excluding only nondeterministic values, and verify the corresponding artifact contents.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor drops a check's output or failure metadata while preserving its name and exit code; this test still passes although the reported gate data changed.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:114–115 projects results through 'map(({ name, ok, exitCode }) => ({ name, ok, exitCode }))'; line 144 compares only those projections. Line 146 separately checks output for the environment check alone. src/gates/run.ts:28–32 also defines 'output', 'failures', 'timedOut', and 'confinementError'.
verification.trigger: The executor loses another check's output or failure metadata while retaining name, ok, and exitCode; the result comparison still passes.

findings.title: Executor stores gate output without the daemon’s dynamic credential registrations
findings.detail: Credential registrations are process-local. The executor loads configured provider credentials, but it does not receive credentials registered dynamically by the daemon, such as GitHub installation tokens and worker tokens. It redacts and persists check events and results using its own incomplete registry before the daemon sees them, so the daemon’s later redaction cannot remove the copies already stored in gate_jobs.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the executor has the daemon’s complete current redaction set before processing output, or defer persistence of output to a boundary that has that set while preserving restart-safe event handling.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon registers a GitHub installation token during operation, and a gate prints that token. An in-place executor that never registered the token stores it unredacted in the job’s events or result.

verification.evidence: src/util/proc.ts:1216–1224 keeps registered credentials in process-local sets: `const credentialValues = new Set<string>()` and `credentialValues.add(secret)`. src/gates/inplace.ts:65 writes check events through `workers.event(...)`, and :69 calls `workers.complete(job.id, run)`. src/db/workers.ts:612–613 persists `this.sanitize(event)`; :717 persists `this.sanitize(run)`. That sanitizer (:129–133) uses local redaction and privacy policy; no daemon credential registrations are transferred.
verification.trigger: A credential registered dynamically only in the daemon appears in gate output. The separate executor does not recognize it and persists it unredacted in gate job events and results, assuming it is not independently covered by the private-output policy.

findings.title: Confinement derives credential paths from the executor environment
findings.detail: The gate receives the daemon’s saved environment, but the executor constructs its read policy from its own process environment. The policy uses environment variables such as AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, GH_CONFIG_DIR, and CARGO_HOME to deny credential paths. When those variables differ between the daemon and executor, a credential path known to the daemon can be omitted from the executor’s deny list, weakening the confinement applied to untrusted gate commands.
findings.suggestion: Build the gate’s confinement policy from the same trusted environment used by the daemon, including its credential-path variables, and refuse execution if that policy cannot be reconstructed.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon has AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE pointing to a credential file under an otherwise allowed toolchain path, while the executor lacks that variable. A gate can read the file through the in-place executor even though the daemon’s local confinement would deny it.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:27 scopes execution with `readPolicyScope.run(cfg.readPolicy, ...)`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:144 derives credential paths from `options.environment ?? process.env`, including `env.AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE` (:169). src/harness/sandbox.ts:351 computes confinement using `writeRoots(opts.cwd, scratch, true)`, independently of the request environment. src/harness/read-policy.ts:204 permits configured toolchains, while :209–212 rejects overlaps only with the credentials discovered in that process.
verification.trigger: Only the daemon has AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE pointing inside an allowed toolchain directory. The executor builds its policy without that credential path, allowing the gate to read a file that the daemon’s policy would protect by refusing the overlap.

findings.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after restart
findings.detail: The request says the local executor covers “the targeted retry” and that a resumed stage with the same stage, round, purpose and SHA attaches to its job. The purpose whitelist excludes both regression retry purposes and baseline retry purposes. On resume, the surrounding stage first asks to resume its initial gate, so it cancels the still-running retry and starts the stage's gate work again.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the recorded retry at its original point, and include its purpose in the resume validation.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running `regression-retry-targeted`; the resumed stage treats the handle as a mismatch, cancels the retry and reruns gate work instead of receiving that job's result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 restricts resumable purposes to `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"]`; lines 35–43 cancel and clear other pending executions. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 starts targeted jobs with purpose `"regression-retry-targeted"`.
verification.trigger: A running in-place regression-retry-targeted job survives a daemon restart. Recovery rejects its handle and cancels it rather than attaching, causing repeated gate work.

findings.title: Executor liveness is process existence, not a fresh heartbeat
findings.detail: The request requires fallback when no executor has a fresh heartbeat and requires the sweep to apply freshness timers against that heartbeat. Executor rows contain no heartbeat timestamp; this method only checks whether the PID and birth time still exist. In addition, `waitStopped` waits indefinitely while that process exists, even after its job lease expires.
findings.suggestion: Record and check a bounded executor heartbeat, and make the stop/fallback path handle an unresponsive owner without assuming that process existence proves progress or safe cleanup.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process becomes unresponsive while its gate is running. Its lease expires, but the daemon regards the executor as alive and waits indefinitely for `stopped` rather than reaching a safe fallback.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 checks executor liveness using `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. After lease expiry fails the job (lines 671–672), src/gates/lan.ts:131 waits for stopped. src/db/workers.ts:366 loops while `this.job(id)?.stopped === 0`, and lines 370–384 perform recovery only if the executor identity disappears; otherwise they sleep without a deadline.
verification.trigger: An executor becomes unresponsive during a gate but its process remains present. Its lease expires, yet the daemon remains in waitStopped indefinitely, preventing safe fallback until the executor resumes or exits.

findings.title: Rollback to an older release does not notify the executor
findings.detail: The request says that when the daemon's release changes, including a rollback, the executor stops leasing and cancels its running jobs. The release marker is written only by this new daemon code. A rollback to the previous release starts a daemon that does not write that marker, so the executor continues to see its own SHA in the database and does not detect the release change.
findings.suggestion: Use a release identity that remains observable across rollback to the previous release, and test an actual old-daemon/new-executor transition.
findings.failure_scenario: A new-release executor is running a gate when deployment rolls back to the base release. The old daemon starts without updating `executor.daemonRelease`, and the executor continues running and leasing as though its daemon release had not changed.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:50 introduces the sole writer of `executor.daemonRelease`, absent from base-release startup. src/gates/inplace.ts:39 uses `store.getSetting("executor.daemonRelease", "") !== releaseSha` to detect a changed release; :53–57 renews leases otherwise. src/db/workers.ts:388 permits leasing while that stale setting matches the executor release.
verification.trigger: Rollback starts the older daemon while the newer executor remains alive. Because the older daemon never updates executor.daemonRelease, the executor fails to detect the rollback and continues running and leasing newer-release jobs.

candidates.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the database setting written by this new daemon. The previous release never writes that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release SHA in place. A running new executor continues its job and can continue leasing queued jobs even though the active daemon is now the older release.
candidates.suggestion: Use release ownership that the previous release can invalidate or otherwise ensure that a rollback stops the executor before the old daemon resumes work.
candidates.failure_scenario: Start an in-place gate on this release, then roll back and start the base-commit daemon. The setting still names this release, so the executor does not cancel the gate as required.

candidates.failure_scenario: An executor is alive but paused or blocked while running a gate. Its lease expires; the daemon enters waitStopped and never completes the gate or starts the fallback.

findings.title: Rollback to an older daemon does not stop the executor
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the persistent `executor.daemonRelease` setting. A daemon from before this change never updates that setting, so after rollback it still contains the newer release SHA. The newer executor continues its running job while the older daemon resumes the run without understanding the in-place handle, allowing both releases to operate on the same worktree.
findings.suggestion: Use a coordinator release and liveness mechanism that also detects replacement by a daemon that does not write this setting, and stop the executor's jobs before the older daemon can resume them.
findings.failure_scenario: A new-release in-place gate is running when the daemon is rolled back to the base release. The old daemon leaves the setting unchanged and starts its own recovery or gate while the executor continues.

verification.trigger: Roll back to the base daemon while an executor gate runs. The setting retains the newer release SHA, so the executor continues running and can keep leasing despite the daemon running another release.

findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A running `regression-retry-targeted` job therefore gets cancelled on restart even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, release, and lease still match. The stage repeats work instead of attaching to the retry, contrary to the requested coverage of targeted retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry progress to resume the targeted retry at its recorded purpose and attach to its matching job.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long targeted regression retry is running. On resume, the saved handle fails the purpose check and the running job is cancelled.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor can block a worktree indefinitely

If the executor is alive but no longer making progress, the sweep eventually fails its lease, but `waitStopped` continues waiting for that same live process to set `stopped`. Consequently the daemon never reaches the in-process fallback or starts another gate in the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a bounded, confirmed process-stop or recovery path before falling back.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor becomes stuck while running a gate but remains alive. Its lease expires, and the daemon waits indefinitely in `waitStopped`.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into a local retry

The daemon treats every failed in-place job as eligible for local fallback in `lan.ts`. A confinement inspection failure can therefore be replaced by a passing second execution, hiding the failed security check and allowing the gate to pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the failure classification across the job boundary and propagate confinement failures without retrying them as local gates.

findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth time; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. Lease expiry therefore does not produce a bounded fallback or a completed cancellation.

candidates.title: Rollback to an older daemon does not stop the executor
candidates.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the persistent `executor.daemonRelease` setting. A daemon from before this change never updates that setting, so after rollback it still contains the newer release SHA. The newer executor continues its running job while the older daemon resumes the run without understanding the in-place handle, allowing both releases to operate on the same worktree.
candidates.suggestion: Use a coordinator release and liveness mechanism that also detects replacement by a daemon that does not write this setting, and stop the executor's jobs before the older daemon can resume them.
candidates.failure_scenario: A new-release in-place gate is running when the daemon is rolled back to the base release. The old daemon leaves the setting unchanged and starts its own recovery or gate while the executor continues.

candidates.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after restart
candidates.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A running `regression-retry-targeted` job therefore gets cancelled on restart even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, release, and lease still match. The stage repeats work instead of attaching to the retry, contrary to the requested coverage of targeted retries.
candidates.suggestion: Persist enough retry progress to resume the targeted retry at its recorded purpose and attach to its matching job.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long targeted regression retry is running. On resume, the saved handle fails the purpose check and the running job is cancelled.

candidates.title: A live but unresponsive executor can block a worktree indefinitely
candidates.detail: Executor freshness is determined solely by whether its PID and birth time still match; there is no heartbeat. If the executor is alive but no longer making progress, the sweep eventually fails its lease, but `waitStopped` continues waiting for that same live process to set `stopped`. Consequently the daemon never reaches the in-process fallback or starts another gate in the worktree.
candidates.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a bounded, confirmed process-stop or recovery path before falling back.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor becomes stuck while running a gate but remains alive. Its lease expires, and the daemon waits indefinitely in `waitStopped`.

candidates.title: Confinement failures are converted into a local retry
candidates.detail: The executor catches every error from `executeGate`, including `ConfinementError`, and marks the job failed. The daemon treats every failed in-place job as eligible for local fallback in `lan.ts`. A confinement inspection failure can therefore be replaced by a passing second execution, hiding the failed security check and allowing the gate to pass.
candidates.suggestion: Preserve the failure classification across the job boundary and propagate confinement failures without retrying them as local gates.
candidates.failure_scenario: The executor cannot verify its Seatbelt confinement, but the daemon's subsequent local confinement check succeeds; the local retry passes and the original security failure is lost.

candidates.title: A live but unresponsive executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
candidates.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth time; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor remains alive but stops making progress, new jobs are sent to it and previously leased jobs eventually enter `waitStopped`, which continues waiting as long as that process exists. Lease expiry therefore does not produce a bounded fallback or a completed cancellation.
candidates.suggestion: Track executor freshness and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for an unresponsive owner while confirming its gate processes have stopped.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor hangs while running a gate and stops renewing its lease. The sweep marks the job failed, but `waitStopped` waits indefinitely because the executor PID still exists, so the run never falls back or finishes.

candidates.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after restart

candidates.failure_scenario: The executor launches a gate without its required confinement; every new executor test still passes because the test fixture disables confinement.

candidates.title: Executor output is redacted with an incomplete credential registry
candidates.detail: Credential registration is process-local. The separate App check at lines 135–139 reports `missing.length ? "fail" : "ok"` but never updates ghOk. Lines 266–277 compute `ok = checks.every((c) => c.status !== "fail")` and return `ok ? 0 : 1`.
verification.trigger: All configured repositories use the App, its token exchange succeeds and installation coverage is complete, but the owner has no gh login. Doctor still reports a failed gh authentication check and exits 1.

candidates.title: Verify that the key is owned and readable by the daemon user
candidates.detail: The startup check inspects permission bits but neither checks the file owner nor attempts to read the file. A regular file owned by another user with mode 0600 passes validation, so the daemon starts even though it cannot read the key. The failure is deferred until a configured repository first needs a token.
candidates.suggestion: Verify ownership and actual readability during configuration loading, and reject the file with a clear startup error when either check fails.
candidates.failure_scenario: The configured key is owned by a different user and has mode 0600. Startup accepts it; the first App-backed GitHub call fails while reading the key.

candidates.title: Prevent an App key inside an agent-readable checkout
candidates.detail: The key path may resolve anywhere, including inside a repository checkout. A mode-0600 file there is accepted, but agents and gate commands run as the same user and can read files in their checkout. This violates the requirement that the App key never reach an agent or gate.
candidates.suggestion: Reject key locations accessible to agents and gates, or enforce an equivalent isolation rule for the configured key path.
candidates.failure_scenario: An operator configures an absolute private_key_path pointing to a mode-0600 PEM file in a managed checkout. An agent or gate running in that checkout can read the private key.

candidates.title: Token exchange ignores caller cancellation and timeout
candidates.detail: The provider creates its own 30-second timeout and does not accept the caller's abort signal or deadline. A GitHub operation can therefore remain in the shared token exchange after its caller is cancelled, and the initial token request plus the App lookup can each consume 30 seconds before the requested gh command starts.
candidates.suggestion: Propagate cancellation and the operation's deadline through identity acquisition, while preserving safe handling of concurrent callers sharing an exchange.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run is cancelled while its first installation-token request is stalled. The run continues waiting for the provider's timeout instead of ending promptly.

candidates.title: Key validation does not establish that the daemon can read the key
candidates.detail: The startup check inspects permission bits but does not verify the file's owner or attempt to read it. A regular 0600 file owned by another user passes this check even though the daemon cannot read it, so startup succeeds and configured GitHub operations fail later.
candidates.suggestion: Validate ownership and actual readability at startup, and report a clear configuration error when either check fails.
candidates.failure_scenario: The configured key path points to a 0600 file owned by another user. loadConfig accepts it, but the first App token exchange fails when readFileSync attempts to open it.

candidates.title: Validate the key file's owner and exact permissions
candidates.detail: The startup check only inspects the file type and selected permission bits. It does not verify that the file belongs to the current user, and it accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 even though the request requires mode 0600. A file owned by another user can pass the check despite being unreadable to the daemon, deferring failure until a GitHub operation.
candidates.suggestion: Require the current user's ownership and mode 0600, and verify that the key is readable at startup.
candidates.failure_scenario: A regular key file owned by another user with mode 0600 passes configuration validation, but the daemon cannot read it when it needs to sign a JWT.

candidates.title: Correct the test that accepts a non-0600 key
candidates.detail: The test explicitly expects a 0400 key to be accepted, asserting behavior contrary to the requested mode 0600 requirement. The permission cases also do not cover ownership or owner execute permissions, so they do not catch the incomplete startup validation.
candidates.suggestion: Expect non-0600 modes to fail and add coverage for a key not owned by the daemon user where the test environment supports it.
candidates.failure_scenario: Changing validation to enforce the requested exact mode causes this test to fail, while the existing incomplete check passes it.

candidates.title: Protect the configured private key outside the config directory
candidates.detail: The configuration accepts an absolute key path or a relative path that escapes the config directory, but the read policy only adds the config directory to its credential deny list. A key at another agent-readable location can therefore be read by an agent or gate running as the same user. The key itself is not registered for output redaction.
candidates.suggestion: Add the resolved key file, including its canonical path and relevant aliases, to the shared read-deny policy used by every agent and gate, or reject paths whose confinement cannot be guaranteed.
candidates.failure_scenario: An operator configures a mode-0600 key at an absolute path inside a checkout. An agent or gate reads that file and can publish the App private key.

candidates.title: Enforce the specified key-file mode and readability at startup
candidates.detail: The mode check accepts owner-executable files such as 0700, and checking the owner-read bit does not establish that the daemon can actually read the file. The request requires a readable mode-0600 file and startup refusal otherwise; an unreadable file currently passes configuration and fails only when an App call is attempted.
candidates.suggestion: Validate the required mode and verify the file can be opened during configuration loading, reporting a clear startup error.
candidates.failure_scenario: A key file has mode 0700, or has mode 0600 but belongs to a different user. Configuration loads even though the required startup validation should refuse it.

candidates.title: Manual landing bypasses the configured App identity
candidates.detail: The request requires “one implementation used by every factory gh invocation for a repository” and says configured repositories use the App. This script invokes gh directly without loading or configuring the identity provider, including for the merge. Consequently manual landing uses the owner's login and can merge even when an App token exchange would fail.
candidates.suggestion: Initialize the configured identity provider in this script and route its repository-scoped gh calls through it.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run scripts/land-pr.sh for an App-configured repository: its private-strings merge step invokes gh with the owner's credentials, so the merge appears owner-authored.

candidates.title: Key validation does not enforce the required mode or readability
candidates.detail: The request says the key must be a regular file with “mode 0600” and that startup refuses otherwise. This check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700, and checks the owner-read permission bit without checking whether the process can actually read the file. For example, a 0600 file owned by another user passes startup validation but cannot be read when an App call is attempted.
candidates.suggestion: Enforce the required permission bits and verify that the configured key is readable during startup.
candidates.failure_scenario: Configure a regular private key owned by another user with mode 0600: startup succeeds, but the first App identity request fails to read the key.

candidates.title: Doctor still requires an owner gh login for an App-only configuration
candidates.detail: The request says doctor reports the active identity and whether the App token exchange works. Doctor unconditionally marks gh authentication as failed before checking the App identity, even when every configured repository uses the App and the exchange and installation coverage succeed. This reports a working App-only setup as failed.
candidates.suggestion: Make the gh authentication check reflect whether any configured repository needs the owner's login.
candidates.failure_scenario: With only App-configured repositories and no owner gh login, doctor reports gh authentication failure despite a successful App token exchange and complete repository coverage.

Verifier: 21 candidates, 21 checked, 4 refuted.

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
findings.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102: `if (run.status === "needs_human") events.set("needs_human", ...)`; :113: `if (!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending") continue;`. The checkpoint is created only when processing that event (:159–162).
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and resumes between polls, before its comment checkpoint exists. Reconciliation sees the resumed status and permanently omits the needs-you comment and reason.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12: `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; :43: `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/index.ts:66–67 mounts the queue only when queue repositories and trusted accounts are configured.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains Closes #42 in a GitHub repository absent from githubQueue.repos. Its lifecycle labels and comments are skipped despite the requirement covering every start path.

findings.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #42` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an error. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders labels as in-progress, needs-you, failed; :68–86 processes them in that order and throws on a failed addition. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 reconciles before selecting candidates; :97 checks failure re-approval only when the failed label exists. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts `latestIssueRun` to `source_ref.kind = 'issue'`, excluding ordinary CLI Closes links.
verification.trigger: An otherwise eligible issue has an old trusted priority label and a failed CLI-linked run. Removing in-progress succeeds but adding failed fails. The poll continues selection with neither label, no active claim, and no latest issue-source run, allowing re-pick without re-approval.

findings.title: An older run can overwrite a newer run's issue labels
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub requests. If another run for the issue is created while a label request is awaiting, the old run remains designated latest and can complete its label transition after the newer run starts. Its completed cursor then prevents correction until the newer run is reconciled on a later poll.
findings.suggestion: Recheck which run owns the issue after awaited operations and before each label mutation and completion checkpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation fetches labels for a failed run, a new run for the same issue starts; the old reconciliation then applies failed and removes in-progress for the active run.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:35–39 builds `latest` once from `store.issueLifecycleRuns()`; :56 checks that snapshot before the awaited label fetch (:60). Afterward, :63–71 re-reads only `store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and checks its desired label, without checking for a newer run.
verification.trigger: A new run for the issue is admitted while the old failed run awaits its label fetch. The stale ownership map still authorizes the old run to remove in-progress and apply failed to the active run's issue until a subsequent reconciliation corrects it.

findings.title: Persist lifecycle events when they occur, not only when a poll observes them
findings.detail: The needs-human, failure, and cancellation comments are created only when reconciliation observes the corresponding current status. No pending effect exists until the comment loop reaches that event. A status that changes between polls, or while an earlier comment write is failing, is therefore never recorded or retried. The single done cursor also suppresses a second needs-human episode for the same run.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle event and its publication-safe content durably at the state transition, then let polling deliver each recorded event.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next poll; reconciliation sees the resumed status and never posts the required reason. Similarly, a failed started-comment write can delay processing until after needs_human has ended.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:99–103 derives events from current run fields and status; :110 processes started before needs_human; :165–167 catches a comment failure and `break`s. Event bodies and pending checkpoints are saved only when that event is reached (:159–162).
verification.trigger: A needs_human episode ends before polling observes it, or a failed started-comment write prevents processing needs_human before the owner resumes. No needs_human checkpoint or original reason survives, so its required comment is never posted.

findings.title: Reconcile issue-linked runs outside queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle processing is restricted to repositories listed in githubQueue with a nonempty trusted list, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. The request applies lifecycle updates to issue-linked runs from every start path; it does not condition those updates on queue admission being enabled for the repository.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and determine the target repository from each linked issue.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository not listed in githubQueue, or with the queue disabled. No lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments are written for that issue.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10-12 defines lifecycleManaged using githubQueue.trusted and githubQueue.repos; line 43 skips issues with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/index.ts:65-67 starts the reconciler's queue only when `!!queue?.repos.length && !!queue.trusted.length`.
verification.trigger: Start an issue-linked run outside configured queue repositories, or with the queue disabled. Its issue receives no lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments.

findings.title: Prevent re-pick while a failed label write is pending
findings.detail: The new re-approval guard depends on the failed label being visible on GitHub. If that write fails, the queue continues selection in the same poll. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only considers issue source references, so it cannot supply a local failure guard for runs linked through a Closes directive.
findings.suggestion: Use the existing admission and claim check to account for the latest linked run and its failure while the GitHub failure-label effect is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails, the GitHub failed-label POST fails, and issue #12 still has its previously trusted priority label. latestIssueRun returns no issue-sourced run, so the queue can immediately select the issue again without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93–95 catches label-write errors with `failure(error)` and continues. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 then proceeds from lifecycle reconciliation to issue selection. Its failure guard at :97 requires the GitHub label, while src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts latestIssueRun to `json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'`. Failed runs also fall outside `ISSUE_CLAIM_STATUSES` at src/db/store.ts:361–367.
verification.trigger: A CLI run linked through Closes #12 fails; removing in-progress succeeds but adding failed errors. With no issue-sourced history, active claim, or failed label, the old trusted priority label permits another queue run without re-approval.

findings.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint
findings.detail: A pending comment is considered delivered when any issue comment contains the predictable marker. The code does not verify the comment author or exact body, although issue comments are untrusted data. A third party can therefore make the reconciler mark a failed write as done without the factory ever posting the required comment.
findings.suggestion: Verify that a matching comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the recorded body before marking the effect complete.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and leaves its effect pending, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's lifecycle marker. On the next poll the factory treats that comment as its own and permanently skips the real update.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 constructs `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:${run.id}:${event} -->`. Lines 122-129 parse comments as `{ body: z.string() }` and execute `if (comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))) { save(effect, "done");`, without checking authorship.
verification.trigger: A comment POST fails, leaving its checkpoint pending. Another participant posts the expected marker; the next poll permanently marks the factory comment delivered without posting it.

findings.title: Lifecycle events can disappear between polls
findings.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human and failure comments only from the current run status. If a run enters one of those states and is resolved or restarted before the next poll, no pending effect was recorded, so that event is never published. The pending-comment tests cover a status change only after a poll has already attempted the comment; they do not cover a transition entirely between polls.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the transitions occur, and add a test that enters needs_human or failed and leaves it before reconciliation runs.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101-102 adds the needs_human event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips it when `!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending"`. src/db/store.ts:2037-2040 permits needs_human to transition to resolved. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:295 schedules reconciliation using `q.pollSeconds * 1000`.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and is resolved before reconciliation observes it. No pending lifecycle effect exists, so neither its needs-you label nor its reason comment is published.

findings.title: Restart-between-effects coverage exercises only the start event
findings.detail: The restart test interrupts the initial in-progress label and started comment. The table-driven terminal-state tests restart only after both writes have completed, and the PR and merge tests likewise do not interrupt their transitions. Consequently, regressions in recovery between a needs-you, failed, cancellation, or merge label change and its associated comment are not covered as requested.
findings.suggestion: Exercise interruption during each applicable lifecycle transition, then restart and assert the final label set and exactly one corresponding comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change loses a failed comment after the failed label is written and the daemon restarts; the existing restart test still passes because it covers only the started event.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1275 parameterizes only interruption point: `test.each(["after label", "after comment"])`; its assertions at :1295–1298 check `limitless:in-progress` and `comment:started`. The failed-status test at :1225–1228 confirms both comments exist before `h.stop()`. Additional failed-comment restart coverage at :1333–1347 interrupts only after `comment:${status}` is already `pending`, leaving the interval between label write and comment checkpoint untested.
verification.trigger: A future regression loses a failed comment when restarting after the failed label write but before the comment checkpoint. Existing tests do not exercise that interval for failed events, so the regression could pass. This confirms a coverage gap, not a demonstrated runtime failure.

findings.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments
findings.detail: The comment body is passed directly to literal credential redaction. The private-string check detects encoded private-string entries, but registered credentials are not necessarily entries in that list. A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
findings.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
findings.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:134-137 applies `redactCredentials` directly to the comment body, then lines 140-148 check only loaded private strings before posting at line 163. src/util/proc.ts:1234-1236 registers literal and JSON-escaped credential variants; lines 1241-1244 pass text directly to the credential matcher without percent-decoding.
verification.trigger: A failure reason contains a percent-encoded registered credential whose literal value is absent from private strings. Literal redaction misses the encoded value, and the public comment exposes the recoverable credential.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint
findings.detail: Retry reconciliation trusts a marker found in any issue comment without checking its author or body. Issue comments are untrusted input, so a commenter who knows a run ID can make the factory record an effect as completed even though the factory never posted it.
findings.suggestion: Verify the comment belongs to the expected GitHub identity and matches the saved publication body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 uses a predictable run/event marker. Lines 128-130 accept any comment containing it and save the effect as done. Lines 159-164 save the effect as pending before POST and mark it done only after POST succeeds.
verification.trigger: A participant preposts the failed-event marker, then the factory's failure-comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On retry, the participant's comment satisfies the checkpoint and the actual failure update is permanently skipped.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to configured queue repositories
findings.detail: The lifecycle reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and it is not started when the issue queue is disabled. The request requires updates for runs started through CLI, MCP, label, and comment paths as well as the queue; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue selection.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover all repositories for which linked runs can be created.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #123` targets a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos; it receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events are lost between polls
findings.detail: The request requires each label change and comment to be a recorded side effect with a durable checkpoint. Here needs-human, failed, and cancelled events are discovered only from the current status. If a run enters and leaves one of those states before a poll observes it, no effect is recorded and its comment is permanently lost. The initial in-progress label can likewise be skipped if the run reaches a later state before its first poll.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the corresponding transitions occur, then reconcile each recorded effect independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the reconciler never posts the needs-you reason or applies its label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 creates the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips absent events unless their checkpoint is already `"pending"`. src/db/store.ts:2037–2038 permits needs_human runs to transition to `status: "resolved"`. No transition history is read by the reconciler.
verification.trigger: A run reaches needs_human and is resolved before the next poll; neither its needs-you label nor its reason is published. Although the proposed scenario calls this resuming, resolution supplies a supported transition that demonstrates the transient-event loss.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a failed CLI issue to be picked
findings.detail: A lifecycle write failure is caught and queue selection continues, but `latestIssueRun` only finds runs with an issue source reference. A failed CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` has no such reference. Until the failed label is successfully written, the queue therefore sees neither the failure label nor that latest failed run and can select the issue without re-approval.

findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails, the GitHub failed-label write errors, and the issue still has its previously approved priority label; the same poll can create a queue run for it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:64–68 derives failedAt from parsed timestamps; src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:99 requires `Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt`, ignoring timeline order when timestamps tie. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1419–1429 appends a trusted priority event after the failure event but explicitly expects rejection for the `"equal"` timestamp case.

candidates.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
candidates.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
candidates.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

candidates.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
candidates.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
candidates.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #42` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an error. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy failure re-approval
candidates.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority labeled event after failure, without requiring that event to correspond to a currently applied approved priority label. An old, still-present priority label can therefore supply the queue priority while a different, subsequently removed label supplies the purported re-approval.
candidates.suggestion: Require a currently applied trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure event.
candidates.failure_scenario: priority:1 was applied before failure; after failure a trusted user applies and removes priority:9. The issue remains failed with priority:1, but becomes eligible.

candidates.title: An older run can overwrite a newer run's issue labels
candidates.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub requests. If another run for the issue is created while a label request is awaiting, the old run remains designated latest and can complete its label transition after the newer run starts. Its completed cursor then prevents correction until the newer run is reconciled on a later poll.
candidates.suggestion: Recheck which run owns the issue after awaited operations and before each label mutation and completion checkpoint.
candidates.failure_scenario: While reconciliation fetches labels for a failed run, a new run for the same issue starts; the old reconciliation then applies failed and removes in-progress for the active run.

candidates.title: Persist lifecycle events when they occur, not only when a poll observes them
candidates.detail: The needs-human, failure, and cancellation comments are created only when reconciliation observes the corresponding current status. No pending effect exists until the comment loop reaches that event. A status that changes between polls, or while an earlier comment write is failing, is therefore never recorded or retried. The single done cursor also suppresses a second needs-human episode for the same run.
candidates.suggestion: Record each lifecycle event and its publication-safe content durably at the state transition, then let polling deliver each recorded event.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next poll; reconciliation sees the resumed status and never posts the required reason. Similarly, a failed started-comment write can delay processing until after needs_human has ended.

candidates.title: Reconcile issue-linked runs outside queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Lifecycle processing is restricted to repositories listed in githubQueue with a nonempty trusted list, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. The request applies lifecycle updates to issue-linked runs from every start path; it does not condition those updates on queue admission being enabled for the repository.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and determine the target repository from each linked issue.
candidates.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository not listed in githubQueue, or with the queue disabled. No lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments are written for that issue.

candidates.title: Prevent re-pick while a failed label write is pending
candidates.detail: The new re-approval guard depends on the failed label being visible on GitHub. If that write fails, the queue continues selection in the same poll. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only considers issue source references, so it cannot supply a local failure guard for runs linked through a Closes directive.
candidates.suggestion: Use the existing admission and claim check to account for the latest linked run and its failure while the GitHub failure-label effect is pending.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails, the GitHub failed-label POST fails, and issue #12 still has its previously trusted priority label. latestIssueRun returns no issue-sourced run, so the queue can immediately select the issue again without re-approval.

candidates.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint
candidates.detail: A pending comment is considered delivered when any issue comment contains the predictable marker. candidates.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and leaves its effect pending, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's lifecycle marker. On the next poll the factory treats that comment as its own and permanently skips the real update.

candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval

The new tests only use a post-failure event for a priority label that remains on the issue.
candidates.suggestion: Require the qualifying post-failure application to correspond to a currently applied, trusted priority label, and test removal of that label while an older priority label remains.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:1 from before failure. After failure, a trusted user applies priority:2 and then removes it; the issue is still eligible even though its remaining priority label was not re-applied after failure.

candidates.title: Restart-between-effects coverage exercises only the start event

The table-driven terminal-state tests restart only after both writes have completed, and the PR and merge tests likewise do not interrupt their transitions. candidates.failure_scenario: A future change loses a failed comment after the failed label is written and the daemon restarts; the existing restart test still passes because it covers only the started event.

candidates.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments

A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
candidates.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
candidates.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

candidates.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint
