Verifier: 19 candidates, 19 checked, 0 refuted.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are lost
findings.detail: Comments and labels are derived only from the run's current status. No durable event is recorded when a run enters needs_human or failed, so a transition that ends before the next poll cannot be reconstructed. The single comment key for each status also suppresses later occurrences of the same status.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when they occur and reconcile each recorded occurrence independently.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll. The poll sees running and never posts the needs-you comment or applies its label. A second needs_human episode after an observed first episode also receives no new comment.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101-102 adds the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`. Lines 112-114 use `const effect = `comment:${event}`` and `if (state(effect) === "done") continue;`, with no episode identifier.
verification.trigger: A needs_human episode begins and ends between polls, so its label and comment are omitted. After one observed episode's comment is done, subsequent episodes receive no new comment.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-configured repositories
findings.detail: The reconciler skips every repository that is absent from githubQueue.repos or has no trusted queue accounts, and it is not started at all when the queue is disabled. The requested lifecycle applies to runs started through every entry point; it is not limited to repositories enabled for automatic issue picking.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration for linked issues.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that has no issue queue configured. The run receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10-12 requires `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length` and membership in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`; line 43 skips with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/index.ts:66-67 starts reconciliation's queue only when queue configuration is enabled.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains Closes #7 in a repository without issue queue configuration; lifecycle labels and comments are never posted despite the requirement covering any start path.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a failed manual run to be re-picked
findings.detail: The transition removes in-progress before adding failed, and a write failure is caught before the queue continues to query candidates. The queue's latestIssueRun lookup only recognizes issue source references, so a terminal CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` supplies no local re-approval guard.
findings.suggestion: Make admission account for terminal runs linked through all supported start paths, including while lifecycle writes are pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails. Removing in-progress succeeds, adding failed fails, and the issue still has its old trusted priority label. The same poll can pick it again without a new approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders labels as in-progress, needs-you, failed; lines 80-86 perform individual writes and throw on failed additions. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 reconciles before selecting issues. src/db/store.ts:1268-1270 restricts `latestIssueRun` to `source_ref.kind = 'issue'`, while lines 1225 and 361-367 restrict claims to active statuses.
verification.trigger: A failed CLI Closes #7 run has no issue sourceRef. Removing in-progress succeeds but adding failed fails. With its old approval still present, neither the active claim nor latest-issue-run guard blocks admission, so the queue can immediately pick it again.

findings.title: An older run can overwrite labels after a newer run starts
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub awaits. Re-reading the old run's status does not check whether another run has since claimed the same issue, so an in-flight reconciliation can apply an old terminal label after a newer run has started.
findings.suggestion: Recheck issue ownership after awaited operations and before each label mutation, coordinating it with run admission.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation of an old failed run is awaiting its label read, a new run for the same issue starts. The old reconciliation then removes in-progress or adds failed based on its stale latest-run map.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:35-39 builds `latest` once from the initial run snapshot. Line 56 checks that map before the awaited label read at line 60. Lines 63-71 reread only `store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and check its desired label; they do not recheck whether a newer run exists.
verification.trigger: A newer run for the issue is created while an old failed run awaits GitHub's label read. Reconciliation can then remove in-progress or add failed for the old run until a later poll corrects the labels.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation skips every repository absent from githubQueue.repos, and the reconciler itself is started only when the queue has configured repositories and trusted accounts. The request requires lifecycle updates for every start path, including CLI and MCP runs, with gh as the fallback identity.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and handle linked issues for all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A user runs `limitless run` with `Closes #7` for a repository that is not in githubQueue.repos. No lifecycle label or comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10-12 defines management through `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 executes `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. The sole reconciliation caller is src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains Closes #7 for a repository outside githubQueue.repos. Its lifecycle labels and comments are skipped. This is the same configuration-gating defect as C2.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear before they are checkpointed
findings.detail: Events are inferred only from the current run snapshot. A needs_human or failed state that begins and ends between polls is never recorded. The same loss occurs when an earlier comment fails: the loop breaks before saving later events as pending, so a status change before the next poll erases them.
findings.suggestion: Durably record each lifecycle transition when it occurs, then reconcile its effects independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human while the started comment write is failing, then is resumed before the next poll. No needs-you comment is ever posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 adds needs_human only when `run.status === "needs_human"`. Lines 110–114 process started first and skip absent events unless already pending. Lines 165–167 handle a failed started write with `failure(error); break;`, preventing needs_human from being checkpointed.
verification.trigger: The started comment fails while the run needs human input. The run resumes before the next poll, so needs_human is neither current nor pending and its comment is permanently omitted.

findings.title: A second needs-human episode is treated as already delivered
findings.detail: Comment checkpoints are keyed only by run and event name. Once a needs_human comment is marked done, a resumed run that later reaches needs_human again cannot post its new reason. Label reconciliation can still switch back to needs-you, leaving the issue with a stale explanation.
findings.suggestion: Key lifecycle effects by a durable transition or status episode rather than only by event type.
findings.failure_scenario: A run needs human input, resumes after the owner responds, and later needs human input for a different reason. The second reason is never commented.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:112 uses `const effect = `comment:${event}`;`; line 114 skips `state(effect) === "done"`. Line 164 saves that effect as done. Neither the key nor its completion state distinguishes separate needs_human episodes.
verification.trigger: After the first needs_human comment succeeds, the run resumes and later needs human input for another reason. The existing completed checkpoint suppresses the second comment.

findings.title: Re-approval can come from a priority label that is no longer applied
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority labeled event, even if that label was subsequently removed. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so the current approval need not be the one applied after failure.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure label.
findings.failure_scenario: Priority:2 was applied before failure; a trusted user applies and removes priority:1 after failure. The issue remains eligible using the old priority:2 label despite the later approval having been withdrawn.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:74–81 derives `approved` from current labels and trusts their latest application. Separately, :99 accepts `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)` without requiring that event's label to remain applied. :129 queries only `LABELED_EVENT, RENAMED_TITLE_EVENT`, excluding removals.
verification.trigger: Trusted priority:2 remains from before failure; trusted priority:1 is applied after failure and then removed. Historical priority:1 satisfies re-approval while priority:2 supplies current approval, allowing the failed issue to be picked again. The latest-run guard at :115–116 accepts the same historical event.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can impersonate a completed lifecycle write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any issue comment containing the predictable marker as proof that the factory posted its pending comment, without checking its author. An issue participant can supply that marker and cause the actual lifecycle comment to be permanently marked done.
findings.suggestion: Verify the recovered comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the pending body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's marker. On the next poll the factory records the failed comment as delivered and never retries it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:123 parses comments using only `z.object({ body: z.string() })`. Lines 128–130 accept `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))` and save the effect as done, without verifying the author or complete body.
verification.trigger: A comment POST fails, leaving a pending effect. Another participant posts the predictable marker; the next poll treats that unrelated comment as delivery and never retries the factory comment.

findings.title: A 404 during label removal is silently recorded as success
findings.detail: The catch treats every HTTP 404 as an already-removed label. GitHub can also return 404 for an inaccessible repository or issue, so a permission or installation failure can be checkpointed as a successful label transition and will not be retried.
findings.suggestion: Confirm the label is absent with a successful fresh read before recording the removal as complete; otherwise log and retry the error.
findings.failure_scenario: The initial label read succeeds, but the App loses repository access before the DELETE. GitHub returns 404 and the reconciliation cursor records the label set as complete even though the label remains.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:85–88 suppresses every removal error matching HTTP 404: `if (add || !/\bHTTP 404\b/.test(String(error))) throw error;` followed by `save(effect, "done")`. Line 92 saves the complete label cursor, and line 56 skips reconciliation when that cursor matches the desired label.
verification.trigger: After labels are read, repository access is lost and a removal returns HTTP 404. For a cancellation or merge requiring only removals, reconciliation records completion although labels remain, preventing subsequent retry even after access returns.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls never produce their comments
findings.detail: Lifecycle comments are derived from the current run status. A needs_human episode that begins and ends between polls is never recorded as pending, so its required comment is permanently lost. The pending-comment tests cover a transition only after a poll has already observed it.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records. Add a test that enters and leaves needs_human between polls, then restarts and checks for exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next issue-queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 invokes lifecycle reconciliation from the polling tick. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:97–102 reads the current run and creates needs_human only if its current status matches. Line 113 skips an absent event unless its effect is already pending.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and resumes between polling ticks. No pending checkpoint was created, and the next poll sees only the resumed status, permanently omitting the needs-you comment.

findings.title: A removed priority label can supply re-approval
findings.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority-label event after failure, even if that label is no longer present. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before failure. The tests only exercise re-approval using the currently present label and miss this combination.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose applicable labeling event is later than the failure event. Add a test with an old current priority and a later trusted priority that has since been removed.
findings.failure_scenario: priority:1 remains from before failure; a trusted user adds and then removes priority:2 after failure. The issue becomes eligible despite having no current priority approval applied after failure.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:74–81 checks current priority labels independently of :99: `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)`. The latter accepts historical applications of removed labels; :129 excludes removal events from the query.
verification.trigger: Trusted priority:1 remains from before failure; trusted priority:2 is applied after failure and removed. The old current label and the removed label's historical event together make the issue eligible, including when the event also follows the latest run's finishedAt.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside the issue queue configuration
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured, and the poller does not start without that configuration. The request requires updates for linked runs from all start paths. The new test explicitly asserts no updates for disabled or unlisted repositories, thereby protecting this omission.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked GitHub issues independently of queue admission configuration, and test a CLI or MCP run when queue polling is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #7 in a GitHub repository that is not enabled for automatic issue picking; the issue receives neither labels nor comments.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10-12 defines lifecycleManaged as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 skips updates with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:144 also disables the poller when queue repositories or trusted accounts are absent.
verification.trigger: Start a run containing Closes #7 for a repository outside githubQueue.repos: lifecycle reconciliation skips it, so no lifecycle labels or comments are posted.

findings.title: Restart coverage does not exercise each lifecycle transition
findings.detail: The interruption matrix only interrupts the initial started event. The needs-human, failure, cancellation, PR, and merge tests restart after their writes have completed, so they do not establish that a restart between each transition's label change and comment preserves the required effect.
findings.suggestion: Exercise interruption after the label update and before the comment for each applicable transition, then reopen the store and verify the final labels and exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that loses a failed or needs-human comment after its label write can pass the current restart tests.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1225–1228 asserts `expect(h.comments.get(7)).toHaveLength(2)` before `h.stop()`. The mid-write restart test at :1275–1298 only exercises startup, asserting `"comment:started"`. The failed/needs-human restart tests at :1347–1349 stop only after asserting `comment:${status}` is already `"pending"`. None interrupts those transitions between the label write and comment checkpoint.
verification.trigger: A regression affecting failed or needs-human recovery specifically after the label write but before the comment checkpoint could pass these tests; that interruption window is untested.

findings.title: Do not accept an arbitrary issue comment as proof of a factory write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any comment containing the predictable lifecycle marker as proof that the factory posted its comment. Issue comments are untrusted: their author is neither retrieved nor checked. An attacker who can comment can therefore suppress a pending lifecycle notification.
findings.suggestion: Authenticate the author of a matching comment against the GitHub identity used for the write, and require an exact, validated marker before recording the effect as done.
findings.failure_scenario: A comment POST fails or the daemon restarts after marking it pending. Another issue participant posts a comment containing `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:<run-id>:failed -->`. On the next poll, reconciliation marks the failed notification done without posting it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 constructs the predictable marker. Lines 122-128 parse comments using only `z.object({ body: z.string() })` and check `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`; lines 129-130 then execute `save(effect, "done"); continue;` without checking authorship.
verification.trigger: A comment write remains pending after failure or restart, and another participant posts its marker. The next poll accepts that comment as proof of delivery and permanently suppresses the factory notification.

findings.title: Tie re-approval to a priority label that is still applied
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority-label event, even if that label has since been removed. The separately computed `approved` set can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so a withdrawn re-approval still permits the issue to run.
findings.suggestion: Require the latest trusted application of a currently applied priority label to be later than the failure event.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains `priority:2` from before failure. A trusted account applies `priority:1` after failure and subsequently removes it to withdraw approval. The old `priority:2` satisfies `approved`, while the historical `priority:1` event satisfies this check, so the failed issue is picked again.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:79 restricts current approval evidence with `e.label.name === l.name`, but :99 checks all priority application events without that restriction: `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)`. :129 requests no removal events.
verification.trigger: An issue retains trusted priority:2 from before failure. A trusted account applies priority:1 after failure and removes it. The removed application satisfies re-approval and the remaining old label satisfies approved, permitting another run.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to repositories in the issue queue
findings.detail: The request covers “any start path,” but reconciliation skips every repository outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. A CLI, MCP, label-triggered, or comment-triggered run against another repository therefore receives none of the required lifecycle labels or comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover linked issues from every supported start path.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #12` for a repository that is not configured in `githubQueue.repos`; no in-progress label or lifecycle comments are posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:43 says `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`; lines 10-12 require the repository to appear in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`. Thus even linked issues from manual runs are excluded outside the queue configuration.
verification.trigger: Run limitless run with Closes #12 in a repository absent from githubQueue.repos: no in-progress label or lifecycle comments are written. This is the same defect as C13.

findings.title: Transitions occurring between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: The requirement says each lifecycle event is a durable side effect and must not lose a label change or comment across restarts. The reconciler derives needs-human, failed, and cancelled events solely from the current run status; it creates no pending effect when the transition occurs. If the run advances again before the next poll, that event is permanently invisible.
findings.suggestion: Durably enqueue lifecycle effects at the state transition and reconcile those recorded effects on each poll.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches `needs_human` and is resumed before the next queue poll, or the daemon restarts and the run is resumed before reconciliation. No needs-you label or reason comment is ever posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 invokes reconciliation during polling; line 295 schedules the next poll using `q.pollSeconds`. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101-102 creates the needs_human event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips absent events unless already pending. src/db/store.ts:2008-2013 updates the current run row and publishes it without recording a lifecycle transition.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and resumes before reconciliation observes it, including across a restart. No pending effect was recorded, so subsequent polls omit both the needs-you label and its reason comment.

findings.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
findings.detail: The request requires a trusted priority application after the failure label. This check accepts any historical trusted priority event after failure, even if that priority label was subsequently removed. A different priority label that was already present before the failure can then supply `approved`, so the issue is picked without a currently applied post-failure approval.
findings.suggestion: Require the post-failure trusted event to be the latest application of a currently present, approved priority label.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue has trusted `priority:2` before failure; afterward a trusted account briefly applies and removes `priority:3`. The remaining pre-failure `priority:2` makes the issue eligible.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:74–81 permits a trusted pre-failure current label to populate `approved`; :99 separately accepts any trusted priority application after failure. :115–116 likewise checks historical events, and :129 excludes label removals.
verification.trigger: Trusted priority:2 remains applied before failure; a trusted account applies priority:3 after failure and subsequently removes it. Its historical application passes the failure and latest-run re-approval checks, so the failed issue becomes eligible again.

candidates.failure_scenario: A regression that loses a failed or needs-human comment after its label write can pass the current restart tests.

candidates.title: Do not accept an arbitrary issue comment as proof of a factory write
candidates.detail: Recovery treats any comment containing the predictable lifecycle marker as proof that the factory posted its comment. Issue comments are untrusted: their author is neither retrieved nor checked. An attacker who can comment can therefore suppress a pending lifecycle notification.
candidates.suggestion: Authenticate the author of a matching comment against the GitHub identity used for the write, and require an exact, validated marker before recording the effect as done.
candidates.failure_scenario: A comment POST fails or the daemon restarts after marking it pending. Another issue participant posts a comment containing `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:<run-id>:failed -->`. On the next poll, reconciliation marks the failed notification done without posting it.

candidates.title: Tie re-approval to a priority label that is still applied
candidates.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority-label event, even if that label has since been removed. The separately computed `approved` set can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so a withdrawn re-approval still permits the issue to run.
candidates.suggestion: Require the latest trusted application of a currently applied priority label to be later than the failure event.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue retains `priority:2` from before failure. A trusted account applies `priority:1` after failure and subsequently removes it to withdraw approval. The old `priority:2` satisfies `approved`, while the historical `priority:1` event satisfies this check, so the failed issue is picked again.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to repositories in the issue queue
candidates.detail: The request covers “any start path,” but reconciliation skips every repository outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. A CLI, MCP, label-triggered, or comment-triggered run against another repository therefore receives none of the required lifecycle labels or comments.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover linked issues from every supported start path.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #12` for a repository that is not configured in `githubQueue.repos`; no in-progress label or lifecycle comments are posted.

candidates.title: Transitions occurring between polls are never recorded
candidates.detail: The requirement says each lifecycle event is a durable side effect and must not lose a label change or comment across restarts. The reconciler derives needs-human, failed, and cancelled events solely from the current run status; it creates no pending effect when the transition occurs. If the run advances again before the next poll, that event is permanently invisible.
candidates.suggestion: Durably enqueue lifecycle effects at the state transition and reconcile those recorded effects on each poll.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches `needs_human` and is resumed before the next queue poll, or the daemon restarts and the run is resumed before reconciliation. No needs-you label or reason comment is ever posted.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
candidates.detail: The request requires a trusted priority application after the failure label. This check accepts any historical trusted priority event after failure, even if that priority label was subsequently removed. A different priority label that was already present before the failure can then supply `approved`, so the issue is picked without a currently applied post-failure approval.
candidates.suggestion: Require the post-failure trusted event to be the latest application of a currently present, approved priority label.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue has trusted `priority:2` before failure; afterward a trusted account briefly applies and removes `priority:3`. The remaining pre-failure `priority:2` makes the issue eligible.

findings.title: A failed run can be picked again before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the latest run failed but the issue does not currently have `limitless:failed`, eligibility falls back to accepting any trusted priority application after the run finished. A failed lifecycle label write can leave precisely that state, so the next queue poll can admit another run without a priority application after the failure label was applied.
findings.suggestion: For a failed latest run, require evidence of the failure-label event followed by trusted priority re-approval even when the label is currently absent.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, the API call adding `limitless:failed` fails, and a trusted user applies a priority label after the run finished. The same poll or a later poll can select the issue before the failure label is applied.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:117-124 checks `context.latest.status === "failed" && failed`; when the GitHub failure label is absent, it falls back to `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > (context.latest?.finishedAt ?? Infinity))`. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:227-232 catches label-write failures and calls `logFailure(...)` without stopping reconciliation. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:203-204 then proceeds from reconciliation into issue selection.
verification.trigger: A failed run has a finishedAt timestamp. Reconciliation removes in-progress but fails to add limitless:failed. A trusted account reapplies priority after finishedAt, and no other claim or eligibility blocker exists. Admission accepts that approval before the failure label is applied and starts another run.

findings.title: Lifecycle events can disappear between polls
findings.detail: The reconciler derives comments only from the run's current status; it does not record transitions when they occur. If a run enters and leaves `needs_human` between polls, no needs-you label or comment is ever recorded. The same approach also makes one comment key cover every occurrence of a status in a run.
findings.suggestion: Durably record each required transition at the point it happens and let polling deliver those recorded effects.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches `needs_human` and is resumed before the next issue-queue poll. The next observation sees its resumed status and never posts the needs-you update.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82: `if (run.status === "needs_human") events.set("needs_human", ...)`; lines 105–110 obtain current runs and call `observe(run, repo, number)`. src/db/store.ts:2084 updates the current row with `UPDATE runs SET ...`; no lifecycle transition checkpoint is written there. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:307 schedules observations at `q.pollSeconds * 1000`.
verification.trigger: A linked run enters needs_human and resumes between lifecycle observations. The next poll sees the resumed status, so no needs-you event or comment is recorded.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs for repositories listed in `githubQueue.repos` with trusted accounts configured, and the poller itself is not started without that configuration. Runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in other repositories therefore receive none of the requested lifecycle labels or durable comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked issues independently of queue admission configuration.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository absent from `githubQueue.repos`. The run starts and opens a PR, but issue 7 receives no lifecycle updates.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:11–13 defines `lifecycleManaged` as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; lines 110 and 116 apply that filter to observation and delivery. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:156 also returns immediately when queue repositories or trusted accounts are absent.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing Closes #7 targets a repository outside githubQueue.repos. Its issue receives neither lifecycle labels nor lifecycle comments, including when the PR opens.

findings.title: Failure and needs-you comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies contain only a generic status and UI link. The requested reason is never read from the run or sanitized for publication, so issue watchers cannot see why the run failed or needs attention.
findings.suggestion: Include the available reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, with a fixed fallback when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a public error such as `tests failed`; the issue comment says only `failed: see …` and does not report the error.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 constructs only `needs you: see ${link}.` and `failed: see ${link}.`; line 95 embeds that fixed text in the comment. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1392 explicitly asserts `.not.toContain("original reason")`.
verification.trigger: A run fails with a public reason such as tests failed. Its issue comment reports failure and a UI link but omits the reason.

findings.title: A blocked publication check permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: If the private-strings check rejects a generated comment, the effect is marked done without posting anything. The request requires a fixed safe message in this case. Marking it done also prevents a later poll from correcting the omission.
findings.suggestion: Create and deliver a fixed safe fallback body when the original text is blocked, retaining a pending effect until delivery succeeds.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI link contains a private string, so `checkBody` throws for a started or terminal comment. The effect is stored as done and no comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93–100 calls `checkBody(...)`, then handles rejection with `save(effect, "done")` and logging. Line 87 skips effects already present. Lines 247–251 likewise mark a pending comment done when publication rechecking fails, without posting a fallback.
verification.trigger: A private-string match in the configured UI URL blocks a lifecycle comment. The effect is permanently acknowledged without posting the required fixed safe message.

findings.title: Failure and needs-you comments omit the reason

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 uses fixed `needs you: see ${link}.` and `failed: see ${link}.` text without reading the reason or question. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1547–1552 supplies an error but expects only the fixed status text and UI link.
verification.trigger: A run fails with a gate error or reaches needs_human with a question. The issue comment omits that reason or question and directs the reader to the UI.

findings.title: A blocked comment is permanently discarded instead of replaced
findings.detail: When publication checking throws, the effect is marked done without posting. The request explicitly requires a fixed fallback message when private-string checking blocks the text. The delivery-time check similarly marks the effect done on any error, including potentially temporary inspection errors, so it will never be retried.
findings.suggestion: Post a checked fixed fallback for blocked text, and leave effects pending when an inspection failure cannot be resolved safely.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the UI link or comment text, or the private-string check fails temporarily; no lifecycle comment is posted on this or later polls.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:98–100 catches publication failures with `save(effect, "done"); logFailure(...)`. Line 87 prevents reconsideration: `if (effects.has(effect)) continue;`. No fallback is posted.
verification.trigger: A private string in the UI URL or a temporary private-string check failure permanently suppresses the corresponding comment, including on later polls.

This does not provide a durable checkpoint for each lifecycle event.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably at the state transition, with an identity for each occurrence, and let the poller deliver those records.

candidates.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, and test both safe and sensitive reasons.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails with a safe error such as "typecheck failed"; the issue comment only says "failed: see" and links to the UI.

candidates.title: A blocked publication is marked done without posting the required fallback
candidates.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done and no comment is posted. The request requires a fixed safe message in this case. The test at test/issue-queue.test.ts:1559 explicitly expects suppression, so it asserts the wrong behavior.
candidates.suggestion: Construct and validate a fixed fallback message, post it when the original text is blocked, and test that it is posted exactly once.
candidates.failure_scenario: A lifecycle comment contains a configured private string; its checkpoint becomes done and the issue never receives the corresponding notification.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled for runs outside the issue queue configuration
candidates.detail: Lifecycle management requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos and the queue to have trusted accounts. The request requires updates for any start path, including manual, MCP and trigger runs. The test at test/issue-queue.test.ts:1743 instead explicitly expects no updates when the queue is disabled or the repository is outside its list.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile linked issues independently of queue admission configuration, and test manual and trigger starts with the queue disabled.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` for a repository that is not enabled in the issue queue; no label or comment is written.

candidates.title: Transitions between polls can be lost
candidates.detail: The reconciler creates event checkpoints only from the current run status. If a run reaches needs_human or failed and then changes status before the next poll, there is no recorded event to reconcile, so its label and comment are never delivered. The tests change status and poll before changing it again; they do not cover an unobserved intermediate transition.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, then have polling deliver those recorded effects. Add a test that transitions through needs_human or failed and resolves before reconciliation.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you label or comment.

candidates.title: Blocked comments are permanently discarded instead of replaced
candidates.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done without posting the required fixed fallback. The same happens if a pending comment fails its publication check at delivery. The checkpoint prevents a later poll from recovering the missing notification.
candidates.suggestion: For a private-text match, checkpoint and publish a fixed safe message; retain a retryable state when the publication check itself cannot be performed.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the UI URL or run ID. A run fails, the failed comment is marked done, and the issue receives no failure comment.

candidates.title: Needs-human and failure comments omit the reason
candidates.detail: Both event bodies contain only a generic status and UI link; neither includes the run's reason. The requested fallback is appropriate when text cannot be published safely, but this implementation uses it for every event, including ordinary publishable reasons.
candidates.suggestion: Include the relevant reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, falling back to a fixed message when it is blocked.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails with a non-sensitive error such as a failed build. The issue comment says only that the run failed and does not tell the watcher why.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation is enabled only for repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts configured, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. Consequently, issue-linked CLI, MCP, label, and comment runs outside that configuration never receive the requested lifecycle labels or comments.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for issue-linked runs independently of queue admission configuration, while retaining queue configuration for picking issues.
candidates.failure_scenario: A repository uses `limitless run` with `Closes #7` but has no issue queue configured. The run starts and fails without any lifecycle updates to issue 7.

candidates.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
candidates.detail: The table requires a “comment with the reason” for both needs_human and failed. Both bodies contain only a generic status and UI link, regardless of the recorded run error or question. The added tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent.
candidates.suggestion: Include the recorded public-safe reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, using the specified fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails with a gate error or needs a specific owner decision; issue watchers receive only “failed: see” or “needs you: see” and cannot see why.

candidates.title: A blocked publication check discards the comment instead of posting a fallback
candidates.detail: The request says “If the check blocks the text, post a fixed message without it.” The catch instead marks the comment done without posting anything; the same behavior occurs when a pending body fails its later check. It will never be retried.
candidates.suggestion: Checkpoint and post a fixed safe fallback when publication text is blocked, retaining retry behavior for write failures.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the run ID or UI URL used in the comment; the check rejects the body and the issue receives no comment for that event.

candidates.title: Polling snapshots lose lifecycle transitions between polls
candidates.detail: The request requires each lifecycle event to have a durable checkpoint, including across restarts. This code discovers needs_human, failed, and cancelled only from the current run status at reconciliation time. A transition that is resolved or otherwise changed before the next poll is never recorded, and a second needs_human episode is also suppressed by the single `comment:needs_human` key.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records, with an identity for each applicable episode.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resolved before the next queue poll; no needs-you label or reason comment is ever recorded or posted.

candidates.title: A failed run can be picked again before its failure label is applied
candidates.detail: The request requires “No re-pick after failure without re-approval” after the failure label was applied. When the failure label is absent, the admission check falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after finishedAt. Reconciliation can remove in-progress and then fail or exhaust its call budget before adding failed, while queue admission still proceeds in the same poll.
candidates.suggestion: Keep admission closed for a failed run until its failure label has been applied and a trusted priority-label event is observed after that application, using the existing admission check.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails, a trusted user applies a priority label before the failed-label write succeeds, and the in-progress label has already been removed. The next candidate check admits the issue without a priority application after the failure label.

findings.title: An initially empty repository discards its first commands
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues stores no enable boundary. When an issue and command later appear, that later poll establishes the boundary from their timestamps and skips the command as if it existed at enablement. The added test explicitly expects this loss.
findings.suggestion: Establish a durable GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue while the repository has no open issues, then create an issue and post a trusted command before the next poll. No run is ever created for that command.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:272–275 derives `newest` exclusively from `issues.nodes` and persists it only with `if (newest) factory.store.githubCommentBoundary(repo, newest)`. Line 282 processes comments only when `boundary` exists; line 301 skips timestamps `<=` that boundary. test/issue-queue.test.ts:3015 explicitly tests that an empty repository stays uninitialized and its subsequent first command never runs.
verification.trigger: An empty successful first poll stores no boundary. An issue and command arriving before the next poll establish the later boundary themselves; that command is skipped permanently.

findings.title: Identity lookup failure bypasses the factory-author exclusion
findings.detail: An identity lookup error is converted to null, but slash commands continue to be processed. With no bot login, the factory-author comparison cannot exclude the App's own account. If that account is trusted, its command is admitted and permanently recorded even though the invariant forbids factory-authored commands.
findings.suggestion: Fail closed for comment processing when the factory identity needed to identify its author cannot be established, leaving comments retryable.
findings.failure_scenario: The trusted list includes the App bot, identity lookup temporarily fails, and the bot has posted `/limitless do work` after the boundary. The poll creates a run from the factory's own comment.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278 catches identity failure with `.catch(() => null)`; line 280 then sets `bot` to `null`. The factory-author guard at line 298 is only `author.toLowerCase() === bot`, while lines 284–285 still parse slash commands and line 318 calls `factory.createRun`.
verification.trigger: With an established boundary, identity lookup fails and a trusted App bot has posted an unedited, unprocessed slash command after the boundary without a factory marker. Its author cannot match null, so the poll creates a run from the factory's comment.

findings.title: Canonicalized names no longer resolve existing mixed-case repository registrations
findings.detail: The queue passes the lowercased repository name into run creation. Repository resolution uses a case-sensitive getRepoBySlug lookup, so an existing mixed-case registration is missed. Resolution then calls GitHub and creates a second repository record with default settings. This can lose the existing registration's merge policy and default branch, and queue admission can fail when the extra GitHub lookup fails.
findings.suggestion: Use canonical keys for comparisons and snapshots while preserving or resolving the registered repository's spelling for run creation.
findings.failure_scenario: A queue configured for Owner/Repo already has a registered Owner/Repo with a custom merge policy. The queue now requests owner/repo, misses that registration, and creates a separate record using the global default policy.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:261 lowercases the repository: `const repo = configuredRepo.toLowerCase()`, then passes it into requests at lines 434–445. src/app.ts:398 calls `resolveRepo(this.store, req.repo, this.cfg.githubMerge)`. src/git/repos.ts:172–173 checks `store.getRepoBySlug(trimmed)`; src/db/store.ts:1222 uses `SELECT * FROM repos WHERE slug = ?`. On a miss, src/git/repos.ts:209–215 inserts the new slug with `mergePolicy: merge`. The schema defines `slug TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE` without NOCASE (src/db/migrations.ts:10).
verification.trigger: An existing Owner/Repo registration has a custom merge policy. Queue requests now use owner/repo, miss the case-sensitive registration, and create a second registration with the global policy.

findings.title: Lowercasing configured repositories bypasses existing registrations
findings.detail: Queue requests now use the lowercased slug, but repository registration and resolveRepo lookups are case-sensitive. An existing registration such as Owner/Repo is therefore not found when the queue creates a run for owner/repo. resolveRepo instead performs a GitHub lookup and creates a second registration with default settings, losing the existing registration's repository-specific settings. If that lookup fails, queue admission fails altogether.
findings.suggestion: Deduplicate using lowercase comparison keys while preserving a configured spelling for repository resolution, or make repository resolution reuse existing registrations case-insensitively.
findings.failure_scenario: A queue configured for Owner/Repo has an existing Owner/Repo registration with a custom merge policy. After upgrade, an approved issue is admitted as owner/repo and resolves to a newly created registration using the default merge policy.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:440 lowercases configured slugs: `repos: [...new Set(repos.map((repo) => repo.toLowerCase()))]`. Queue admission passes that slug to `issueRunRequest` (src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:434–436), which preserves it as `repo` (src/integrations/github.ts:109–111). Factory calls `resolveRepo(this.store, req.repo, this.cfg.githubMerge)` (src/app.ts:398). Lookup uses `SELECT * FROM repos WHERE slug = ?` (src/db/store.ts:1222), against `slug TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE` without NOCASE (src/db/migrations.ts:10). On a miss, resolveRepo inserts the lowercase `slug` with `mergePolicy: merge` (src/git/repos.ts:209–215).

findings.title: Classify the moved tip before discarding a release intent
findings.detail: Every `moved` result from a replay marks the confirmed lease lost and clears the intent without examining the returned tip. The claim client can return `moved` for a malformed record or a valid record that does not meet the supersession conditions. The recovery rules require malformed content to remain pending, and only a higher generation or the same generation under another holder or run establishes supersession. Clearing the journal also makes the row forgettable, losing confirmed ownership history and the final release record.
findings.suggestion: Classify `result.tip` using the same recovery rules as the initial read; retain the intent for malformed or otherwise unclassifiable tips, and mark it lost only when the tip establishes supersession.

findings.title: Release-intent replay bypasses lease-time validation
findings.detail: Reconciliation delegates a pending release to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which can replay the release with `client.write` without a GitHub-time sample or `beforeSend` predicate. Both startup recovery and ordinary operations use that path, so an expired generation can mutate the claim after its lease window has closed.
findings.suggestion: Ensure release replay uses the same fresh time decision and send-time revalidation as other same-generation writes.
findings.failure_scenario: A release intent is journaled, the process stops before sending it, and recovery runs more than ten minutes later while the old tip remains current. Recovery writes the expired generation's release without checking whether it is renewable.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:65 calls `recoverLeases({ client, store })`; :89 calls `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)`. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:118–121 replays releases with `client.write(..., { signal, onCommit: ... })`, without `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206–208 only aborts when `opts.beforeSend?.()` returns false.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
findings.detail: The loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes applied in this manager instance. Confirmed held rows loaded at startup, and acquisitions confirmed by intent reconciliation, never enter that map. Even if `active` would accept their handles, the loop never renews them.
findings.suggestion: Enumerate confirmed held rows when starting or reconciling and make their handles available to the renewal loop.
findings.failure_scenario: A manager restarts with a confirmed held lease and starts the loop. Every tick skips that lease; it expires even though the associated run is active.

Its only insertion is :192, `handles.set(key(repo, ref), held)`, after a direct applied write. The renewal loop at :242 iterates only `handles.values()`.
verification.trigger: Restart with a confirmed held lease, then start with an active hook returning true. Without another successful acquire or mutation, every tick skips the recovered lease and it expires.

findings.title: A different run cannot reconcile an earlier pending acquisition
findings.detail: The cross-run check returns `refused` before reconciliation whenever the existing row has an intent. This violates the requirement to reconcile pending intents before every operation, and prevents the caller from clearing a dropped first acquisition unless a separate loop happens to run.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the existing intent under the mutex before deciding whether the row blocks the requested run.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent on an absent ref and ends. Run B calls `acquire` before the renewal loop is started; it receives `refused` indefinitely even though reconciliation would drop A's intent and allow B to acquire generation 1.

findings.title: Reconciled and recovered leases are never registered for renewal
findings.detail: The renewal loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated solely by an immediately applied write. Recovery or later reconciliation can confirm a held acquisition without adding a handle to that map. Confirmed held rows already present when the manager starts are likewise omitted. Those leases therefore receive no periodic renewal even when the active hook would return true.
findings.suggestion: Register confirmed held handles after recovery and successful reconciliation, and ensure the loop can discover existing confirmed held rows.

candidates.title: Reconcile a pending intent before refusing another run
candidates.detail: The different-run check returns `refused` before reconciliation whenever an intent exists. An unresolved intent must produce `wait`, and a resolvable failed first acquisition must be dropped and forgotten before the next run is considered. This ordering can leave the next run refused even though the first run never acquired the ref.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile the row first, return `wait` if it remains pending, and then evaluate ownership using the refreshed row.

candidates.title: Release replay bypasses lease-time revalidation
candidates.detail: `reconcileLeaseIntent` can replay a pending release by calling `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook. Calling it directly here and during startup therefore permits a same-generation release after its lease has expired, without a fresh GitHub-time sample or send-time check.
candidates.suggestion: Make release reconciliation apply the same fresh-time decision and send-time predicate as other same-generation writes.
candidates.failure_scenario: A release intent is persisted before its ref update, the process stops, and recovery runs after the lease window and renewable period have elapsed while the old tip remains unchanged. Recovery sends the release anyway.

candidates.title: Renewal loop omits confirmed leases recovered from storage
candidates.detail: The loop only visits the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by an immediately applied write in this manager instance. Such leases never reach the `active` hook or get renewed by the loop.
candidates.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, while retaining the generation checks.
candidates.failure_scenario: An acquisition is applied on GitHub but returns unconfirmed; a later loop tick reconciles it to held. No handle was added to `handles`, so subsequent ticks do not renew it and the lease expires.

candidates.title: Replaying a release bypasses lease-time validation
candidates.detail: Reconciliation can replay a pending release through `reconcileLeaseIntent`, whose write has no `beforeSend` time check. This path runs before the manager samples GitHub time or checks the lease window, including during startup recovery and loop ticks. A release interrupted before its ref update can therefore mutate a generation after its lease has expired.
candidates.suggestion: Make release replay use the manager’s fresh time decision and send-time revalidation, or leave the intent pending until it can be replayed safely.
candidates.failure_scenario: A release commit is journaled but its ref update is interrupted; the process restarts more than ten minutes later while the old tip remains current. Recovery writes the release without checking whether the generation is still renewable.

candidates.title: Different-run requests skip pending-intent reconciliation
candidates.detail: The early refusal executes before reconciliation whenever another run owns a row with an intent. An unresolved first acquisition that is subsequently proven unchanged remains in the database and prevents the next run from acquiring until a timer happens to reconcile it; if the loop has not started, it blocks indefinitely. The request requires reconciliation before every operation and forgetting an unconfirmed acquisition when dropped.

candidates.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent for an absent ref, then ends. GitHub later becomes readable and run B calls acquire before the renewal loop starts; B receives `refused: live` and A’s droppable intent remains.

candidates.title: Recovered and reconciled holdings are never added to the renewal loop

findings.title: Treat browser availability as a positive setup outcome
findings.detail: The engine labels the browser available whenever a preview exists and no `browser_unavailable` event was recorded. That event only covers failures while constructing the MCP configuration; it does not establish that the MCP server or Chromium subsequently started successfully. A verifier that reports a genuine browser startup failure as blocked will therefore have its result converted to unclear and sent into an implementation feedback round.
findings.suggestion: Persist and use a positive, same-invocation browser setup outcome, and retain environment-block handling when successful setup cannot be established.
findings.failure_scenario: The preview starts and browserMcp produces a configuration, but the MCP server or Chromium fails to launch. No `browser_unavailable` warning is emitted, so a marked browser check reported blocked becomes unclear even though the browser was unavailable.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:2378–2384 assigns "available" whenever a preview exists and no event has code === "browser_unavailable". src/harness/browser-mcp.ts:252–290 merely returns launch configuration; its catch at :291–299 emits that warning only for configuration errors. Runtime MCP errors become ordinary tool results: src/harness/codex.ts:165–169 emits `type: "tool_result"` with `isError: item.status === "failed"`. src/pipeline/verification.ts:22–28 then changes marked blocked rows to `status: "unclear"`, clears `blockedReason`, and empties `covering_tests`.

The engine converts the infrastructure block to unclear and bypasses environment-only handling.

That warning only reports failures while constructing the MCP configuration; it does not confirm that the CLI successfully started the MCP server or completed its handshake. An MCP startup failure can therefore leave a verifier without browser tools while the engine converts its environmental block into unclear and sends implementation feedback.

findings.title: Browser availability is inferred without a successful setup record
findings.detail: The request requires conversion when same-attempt records show both a ready preview and successful browser setup. This code instead treats the absence of a `browser_unavailable` event as success. The harness emits that event for configuration failures, but successful configuration does not establish that the MCP server or browser actually started. The same problem occurs after recovery establishes that a stale POST was not accepted. The run can therefore remain waiting indefinitely without its questions appearing on the issue.

findings.title: Retired unsent question sets cannot be published if they become eligible again
findings.detail: Superseding an unsent question effect marks it done, and observe() will never create that effect again because it already exists. A temporary linkage or status change can therefore permanently suppress a question set that was never posted.

findings.title: Privacy reinspection can close an uncertain POST without recovery
findings.detail: The pending body is reinspected before marker recovery, and any inspection failure immediately marks the effect done. candidates.suggestion: Add cases that lose the POST response, change or break privacy configuration, reopen the database, and assert that marker recovery occurs before the checkpoint closes without reposting unsafe text.
candidates.failure_scenario: An accepted question POST loses its response and the private-strings file becomes unreadable before reopening; the current tests do not detect that the effect is closed without querying GitHub.

candidates.title: Lifecycle delivery errors can log untrusted or private content
candidates.detail: The delivery catch passes the exception to logFailure, which logs its string after only literal credential redaction. Errors from parsing GitHub recovery responses can include response text, and subprocess errors can include command arguments or output. These diagnostics are not fixed codes and are not checked against configured private strings.
candidates.suggestion: Log a fixed delivery or recovery failure code without exception text, while retaining the checkpoint for retry.
candidates.failure_scenario: A malformed recovery response contains a configured private string in its JSON parse error; the exception is written to the lifecycle log.

candidates.title: Inspection failure closes an uncertain POST before recovery
candidates.detail: The saved body is inspected before the pending-page recovery branch. If inspection now fails, the effect is marked done without looking for the checkpointed author's marker, even though a previous POST may have been accepted. This loses the recorded outcome of an uncertain publication and violates the requirement to recover it before closing the checkpoint.
candidates.suggestion: Recover uncertain POSTs using the independently generated marker and checkpointed identity before deciding whether a new POST may be made; retain the checkpoint if recovery cannot be confirmed.
candidates.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts a question comment but the response is lost. Before the next poll, private-string inspection becomes unavailable; the next reconciliation marks the effect done without querying GitHub or recording the accepted comment.

candidates.title: A superseded unsent set can never be published if it becomes current again
candidates.detail: The request says to “publish each unanswered question” and “publish each set once across restart.” Superseding an unsent effect marks it `done`, but observation refuses to create another effect with the same question IDs. If the run later returns to waiting with the same unanswered questions, there is no publication even though that set was never posted.
candidates.suggestion: Distinguish a superseded, never-published effect from a completed publication and permit a fresh eligible attempt when the same set becomes current again.
candidates.failure_scenario: A question is checkpointed while waiting, the run changes to running before its POST, reconciliation retires the effect, and the run later returns to waiting with the same open question. No question comment is posted.

candidates.title: A failed body inspection closes an uncertain POST without recovery
candidates.detail: The request requires: “Recover an uncertain prior POST by its marker before closing its checkpoint.” An effect with a recovery page is instead marked done if reinspection of its stored body fails, before GitHub is searched. This loses the distinction between an accepted POST and one that never reached GitHub.
candidates.suggestion: Recover an issued POST using its independently generated marker and checkpointed identity before closing the checkpoint; apply publication checks before any subsequent POST.
candidates.failure_scenario: A question POST has an uncertain result, then the private-string configuration becomes unreadable before restart. Reconciliation marks the effect done without checking whether the comment exists, so an unaccepted question is never published.

candidates.title: Lifecycle delivery errors include exception output in diagnostics
candidates.detail: The request says “Diagnostics contain fixed codes, never withheld content or exception output.” The delivery and recovery catch passes the exception to `logFailure`, which logs its string after credential redaction only. GitHub or parsing errors can contain private strings or untrusted response text, and configured private strings are not redacted there.
candidates.suggestion: Log a fixed delivery or recovery failure code without including the exception text.
candidates.failure_scenario: A GitHub recovery response fails JSON parsing and its error message includes response text containing a configured private string; that text is written to the lifecycle log.
